text: RNA-seq was performed on 10 ng of total RNA collected from three independent wells of NPCs from a 24-well plate. NPCs were not treated with EVs or treated for 12 hours with EVs collected by ultracentrifugation from 25 ml of conditioned medium collected from 28 to 37 days in culture COs (control ventral, EPM1 ventral). NPCs were lysed in 1 ml of TRIzol (QIAGEN) per well, and RNA was isolated using the RNA Clean & Concentrator Kit (Zymo Research) including the digestion of remaining genomic DNA according to producer’s guidelines. RNA was further processed according to (75). Briefly, cDNA synthesis was performed with SMART-Seq v4 Ultra Low Input RNA Kit (Clontech catalog no. 634888) according to the manufacturer’s instruction. cDNA was fragmented to an average size of 200 to 500 bp in a Covaris S220 device (5 min; 4°C; PP 175; DF 10; CB 200). Fragmented cDNA was used as input for library preparation with MicroPlex Library Preparation Kit v2 (Diagenode, catalog no. C05010012) and processed according to the manufacturer’s instruction. Libraries were quality controlled by Qubit and Agilent DNA Bioanalyzer analysis. Deep sequencing was performed on a HiSeq 1500 system according to the standard Illumina protocol for 50-bp paired-end reads with v3 sequencing reagents.

text: Paired end reads were aligned to the human genome version GRCh38 using STAR v2.6.1d (76) with default options “--runThreadN 32 --quantMode TranscriptomeSAM GeneCounts -- outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate”. Reads-per-gene counts were imported in R v4.1.0. Expression data from Bulk RNA-seq samples were loaded on Rstudio, focusing on transcript per million values. Data normalization was performed by calculating z-scores across expression values, facilitating comparability between samples, and rows with missing values were excluded to ensure data integrity. Hierarchical clustering was used to uncover patterns in expression profiles. Clusters were visualized on a heatmap, with both rows (genes) and columns (samples) grouped based on similarity. Gene clusters were extracted, and a final list of genes within each cluster was compiled and exported for further analyses. The R packages ComplexHeatmap (77), circlize (78), colorspace (79), GetoptLong (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GetoptLong/), and ggpattern (https://github.com/coolbutuseless/ggpattern) were used for heatmap visualization, clustering, and customization. Dendsort (80) refined hierarchical clustering, while RColorBrewer (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RColorBrewer/) and colorspace (79) managed color gradients. Pheatmap (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pheatmap/) enabled targeted gene display and write.table exported clustered gene lists.

text: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder affecting approximately 65 million people worldwide, spanning all age groups1. For most individuals, the primary treatment involves antiepileptic drugs (AEDs). Despite over 20 available AEDs, one-third of adult individuals and about 20–25% of children with epilepsy experience uncontrolled seizures, defining them as drug-refractory epilepsy (DRE) cases if they fail to achieve seizure freedom after trials of two AEDs2. DRE is notably common in genetic forms of epilepsy, such as Dravet syndrome (DS), a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy that begins in infancy3. Over 80% of DS cases are linked to variants in the SCN1A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1, leading to a haploinsufficiency4. Individuals with DS often suffer from spontaneous seizures, developmental delays, autism spectrum disorder characteristics and an elevated risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy5,6. Recently, the Food and Drug Administration approved three new anticonvulsants, but the inherent drug resistance of DS underscores the urgency to explore alternative therapeutic approaches7. Epilepsy arises from various etiologies beyond genetic mutations, including structural, infectious, metabolic and immune factors8. Neuroinflammation is a unifying feature across these conditions. Elevated proinflammatory cytokines and reactive astrocytes and microglia are frequently observed in drug-resistant epileptogenic brain tissues and animal models, implicating cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), TNF and IL-6 in seizure promotion9. Neuroinflammation in epilepsy can be initiated by the innate immune response to various pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns10–12. DNA is one type of damage-associated molecular pattern linked to epileptogenesis, with mitochondrial DNA damage, defective DNA repair and activation of DNA-sensing Toll-like receptors (TLRs) implicated in seizure development13–15. Cyclic GMP–AMP synthase (cGAS) is a crucial type of DNA sensor for cytosolic DNA and activates stimulator of interferon genes (STING) to induce type I interferon (IFN-I) expression through the TBK1 signaling pathway16,17. Previous work showed that cGAS–STING–IFN-I activation disrupts neuronal activity by inhibiting the MEF2C transcriptional network, a key regulator of neuronal function, where MEF2C haploinsufficiency is known to cause seizures18,19. These findings highlight the role of the cGAS-mediated DNA-sensing pathway in regulating neuronal activity and network function. In this study, we investigated the involvement of the cGAS–STING–IFN-I pathway in DS. We identified a strong IFN-I signature in the microglia of individuals with DRE from single-cell transcriptomic data. Using the Scn1a model of DS, we showed that cGAS reduction and inhibition alleviated seizure phenotypes, reduced inflammation and normalized transcriptional changes in neurons and glia. These results highlight the potential of targeting cGAS as a therapeutic strategy for DS.

text: Microglia, the resident immune cells in the brain, are known to modulate neuronal activity by suppressing neuronal activation, and the loss of the microglia homeostatic receptor P2RY12 can promote seizures20,21. We first analyzed a published single-cell transcriptomic dataset of immune cells from 11 brain tissues (hippocampal and cortical) from 6 individuals (4 children and 2 adults) with DRE, which identified profound proinflammatory signatures22. Fifteen microglia subclusters were identified among all immune cells (Fig. 1a). Expression of IFN-stimulated genes (STAT1, PARP14, RNF213, IFIT3 and others) was enriched in clusters 3 and 4 but was highest in cluster 4 (Fig. 1b). Genes associated with IFNα and IFNγ response, as well as transcription factor (TF) motifs of IFN response factors and IFN-sensitive response elements, were enriched in the marker genes of cluster 4 (Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Table 1). Analysis of another published single-nuclei dataset from individuals with drug-refractory temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and healthy individuals23 identified a shift in microglia clusters comparing TLE to healthy tissue (Fig. 1f). IPA upstream regulator analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on the upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in TLE microglia identified IFN-I signaling to be a top player in the microglial response to epileptic lesions (Fig. 1g,h and Supplementary Table 2). Considering the role of cGAS as a sensor for double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), we hypothesized that repetitive seizures might cause DNA damage in neurons and DNA release from degenerating neurons, which microglia could engulf14,24, leading to cGAS–STING activation. Supporting this hypothesis, immunostaining revealed a significant increase in 53BP1, a DNA damage marker, in cortical neurons from epileptic lesions in individuals with DRE compared to healthy individuals (Fig. 1i,j and Supplementary Table 3). Further, to confirm the activation of the cGAS–STING–IFN pathway in microglia of individuals with epilepsy, we performed immunofluorescence staining of STING and the microglia marker IBA1. Indeed, microglial STING expression was increased in the cortical regions of human epilepsy brains compared to in healthy tissue (Fig. 1k,l), suggesting the involvement of cGAS–STING activation in promoting the microglial IFN response associated with epilepsy in humans.

text: SCN1A haploinsufficiency-induced DS is a well-established form of DRE in need of novel therapeutic targets due to its devastating and lifelong nature. Thus, we were interested in understanding if maladaptive responses in microglia could contribute to disease progression in DS. We first performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of both frontal cortex and hippocampal tissue of 6-month-old conditional Dravet (PvalbCre/+Scn1afl/+) and littermate control (PvalbCre/+Scn1a+/+) mice. In total, 86,698 nuclei passed quality control and were clustered into different cell types based on the expression of specific marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 1). Microglia, with other immune cells, marked by the expression of Cx3cr1, P2ry12 and Csf1r, were further subclustered. Macrophage and T cell groups were removed based on the expression of Mrc1 and Skap1, respectively. Final microglia cells were grouped into five distinct clusters with cluster shifts observed in the hippocampi but not the cortices of the conditional Dravet mice (Fig. 2c). Specifically, a significant loss of microglia cluster 1 and an expansion of microglia cluster 2 were observed (Fig. 2d,e). Pseudobulk analysis of DEGs showed upregulation of genes associated with antigen presentation (H2-K1, H2-D1 and Nlrc5) and IFN response (Stat1 and Sp100; Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 4). Using Single Cell Regulatory Network Inference and Clustering (SCENIC) to predict TF activity in different microglia clusters, oxidative stress and IFN-related TFs such as Nfe2l2, Stat1 and Stat2 were identified to be highly active in cluster 2 (Fig. 2f). Additional analyses using high-dimensional weighted correlation network analysis (hdWGCNA) revealed three modules of highly correlated genes: turquoise, brown and blue. Specifically, the turquoise module was mostly expressed by cluster 2 microglia, and the blue module was mostly expressed by cluster 1 (Fig. 2g). Hallmark analysis of feature genes of each module suggested that the turquoise module was enriched for IFNγ and IFNα response, whereas the blue module was enriched for pathways important for homeostatic microglia function, such as TGFβ signaling (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 4).Fig. 2Neuronal hyperexcitability activates microglial cGAS–STING in vivo.a, Volcano plot of DEGs comparing PvalbCre/+Scn1afl/+ versus PvalbCre/+Scn1a+/+ microglia. (d, l and k).Source data Because EVs can carry dsDNA25–27, we next examined tissue-derived EVs using nano-flow cytometry measurement (NanoFCM). Scn1a+/− mice exhibited a selective reduction in small EVs within the exosome size range of approximately 40 to 100 nm in the hippocampus (Fig. 3e). Small EVs have been implicated in the export of nuclear and mitochondrial dsDNA from cells, and their reduction is therefore consistent with reduced dsDNA clearance and elevated cytosolic accumulation in microglia. To directly assess whether neuronal hyperexcitability could trigger microglial cGAS activation, we turn to an in vitro cell culture system (Fig. 3f). Hyperexcitability of neurons was triggered with 10 mM pentylenetetrazole (PTZ), which disrupts inhibitory synaptic transmission mediated by GABAA receptors. Using a genetically encoded calcium sensor GCaMP8-fast transduced with a lentivral vector (Lenti-hSynapsin-jGCaMP8f), we confirmed spontaneous epileptiform activities after acute perfusion with 10 mM PTZ, as evidenced by synchronized high-amplitude ictal-like events and high-amplitude interictal spikes (Fig. 3g). After 24 h, we collected conditioned medium from PTZ-treated or nontreated primary neurons and applied it to primary microglia with or without cGAS (Fig. 3f). Western blot analysis showed that both Herring testis DNA (HT-DNA), serving as a positive control, and conditioned medium from PTZ-treated neurons increased TBK1 phosphorylation in Cgas+/+ microglia compared to conditioned medium from untreated neurons. Deleting Cgas abolished the increase in phospho-TBK (pTBK) induced by conditioned medium from PTZ-treated neurons (Fig. 3h,i). To exclude the possibility that PTZ directly affects microglial pTBK1, primary microglia were treated with 10 mM PTZ or conditioned medium for 1 h, followed by microglia collection 24 h later (Fig. 3j). Western blot analysis revealed no difference in TBK1 phosphorylation between the control and PTZ-treated groups (Fig. 3k). Together, our findings suggest that DNA released from hyperexcitable neurons can activate cGAS–STING in microglia.

text: Our results so far provide strong evidence of microglial activation of cGAS–STING in the presence of seizure-associated hyperexcitability. We next used the acute PTZ model to assess the contribution of cGAS to seizure susceptibility under conditions of transient network disinhibition. Cgas−/− mice and littermate Cgas+/+ controls were treated with PTZ (50 mg per kg (body weight), intraperitoneal (i.p.)), with a second challenge performed 3 weeks later to assess the effects on seizure sensitization (Fig. 4a). Seizure severity was quantified using the modified Racine scale, recording the maximum score during each session. Male Cgas−/− mice consistently exhibited lower seizure scores than Cgas+/+ littermates in both PTZ treatments (Fig. 4b). Cre recombinase expression was induced through tamoxifen administration at 2 months of age. We assessed the susceptibility to seizures in both groups by administering PTZ (50 mg per kg (body weight), i.p.) at 19–23 months of age. Cgastm1cfl/fl; CX3CR1CreERCre/+ mice showed significantly lower maximum seizure scores than control littermates (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Our analysis of human TLE snRNA-seq data revealed robust activation of IFN-I signaling in microglia (Fig. 1f–h). We therefore tested whether Cgas deletion reduces seizure severity in the kainic acid model, a limbic excitotoxic paradigm that more closely reflects TLE20,21. Cgas−/− and Cgas+/+ mice were administered kainic acid (18 mg per kg (body weight), i.p.) at 2–6 months of age. Consistent with the PTZ model, male Cgas−/− mice displayed significantly reduced seizure scores compared to Cgas+/+ controls, while female Cgas−/− mice showed a similar trend (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). text: Building on the evidence that cGAS promotes PTZ- and kainic acid-induced seizures and the elevation of cGAS–STING signaling in Dravet mice, we next examined if cGAS contributes to disease progression in DS. Scn1atm1Kea mice on a pure 129S6/SvEvTac background (Scn1a+/− 129S6) do not have overt DS phenotypes, but when backcrossed with C57BL/6J (B6) mice and on the N1 strain, they exhibit spontaneous seizures, early lethality and susceptibility to febrile seizures28. We crossed Scn1a+/− 129S6 mice with Cgas+/− B6 mice to generate N1 Scn1a+/+ and Scn1a+/− mice that are Cgas+/+ or Cgas+/− (Extended Data Fig. 2g). We began monitoring survival at postnatal day 20 (P20), assessed hyperthermia-induced seizure susceptibility by raising body temperature at P35–P45 and collected the surviving mice at around P120 (Fig. 4e). Scn1a+/− mice showed increased cGAS protein levels and showed a trend of elevated TBK1 phosphorylation, which was mitigated by Cgas+/− (Fig. 4f–h), confirming that the cGAS–STING pathway is activated in DS mice. Febrile seizure, a hallmark of DS, is commonly induced by infections and accompanied by inflammatory responses29,30. To mimic febrile seizures, N1 mice were challenged by gradually raising body temperature with a heat lamp to a maximum of 42.5 °C or until clonic and tonic-clonic seizures occurred. N1 Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice exhibited a higher temperature threshold for seizures (mean = 42.2 °C) than Scn1a+/− littermates (mean = 41.7 °C; Fig. 4i). However, no significant survival benefit was observed comparing N1 Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice to Scn1a+/− littermates (Extended Data Fig. 2h). To assess whether cGAS reduction could mitigate the worsened epileptic phenotypes of Scn1a+/− mice on the B6 background28,31, we backcrossed Scn1a+/− 129S6 mice with Cgas −/− or Cgas+/+ B6 mice for three generations (Extended Data Fig. 2i) and performed experiments (Fig. 4j). Consistent with the observation in N1 Scn1a+/− mice, we observed no survival benefit for N3 Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice compared to Scn1a+/− littermates (Extended Data Fig. 2j). We next implanted 32-channel tetrodes into N3 DS brains at P60 and conducted 24-h local field potential (LFP) recordings with video monitoring to capture spontaneous epileptiform activity across brain regions, including the primary visual cortex, primary somatosensory cortex, CA1, dentate gyrus and thalamus (Fig. 4k). An automated algorithm was used to quantify epileptic spikes and identify epileptiform events with continuous spikes lasting over 10 s (Fig. 4l). Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice exhibited fewer epileptiform events than Scn1a+/− littermates, especially in the hippocampi, suggesting reduced spontaneous spiking (Fig. 4m,n). N3 Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice showed similar seizure thresholds as Scn1a+/− mice after hyperthermia challenge (Fig. 4o) and had reduced poststimulation mortality rates, where only 28.6% died up to P120 compared to 71.4% of Scn1a+/− littermates (Fig. 4p). Together, genetic cGAS reduction ameliorates epileptic phenotypes in DS mice across genetic backgrounds and disease severities.

text: To test the translational relevance of cGAS targeting in DS, we next evaluated whether pharmacological inhibition of cGAS mitigates DS-associated phenotypes in a cohort of N1 Scn1a+/+ and Scn1a+/− mice by crossing Scn1a+/− 129S6 mice with wild-type B6 mice. Starting at P15, the mice received daily i.p. injections of 5 mg per kg (body weight) of the brain-penetrant cGAS inhibitor (cGASi) TDI-6570 (ref. 19) or control until P21, followed by a daily single dose of almond butter containing 5 mg per kg (body weight) cGASi or control. At P35, the mice were challenged with hyperthermia-induced seizures and collected at P42 (Fig. 5a).Fig. 5Pharmacological cGAS inhibition ameliorates DS-associated seizure phenotypes.a, Schematic showing the treatment and experiments performed in N1 mice along the timeline. b,c, Western blot image (b) and quantification of cGAS protein levels normalized to GAPDH in hippocampal lysates of N1 Scn1a+/+ control (n = 7), Scn1a+/− cGASi (n = 8, one outlier was removed with the robust regression and outlier removal (ROUT) test, Q = 1% for quantification) and Scn1a+/− control (n = 7) mice (c). Data in care presented as mean values ± s.e.m. and were analyzed by ordinary one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test. d, Survival of Scn1a+/− control (n = 32) and Scn1a+/− cGASi (n = 33) mice monitored until collection. Data were analyzed by log-rank Mantel–Cox test. e, Seizure-free ratio and temperature of Scn1a+/+ control (n = 4), Scn1a+/+ cGASi (n = 4), Scn1a+/− control (n = 12) and Scn1a+/− cGASi (n = 15) mice during hyperthermia-induced seizures. Data were analyzed by log-rank Mantel–Cox test comparing Scn1a+/− control and Scn1a+/− cGASi mice.Source data Scn1a+/− control mice showed elevated cGAS expression compared to Scn1a+/+ controls, which was prevented by cGASi treatment, indicating target engagement (Fig. 5b,c). cGASi treatment also reduced the expression of the IFN-I-induced chemokine CCL5 in Scn1a+/− mice (Extended Data Fig. 3d). Notably, cGASi markedly reduced early mortality in Scn1a+/− mice (Fig. 5d) and increased the mean hyperthermia-induced seizure threshold from 40.9 °C to 41.7 °C without affecting baseline body temperature (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 3e). None of the Scn1a+/+ mice treated with control or cGASi experienced premature death or hyperthermia-induced seizures even at 42.5 °C, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of cGAS inhibition for DS.

text: We next interrogated cell-type-specific transcriptomic changes induced by cGAS reduction in Scn1a+/− mice. We focused on the hippocampus due to the strong inflammatory signatures induced by DS (Fig. 1i,j). snRNA-seq was performed in 4- to 5-month-old N3 Scn1a+/+Cgas+/−, Scn1a+/+, Scn1a+/− and Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice (n = 4 per genotype). In total, 137,028 nuclei were analyzed and grouped into different cell types after passing stringent quality control (QC; Extended Data Fig. 4). Among the six subclusters from 5,732 microglia nuclei, cluster 6 was mostly present in Scn1a+/− mice, whereas cluster 3 was almost exclusively present in Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice (Fig. 6a). Pseudobulk DEG analysis identified an upregulation of disease-associated astrocyte (DAA) markers33, such as Gfap, Cd9, Id3 and Aqp4, in PvalbCre/+Scn1afl/+ astrocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7c and Supplementary Table 4). Correlation analysis of cluster 4 marker genes and DAA marker genes showed a significant positive correlation with a Pearson’s r of 0.71, suggesting the expansion of DAAs in the conditional Dravet mouse model (Extended Data Fig. 7d and Supplementary Table 4). Using western blotting, we confirmed an increase in the expression of GFAP in the hippocampus of conditional Dravet mice (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Further analysis of the N3 Scn1a+/− snRNA-seq dataset showed that among the eight astrocyte clusters, cluster 4 was expanded in Scn1a+/− mice and was rescued by Cgas+/− (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). Confirming our observation in the conditional dataset, cluster 4 showed high expression of DAA marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Pseudobulk analysis showed that Cgas+/− rescued 358 of 549 Scn1a+/− induced astrocyte DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Table 5). A negative correlation of r = −0.88 between overlapping DEGs was observed (Extended Data Fig. 8e). The elevated expression of DAA marker genes (Gfap, Aqp4, Cd9, Clu, Apoe and so on) in Scn1a+/− mice was abolished by Cgas reduction (Extended Data Fig. 8f). GO analysis identified gliogenesis, glial cell differentiation and regulation of protein catabolic process to be the top pathways upregulated by Scn1a+/− and modified by Cgas+/− (Extended Data Fig. 8g). APOE+ lipid-accumulated reactive astrocytes have been reported to promote disease progression in epilepsy23. Notably, Apoe was a top DEG rescued by cGAS reduction. Indeed, immunostaining of APOE and GFAP revealed that both the immunointensity of GFAP and the colocalization between APOE and GFAP were increased in the CA1 region of the hippocampus of Scn1a+/− mice and reduced by Cgas+/− (Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Together, cGAS reduction markedly ameliorated the inflammatory signature in microglia and astrocytes of DS mice.

text: Our study identifies IFN-I signaling as a key inflammatory pathway contributing to disease progression in DS. Transcriptomic analysis of human DRE tissue and DS mouse models revealed elevated IFN-I signatures in microglia, highlighting sustained neuroinflammation as a hallmark of pharmacoresistance. This aligns with observations of persistent inflammation in individuals with prolonged seizures and provides molecular insights into resistance to AEDs. Notably, IFN-I signaling mediates a unique inflammatory response in epilepsy, distinct from other DAM signatures, underscoring its specific role in epileptogenesis. Our findings further implicate cGAS, a cytosolic DNA sensor, as a critical upstream regulator of IFN-I signaling in epilepsy. Activation of the cGAS–STING pathway was elevated in both human DRE tissue and DS mouse models, likely driven by neuronal DNA damage induced by neuronal activity and exacerbated under pathological conditions39,40. Supporting this, our in vitro studies showed that conditioned medium from hyperactive neurons activated the cGAS pathway in microglia, linking neuronal hyperactivity to microglial IFN-I signaling. Because the human specimens were obtained from surgical pathology and autopsy archives, the control and epilepsy groups were not age matched, and the precise cortical regions available for analysis varied across individuals. Future studies using larger age- and region-matched human cohorts will be essential to rigorously quantify alterations in the cGAS–STING pathway in drug-resistant epilepsy. Clinical evidence reinforces this connection: individuals with type I interferonopathies like Aicardi–Goutières syndrome often develop epilepsy41, and IFN-I therapy for chronic viral hepatitis can induce seizures that resolve following cessation of treatment42–44. Activation of IFN signaling is also identified in DRE associated with tuberous sclerosis complex45. IFN-I signaling is triggered by pattern recognition receptors responding to damage-associated molecular patterns and pathogen-associated molecular patterns, with nucleic acid-sensing pattern recognition receptors such as TLR3 and TLR9 previously implicated in seizure models10,14. Our findings expand on this by positioning cGAS as a central mediator of neuroinflammation and a potential therapeutic target in epilepsy. We found that genetic deletion of Cgas lowered the severity of and increased latency to seizures in pharmacologically induced PTZ and kainic acid models and reduced hyperthermia-induced seizure susceptibility and spontaneous epileptiform activity in two DS mouse lines with different genetic backgrounds. Our findings indicate that recurrent seizures drive sustained activation of the cGAS–STING pathway, which in turn contributes to the maintenance of the epileptic state in a chronic mouse model. In addition, aberrant activation of cGAS–STING exacerbates seizure severity in acute PTZ- and kainic acid-induced models. Conversely, inhibition of cGAS–STING signaling mitigates seizure severity in these acute models, collectively supporting a detrimental role for this pathway in both acute seizure generation and chronic epileptogenesis. Although microglia have been reported to exert protective functions in certain acute seizure paradigms20,46–49, our findings suggest that activation of the cGAS–STING pathway represents a distinct innate immune program that promotes proinflammatory signaling and worsens seizure severity. Seizure-associated cellular stress may lead to cytosolic DNA accumulation, triggering cGAS–STING activation and shifting microglia toward a neuroinflammatory state that exacerbates network hyperexcitability. Seizure-associated cellular stress may lead to cytosolic DNA accumulation, triggering cGAS–STING activation and shifting microglia toward a neuroinflammatory state that exacerbates network hyperexcitability. PTZ and acute kainic acid paradigms provide complementary seizure-challenge systems, which allowed us to test whether cGAS signaling modulates acute seizure susceptibility outside the Scn1a background. Together, our results support a seizure-amplifying role for cGAS with disease-specific relevance established primarily in the DS model. cGAS reduction also diminished IFN-I signaling and proinflammatory pathways, such as antigen presentation, complement activation and TLR signaling, in microglia, as well as DAA signatures. Astrocytes, which interact with microglia and neurons, promote epileptogenesis through neuroinflammation, lipid metabolism and gliotransmission23,50,51. We observed that cGAS reduction decreased APOE accumulation in DS astrocytes, aligning with reports that APOE-high reactive astrocytes exacerbate neuronal hyperactivity and epilepsy progression23. Although widely used for screening antiepileptic drugs, induced seizure models assess seizure susceptibility and severity under provoked conditions and do not fully recapitulate endogenous spontaneous seizure activity. These results demonstrate concordant effects of genetic and pharmacological perturbations within the Scn1a model of DS, supporting a shared mechanistic pathway in this genetic epilepsy model. Therefore, to better reflect the etiological and phenotypic diversity of complex human epilepsies, future studies using complementary models will be necessary to determine whether this cGAS reduction effect extends to other seizure types. In neurons, cGAS reduction restored transcriptomic changes related to synaptic transmission, ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors but did not affect Scn1a expression nor Nav1.1 protein levels, suggesting a mechanism not specific to DS. Neuronal DNA damage, mitochondrial DNA defects and DNA release (common in epilepsy13–15) likely activate cGAS. Elevated 53BP1 levels in neurons from human DRE tissue confirmed increased DNA damage. In vitro, conditioned medium from PTZ-treated neurons increased TBK1 phosphorylation in Cgas+/+ but not Cgas−/− microglia, linking neuronal DNA release to cGAS activation. By contrast, direct PTZ exposure failed to induce TBK1 phosphorylation in primary microglia, arguing against a cell-autonomous effect of PTZ on cGAS–STING activation. Consistent with this, our in vivo analyses in DS mice demonstrate increased microglial cytosolic dsDNA and EV-associated DNA following seizure activity, providing direct evidence that hyperactive neurons indirectly drive microglial cGAS–STING activation in vivo. This aligns with previous studies showing that self-DNA from degenerating neurons activates DNA sensors like TLR9 during seizures14. Our findings support that targeting the cGAS–STING–IFN-I pathway offers promise for treating DS. The brain-permeable cGASi TDI-6570 reduced early mortality and hyperthermia-induced seizure susceptibility and corrected many transcriptomic changes in DS mice. Microglial inflammatory signatures varied between young (N1) and older (N3) DS mouse lines, reflecting differences in disease stage and genetic background. Nonetheless, the consistent elevation of cGAS in DS models highlights its role in acute and chronic epilepsy. TDI-6570 also increased Mef2c expression, a TF critical for synapse regulation and neuronal development37,54,55, and rescued the expression of its target genes. Given that MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome includes epilepsy as a common symptom18 and neuronal MEF2C is negatively regulated by STING–IFN-I activation19, rescue of the MEF2C transcriptional network likely contributes to the protective effects of cGAS inhibition. Pharmacological inhibition of cGAS was notably more effective than genetic reduction in improving survival and hyperthermia-induced seizure thresholds. This difference may stem from variations in timing, level and mode of inhibition. Genetic reduction occurs embryonically, whereas cGASi is administered postnatally. IFN-I-responsive microglia are crucial in maintaining excitatory/inhibitory balance in neurodevelopment24, and this function may be disrupted by genetic reduction of Cgas. Further, compensatory changes may arise with genetic manipulation but not with inhibitor treatment. Additionally, Cgas+/− reduces both enzymatic and nonenzymatic functions of cGAS, whereas cGASi specifically targets enzymatic activity. The role of cGAS’s nonenzymatic functions remains less understood. The exact cell type(s) in which cGAS activity drives disease progression in DS remains an important unanswered question. Microglia express the highest levels of cGAS and STING and play a central role in DNA sensing and neuroimmune signaling19. Microglia cGAS–STING activation triggers IFN-I production, which disseminates antiviral responses to other CNS cell types. For instance, during herpes simplex virus type 1 infection, microglial cGAS–STING activation induces IFN-I production, which activates STING-dependent antiviral programs in neurons and primes TLR3–IFN-I pathways in astrocytes56. Similarly, STING-mediated inflammatory responses have been shown to propagate in CNS and peripheral neurons57–59. Our snRNA-seq data support these findings, showing that Tlr3 is upregulated in Scn1a+/− astrocytes, a change reversed by Cgas+/−. Furthermore, a microglial-specific Cre-induced cGAS activation model demonstrated heightened IFN-I responses in both microglia and astrocytes, which was sufficient to cause cognitive impairments52. We further observed that PTZ-induced seizure activity was reduced in mice with microglia-specific Cgas deletion, supporting a role for microglia cGAS–STING signaling in seizure generation. In DS, it is conceivable that microglial cGAS activation by engulfed neuronal DNA drives IFN-I production, amplifying inflammatory responses in neurons and astrocytes. This exacerbates neuronal hyperexcitability, leading to neuronal damage and creating a feed-forward cycle of inflammation and sustained hyperexcitability. Suppressing cGAS activation caused by dsDNA released from hyperexcitable neurons could disrupt this vicious cycle, potentially halting DS progression. Future studies using conditional knockout models and systematically investigating the cell-type-specific roles of cGAS in the CNS are essential to fully elucidate its contributions to epilepsy. These efforts could advance our understanding of cGAS as a therapeutic target and clarify its broader role in neuroinflammatory and neurological diseases.

text: Mice were housed no more than five per cage, given ad libitum access to food and water and maintained in a pathogen-free barrier facility at 21–23 °C with 30–70% humidity on a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle. All mouse protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Weill Cornell Medicine. For the conditional DS snRNA-seq experiments, frozen whole brains from PvalbCre/+Scn1a+/+ (n = 3) and PvalbCre/+Scn1afl/+ (n = 3) mice on the B6 background were obtained from J. Palop (University of California, San Francisco). For the pharmacological model of seizures, Cgas−/− mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 026554) were crossed with B6 mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 000664) to generate F1 Cgas+/− mice. F1 Cgas+/− mice were then crossed again to generate littermate Cgas+/+, Cgas+/− and Cgas −/− mice. For targeting microglia-specific Cgas deletion in adult mice, Cx3cr1CreER mice60 (The Jackson Laboratory, 020940) were crossed with floxed cGastm1c mice61 (MMRRC, 065342-UCD) to generate Cgastm1c fl/fl; CX3CR1CreER Cre/+ and littermate Cgastm1c fl/fl; CX3CR1CreER +/+ control mice. Both groups received tamoxifen injection (20 mg per kg (body weight), i.p.) once daily for 5 consecutive days at 2 months of age. For the DS model, female Cgas+/− mice were crossed with male 129S-Scn1atm1Kea/Mmjax mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 037107) to generate N1 Scn1a+/+, Scn1a+/−, Scn1a+/+Cgas+/− and Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice. Mice of both sexes were included for mortality, hyperthermia-induced seizure, histological and biochemical analyses. A separate breeding of female Cgas−/− mice with male 129S-Scn1atm1Kea/Mmjax mice was used to generate N1 Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice, which were crossed again with Cgas−/− mice to generate N2 Scn1a+/−, Cgas+/− and Scn1a+/−Cgas−/− mice. Male N2 Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice were crossed with female B6 mice to generate N3 Scn1a+/+, Scn1a+/−, Scn1a+/+Cgas+/− and Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− mice. Mice of both sexes were included in the analysis. Mice that received electrode implantation surgeries were used for LFP recording and subsequent hyperthermia-induced seizure induction and were excluded from mortality, transcriptomic, histologic and biochemical analysis. For cGASi treatment, male 129S-Scn1atm1Kea/Mmjax mice were crossed with female B6 mice to generate N1 Scn1a+/+ and Scn1a+/− mice. Mice of both sexes were included for mortality, hyperthermia-induced seizure, transcriptomic, histological and biochemical analyses.

text: The procedures used to isolate nuclei from frozen mouse brains were adapted from a previous study, with modifications62,63. All procedures were performed on ice or at 4 °C. In brief, postmortem brain tissue was placed in 1,500 µl of Sigma nuclei PURE lysis buffer (Sigma, NUC201-1KT) and homogenized with a Dounce tissue grinder (Sigma, D8938-1SET) with 20 strokes with pestle A and 15 strokes with pestle B. The homogenized tissue was filtered through a 35-µm cell strainer, centrifuged at 600g for 5 min at 4 °C and washed three times with 1 ml of PBS containing 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA), 20 mM DTT and 0.2 U µl−1 recombinant RNase inhibitor. Nuclei were then centrifuged at 600g for 5 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 800 µl of PBS containing 0.04% BSA and 1× DAPI, followed by fluorescence-activated cell sorting to remove cell debris. The sorted suspension of DAPI-stained nuclei was counted and diluted to a concentration of 1,000 nuclei per µl in PBS containing 0.04% BSA.

text: In 6-month-old conditional Dravet mice, we sequenced and integrated samples from the frontal cortical and hippocampal tissue of PvalbCre/+Scn1a+/+ (n = 3) and PvalbCre/+Scn1afl/+ (n = 3) mice. In the 4- to 5-month-old N3 Dravet cohort, we sequenced and integrated samples from the hippocampi of Scn1a+/+ (n = 4), Scn1a+/− (n = 4), Scn1a+/+Cgas+/− (n = 4) and Scn1a+/−Cgas+/− (n = 4) mice. In the 1.5-month-old N1 Dravet cGASi treatment cohort, we sequenced and integrated samples from the hippocampi of Scn1a+/+ control (n = 4), Scn1a+/− control (n = 4), Scn1a+/+ cGASi (n = 4) and Scn1a+/− cGASi (n = 4) mice. Gene counts were obtained by aligning reads to the mm10 genome with Cell Ranger software (v6.1.2; 10x Genomics). To account for unspliced nuclear transcripts, reads mapping to pre-mRNA were counted. Cell Ranger 6.1.2 default parameters were used to call cell barcodes. We further removed genes expressed in no more than three cells, cells with unique gene counts over 5,000 or less than 300, cells with unique molecular identifier counts over 15,000 and cells with a high fraction of mitochondrial reads (>1% or >5% for the N3 cohort). Potential doublet cells were predicted using DoubletFinder64 for each sample separately, with high-confidence doublets removed. Normalization and clustering were performed with the Seurat package v5.0.0. In brief, counts for all nuclei were scaled by the total library size multiplied by a scale factor (10,000) and transformed to log space. A set of 2,000 highly variable genes was identified with SCTransform from the SCTransform R package in variable stabilization mode. This returned a corrected unique molecular identifier count matrix, a log-transformed data matrix and Pearson residuals from the regularized negative binomial regression model. Principal-component analysis was performed on all genes, and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding was run on the top 15 principal components. Major cell types in the brain were identified by the expression of known cell identity markers65–67 for excitatory neurons (Slc17a7 and Nrgn), inhibitory neurons (Gad1 and Gad2), immune cells (Cx3cr1, P2ry12 and Csf1r), oligodendrocytes (Plp1, Mbp and Mobp), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (Vcan and Pdgfra), astrocytes (Clu, Plpp3 and Pla2g7), vascular cells (Bmp6, Adam12and Cped1) and choroid plexus epithelial cells (Clic6 and Ttr). Cell clusters were identified with the Seurat functions FindNeighbors and FindClusters. In this analysis, the neighborhood size parameter pK was estimated using the mean variance-normalized bimodality coefficient (BCmvn) approach, with 15 principal components used and pN set as 0.25 by default. For each cluster, we assigned a cell-type label using statistical enrichment for sets of marker genes and manual evaluation of gene expression for small sets of known marker genes66–69. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using the FindMarkers function and MAST70. To identify GO and pathways enriched in the DEGs, DEGs were analyzed using the clusterProfiler package in R (v4.10.1) or the MSigDB gene annotation database71,72. To identify gene activation networks and upstream regulators, DEGs were analyzed using IPA (Qiagen). To control for multiple testing, we used the Benjamini–Hochberg approach to constrain the false discovery rate.

text: Hemibrains from transcardially perfused mice were placed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 28 h, followed by 30% sucrose in PBS for 48 h at 4 °C. Sections were cut coronally at 40 µm using a freezing microtome (Leica) to produce eight to ten free-floating series per mouse and placed in cryoprotective medium at −20 °C until use. All washing steps were 5 min long and were repeated three times. Sections were washed in 1× Tris-buffered saline with Tween-20 (TBST), permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in TBST for 10 min and washed. Sections were then placed in an antigen-retrieval solution (Antigen Decloaker, Biocare Medical, CB910M) and placed in a 90 °C incubator for 15 min, when applicable. Sections were washed and then blocked in 5% normal donkey serum (Vector, BMK-2202) in TBST for 2 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies were diluted in 5% normal donkey serum in TBST and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The following day, sections were washed thoroughly and incubated in appropriate secondary antibodies (1:500; Invitrogen) for 1 h. Sections were washed, mounted on slides using Vectashield antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, H-1200; Sigma, D9542) and imaged. Paraffin-embedded human brain sections (5 µm) mounted on slides were incubated in an oven at 60 °C for 10 min with aluminum foil underneath to catch melted paraffin. Slides were deparaffinized with xylene for 5 min three times, followed by 100% ethanol for 2 min twice and 95% ethanol for 2–5 min, and washed three times in distilled water for 2 min each. Slides were then placed in an antigen-retrieval solution made of 1× citrate buffer, pH 6.0 (Electron Microscopy Sciences, 64142-08) in distilled water and placed in a pressure cooker (Cuisinart) at high pressure for 15 min. Slides were washed three times (2 min each) with cool distilled water, followed by three washes (2 min each) with 1× PBS. Slides were then blocked with 5% donkey serum in 1× PBS for 1 h and incubated in primary antibodies diluted in 1% donkey serum in 1× PBS overnight in a humidified slide chamber. The following day, slides were washed in 1× PBS for 2 min three times and incubated with secondary antibodies diluted in 1% donkey serum in 1× PBS for 1 h in a humidified slide chamber. Slides were then washed in 1× PBS for 2 min three times and coverslipped with Vectashield mounting medium with DAPI. For IBA1/STING, GFAP/APOE and PDE10A/NeuN staining, the CA1 or CA3 region of the hippocampus was imaged with a 1-μm interval z-stack over a total distance of 8 μm per slice. For MEF2C staining, the CA1 region was imaged with 4 × 1 tiles and a 1-μm interval z-stack over a total distance of 10 μm per slice. Final images were processed with maximum intensity projection. For IBA1 staining, cells located near the tissue section edge were excluded from quantitative analyses to avoid potential sectioning artifacts that could influence measurements of microglial process length and branching complexity. For all human brain imaging, four to five images over different areas per section were acquired with a Keyence BZ-X700 microscope using a ×20 objective. Quantification was performed with ImageJ software V2.1.40LL (NIH). All images of dsDNA staining were acquired using a Nikon A1 laser confocal microscope. The large images containing the hippocampus were obtained by tile scanning under ×20 magnification. Single z-stack areas of the hippocampal CA1 were imaged under ×100 magnification. Six windows inside the CA1 area were randomly selected for z-stack imaging under identical conditions. Images were processed and analyzed in Fiji-ImageJ. For dsDNA puncta in microglia cytoplasm, z-stack images of ten layers with a 1-μm z-step containing a single microglia cell were projected by maximum intensity. dsDNA puncta inside the microglia cell body and main branches but outside the nucleus were quantified as ‘cytosolic dsDNA puncta number’ in single microglia.

text: For mouse brain samples, half hippocampi were sonicated on ice in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89901) supplemented with Halt phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 78420) and cOmplete protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, 11697498001). After sonication, brain lysates were centrifuged at 20,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. Supernatants were collected, and protein concentration was measured by BCA (Pierce, 23225). Samples were boiled at 95 °C for 5 min or 55 °C for 30 min (for Nav1.1 only). Fifty micrograms of protein was loaded onto NuPage Bis-Tris gels (Thermo Fisher) and run in SDS running buffer at 80 V for 30 min and 130 V for ~1 h. Gels were transferred to PVDF membranes (Bio-Rad) for 1.5 h at 0.36 A in a cold room. Membranes were blocked for 1 h in 5% milk in TBST. Primary antibodies were diluted in 1% milk in TBST and incubated at 4 °C overnight. The following day, membranes were washed three times for 5 min each in TBST and incubated with secondary antibodies in 1% milk in TBST for 1 h at room temperature. Membranes were washed three times, treated with ECL (Bio-Rad) for 60 s and developed using a Bio-Rad imager. Blots were scanned at 300 d.p.i. and quantified using Image Lab. Primary antibodies used for western blotting were anti-cGAS (clone D3O8O, Cell Signaling Technology, 31659; 1:500), anti-STING (clone D1V5L, Cell Signaling Technology, 50494; 1:1,000), anti-TBK1 (clone D1B4, Cell Signaling Technology, 3504; 1:1,000), anti-pTBK1 (clone D52C2, Cell Signaling Technology, 5483; 1:500), anti-GAPDH (GeneTex, GTX100118; 1:10,000), anti-Nav1.1 (clone K74/71, NeuroMab; 1:500), anti-GFAP (Abcam, ab7260; 1:1,000) and anti-β-actin (Millipore Sigma, A3854; 1:10,000). Secondary antibodies used for western blotting were Peroxidase-AffiniPure Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch Labs, 111-035-144; 1:10,000) or Peroxidase-AffiniPure Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch Labs, 115-035-146; 1:10,000).

text: PTZ powder (Sigma-Aldrich, P6500) and kainic acid monohydrate (Tocris, 7065) were dissolved in 0.9% sodium chloride injection, USP (Hospira) to final concentrations of 5 mg ml−1 (PTZ) and 2.5 mg ml−1 (kainic acid), respectively. Mice were placed in a circular open-field chamber (8228, Pinnacle Technology) and video recorded with a FLIR camera (Teledyne FLIR) for baseline activity for 10 min. Mice were then injected i.p. with the PTZ solution at 50 mg per kg (body weight) or kainic acid solution at 18 mg per kg (body weight) and observed simultaneously by two investigators under video for 30 min (PTZ) or 90 min (kainic acid) to assess seizure activity. Seizures were scored based on a modified Racine scale77, where 0 indicates no seizure response; 1 indicates sudden behavioral arrest or immobility; 2 indicates tail twitching, myoclonic jerks or facial automations; 3 indicates head nodding and neck jerks; 4 indicates clonic seizures while the animal falls into a sitting position; 5 indicates tonic-clonic seizures with the animal falling on its side; 6 indicates wild-jumping; 7 indicates tonic extension of limbs; and 8 indicates death. Maximum Racine score and latency to seizure were analyzed.

text: Hyperthermia-induced seizure was performed based on a previously published protocol with modifications78. Mice were placed in an open-field chamber with a RET-4 probe (Phisitemp) inserted in the rectum to continuously measure rectal temperature. Mice were allowed to habituate and were recorded at baseline for 10 min. The mice were then heated with an infrared heat lamp (HL-1, Phisitemp) at a constant distance from the chamber to gradually increase the body temperature using a TCAT-2DF thermo controller (Phisitemp). For every 0.5 °C the body temperature was increased, the heat lamp was turned off for 30 s. The cycle repeated until clonic or tonic-clonic seizure was recognized by LFP recording (in N3 mice) and video analyses (in both N1 and N3 mice) or the body temperature reached 42.5 °C. The heating lamp was then switched off, and an ice block was placed in the chamber to allow recovery. Mice were monitored until body temperature returned to the baseline or until death occurred. For tissue EV and dsDNA immunofluorescence analysis, brains were collected 3 h following hyperthermia-induced seizures (Fig. 3a).

text: Mice were initially anesthetized with 3.5% isoflurane, mounted on a stereotaxic frame and maintained under ~1.2% isoflurane. Body temperature was maintained at 37 °C with a regulated heating blanket (World Precision Instruments). A craniotomy was drilled for electrode insertion. Animals were implanted with a custom 32-channel 3D electrode array (Kedou Brain-Computer Technology) that contains eight tetrodes over the somatosensory cortex, CA1 of the hippocampus, dentate gyrus, primary visual cortex and thalamus (somatosensory cortex: antero–posterior (AP) –1.8 mm, mediolateral (ML) 2.1 and 2.3 mm, dorsoventral (DV) 1.0 mm; CA1: AP –1.8 mm, ML 1.5 mm, DV 1.5 mm; dentate gyrus: AP –3.0 mm, ML 1.8 mm, DV 2.2 mm; primary visual cortex: AP –3.0 mm, ML 2.1 and 2.3 mm, DV 0.8 mm; thalamus: AP –1.8 mm, ML 1.0 and 1.2 mm, DV 3.8 mm; Fig. 2k). Stainless steel screws were implanted into the skull to provide electrical ground and mechanical stability for drives, and the whole construct was bonded to the skull using C&B-Metabond luting cement (Parkell). Two weeks after implantation, animals were put in a circular open-field chamber (8228, Pinnacle Technology) to record spontaneous activity continuously for 24 h with food and water supply. Electrophysiological data were acquired using an Intan RHD headstage (Intan Technologies), and the Open Ephys acquisition board and software sampled at 1 kHz (ref. 79). Locomotion was simultaneously acquired with a FLIR camera (Teledyne FLIR) and open-source Bonsia software80 recording at 50 Hz.

text: Detection and quantification of epileptic activities were performed using a custom script written in MATLAB based on an automated algorithm81 (https://github.com/Jackson-Kyle-CCOM/Automated-EEG-Algorithm). LFP recording signals were first band-pass filtered between 5 and 90 Hz. The baseline activity value was autonomously calculated based on a period of 10 min of low activity. The lower threshold value was defined as 5 standard deviations from baseline value. An upper threshold value of 6,000 μV was used to remove electroencephalogram artifacts due to noise and animal behavior. LFP spikes for whole recording were then determined following those key parameters. The interspike interval was set at 100 ms, and the maximum peak width was set to 200 ms to identify interictal spike, polyspikes and other abnormal spiking patterns or LFP artifacts. Seizure-like ictal82,83 epileptiform was defined to contain sequential peaks that lasted for at least 10 s with an interspike interval of less than 5 s.

text: Primary neurons were isolated from mouse embryos at embryonic day 16. Briefly, the brains were isolated and minced. Tissues were dissociated in 0.25% Trypsin-EDTA (Gibco, A5200-056) for 15 min at 37 °C. For every four brains, 300 μl of DNase I (Millipore Sigma, 260913) was added to the tissue, and the supernatant was discarded. Next, the tissue was washed twice with 2.7 ml of HBSS (Gibco, 14025) and incubated for 5 min at room temperature. The supernatant was discarded. Ten milliliters of MEM (Gibco, 11095-080) with 10% FBS (Gibco, 26140-079) was then added, and moderate pipetting was performed to dissociate the cells. Primary neuron cells were then counted and seeded on six-well plates with FBS-MEM, 1× B27 plus (Lifetechnology, A35828-01) and 1× N2 (Lifetechnology, 17502-048). Cells were maintained by half changing the medium with 10 μM uridine and 5-FDU every 3–4 days.

text: Brains were dissected from mouse pups at P1–P3. The meninges were removed, and the cortical tissue was finely chopped with a razor blade and digested in 2.5% trypsin (Gibco, 15090-45) with DNase I (Millipore Sigma, 260913) at 37 °C for 22 min. The reaction was stopped with DMEM (Corning, 10-017-CV) supplemented with 20% heat-inactivated FBS (Gibco, 26140-079). In total, 200 μl of DNase was added, followed by 5 ml of 20% FBS/DMEM, and tissue was triturated and spun at 200g for 15 min. The pellet was resuspended in DMEM supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated FBS (Gibco, 26140-079) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15070063), plated in T75 flasks precoated with 5 μg ml−1 poly-D-lysine (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A389401) and rinsed with water. Mixed glial cultures were maintained in growth medium (DMEM with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin) at 37 °C and 5% CO2. On day 4, the medium was collected and spun down at 200g for 10 min to remove the debris. The supernatant was collected back to the flasks with fresh medium. On day 7, the medium was supplemented with 5 ng ml−1 recombinant mouse granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (R&D Systems, 415-ML-020-CF) to promote microglial proliferation. When flasks were ready for collection on days 10–13, to isolate microglia, the flasks were shaken at 400 rpm for 2 h, the medium was spun down at 200g for 15 min, and cells were plated for experiments on poly-D-lysine-coated plates.

text: For neuronal calcium imaging experiments, neurons were transduced with hSyn-jGCaMP8f lentivirus84,85 at 7 days in vitro. At 14 days in vitro, primary neuron coverslips were placed into a glass-bottom chamber at 33 °C containing 10 mM PTZ calcium imaging buffer (20 mM HEPES, 119 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 30 mM glucose, 2 mM CaCl2, 10 mM PTZ, pH 7.2–7.4). Fluorescence time-lapse images were collected on a Nikon FN1 microscope using a ×60/1.0-NA objective (CFI APO 60XW NIR, Nikon) and a C-FL GFP filter cube. An X-CITE LED illuminator (Nikon) was used for excitation. Images were collected using an ORCA-Fusion CMOS camera (Hamamatsu) with 4 × 4 binning (576 × 576 pixel resolution, 16-bit grayscale depth, 0.43 m per pixel) and NIS-Elements AR software (Nikon). Exposure time was set to 20 ms. For spontaneous activity, images were acquired at 30 Hz for 4 min. We selected regions of interest covering all identifiable cell bodies using a semiautomated algorithm in NIS-Elements AR (Nikon). Further quantifications were performed using custom-written MATLAB (Mathworks) scripts. The fluorescence time course (ΔF / F0) of each image frame was calculated as (Ft – F0) / F0, where F0 was an average of all frames acquired during the first 0.5-s window as a baseline and Ft is the fluorescence intensity at a given time. Photobleaching was corrected by fitting exponentially weighted moving averages86.

text: All data are reported as mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analyses were performed using R v4.3.3 and GraphPad Prism v.10.2.0. For data analysis using GraphPad, significant outliers were removed using Prism’s outlier calculator with ROUT test (Q = 0.1%) and Grubb’s test (α = 0.05). Shapiro–Wilk and Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests were performed to determine the normality of all data. Normally distributed data were analyzed using an ANOVA or t-test. Non-normal data were analyzed using a Kruskal–Wallis or Mann–Whitney test. Morality and hyperthermia-induced seizure data were analyzed with a log-rank Mantel–Cox test. Gene set overlap analysis was performed with a Fisher’s exact test using the GeneOverlap package in R88. All statistical details can be found in the figures and figure legends. A subset of mice from the immunohistochemistry cohort was randomly selected for snRNA-seq studies. Animals were blinded from genotypes when performing image analysis and quantification for all immunohistochemistry experiments. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size, but our sample sizes are similar to those reported in a previous publication19. Data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested.

text: Epilepsy affects more than 50 million people worldwide, with the greatest burden occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where most affected individuals reside and treatment gaps frequently exceed 60% . Treatment gap has been defined as the proportion of individuals with active epilepsy who have not accessed biomedical treatment services for ≥ 30 consecutive days within the preceding 90 days . Large number of people with epilepsy live in LMICs, the majority of whom do not receive appropriate treatment . Frequent or prolonged seizures may result in irreversible brain injury and cognitive impairment, particularly among children and adolescents, thereby imposing substantial psychological and social burdens on affected individuals and their . Limited data are available regarding childhood epilepsy in Sudan . The prevalence of epilepsy in Khartoum State, the capital of Sudan, has been estimated at 4 per 1,000 . Continuous access to antiseizure medications (ASMs) is essential for effective seizure control, and seizure remission rates of 60–80% depend largely on sustained medication adherence . Medication adherence is defined as the extent to which a patient’s medication-taking behaviour corresponds with recommendations provided by a healthcare professional . Several tools have been used to assess adherence, including the Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS), MMAS-4, MMAS-8, and one-month recall methods . Poor adherence has been associated with increased seizure frequency, greater emergency healthcare utilisation, and poorer clinical outcomes, whereas improved adherence contributes to better seizure control and quality of life . The Proportion of Days Covered (PDC) provides a quantitative measure of adherence, with a threshold of PDC ≥ 80% commonly used to define adequate adherence in chronic disease management . Adherence rates vary considerably, particularly among children, and are generally lower in LMICs because of shortages of trained healthcare personnel, limited medication availability, inadequate healthcare infrastructure, and insufficient patient education . These challenges are particularly pronounced in rural settings, where specialist services are scarce, leading the World Health Organization to advocate for epilepsy management at the primary healthcare level . A pre-conflict study conducted at Wad Medani Pediatric Teaching Hospital in Gezira State, central Sudan, reported good medication adherence in 48 patients (71.6%) . Another sudanese study conducted on children with epilepsy before the armed conflict found that 170 patients (48.6%) demonstrated high adherence on the Morisky Scale, whereas 86 (24.6%) and 94 (26.9%) had medium and low adherence, respectively . Sudan has experienced decades of complex and protracted conflict, with a new phase of civil war beginning in April 2023 in Khartoum before spreading to Gezira and Sinnar states, in addition to other major regions of the country (lasted for two years or more in some areas). In Gezira State, the setting of the present study, armed conflict persisted for approximately one year. In Gezira State, the setting of the present study, armed conflict persisted for approximately one year. Nearly 13 million people have been forcibly displaced, including 8.9 million internally displaced persons and 3.7 million refugees in neighbouring countries, placing severe pressure on Sudan’s collapsing infrastructure and the already limited capacities of host nations . Armed conflict further disrupts healthcare systems, medication supply chains, and continuity of follow-up care, placing children with epilepsy at particular risk . On-going conflict has led to the breakdown of referral networks and disruption of continuity of care . text: A retrospective, hospital-based, single-cycle clinical audit was conducted at Wad Medani Pediatric Teaching Hospital between 1 July 2025 and 1 October 2025. The audit evaluated treatment continuity and adherence to ASMs among children with epilepsy receiving routine care at the hospital epilepsy clinic during the armed conflict. The Proportion of Days Covered (PDC) was estimated using caregiver-reported medication availability because pharmacy refill records were unavailable.

text: Data were collected retrospectively from clinic records and supplemented by structured caregiver interviews conducted during clinic visits. Extracted variables included demographic characteristics (age, sex, and displacement status), seizure classification, epilepsy syndrome (where identifiable), prescribed ASMs, and the use of monotherapy or polytherapy. Demographic and clinical information, including age, sex, epilepsy diagnosis, seizure type, prescribed antiseizure medications, and hospital admissions documented in the medical record, were extracted from hospital records. Information relating to medication availability during the preceding 90 days, treatment interruptions, displacement status, loss of medical records, transportation difficulties, medication stock-outs, financial barriers, and other factors affecting treatment continuity was obtained through structured caregiver interviews conducted during clinic attendance. The structured interview consisted of a standardised data collection form developed for this clinical audit. Caregivers were asked a predefined set of questions regarding medication access, continuity of treatment, displacement-related challenges, and epilepsy-related events occurring during the conflict period. The same form was used for all participants to ensure consistency of data collection.

text: Treatment gap was defined as the complete absence or interruption of prescribed ASM therapy for ≥ 30 consecutive days within the preceding 90 days, consistent with commonly used operational definitions in epilepsy treatment-gap research. Medication adherence was assessed using the Proportion of Days Covered (PDC) over the preceding 90 days, with adherence defined as PDC ≥ 80%. Barriers to treatment continuity, including financial constraints, insecurity or transportation difficulties, medication stock-outs, and displacement-related loss of medication access, were recorded based on caregiver reports. Dose rationing was documented qualitatively when reported but was not formally quantified. Clinical outcomes included increased seizure frequency, emergency department attendance for seizures within the preceding 3 months, hospital admission, seizure-related injury or burns, and any history of status epilepticus since the onset of the armed conflict. The 3-month period corresponded to the return of displaced individuals and healthcare personnel following the retreat of the Rapid Support Forces from the study area.

text: Due to the absence of pharmacy dispensing databases and electronic refill records during the conflict, medication adherence was estimated using a caregiver-reported PDC approach. Caregivers reported the number of days during the preceding 90 days in which the child had access to prescribed ASMs based on household medication possession and availability. PDC was calculated as follows:\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned}\:\mathrm{P}\mathrm{D}\mathrm{C}=&(\mathrm{N}\mathrm{u}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{r}\:\mathrm{o}\mathrm{f}\:\mathrm{d}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{y}\mathrm{s}\:\mathrm{w}\mathrm{i}\mathrm{t}\mathrm{h}\:\mathrm{A}\mathrm{S}\mathrm{M}\:\mathrm{a}\mathrm{v}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{i}\mathrm{l}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{b}\mathrm{l}\mathrm{e}\:/\:90)\\&\:\times\:\:100\end{aligned}$$\end{document} Children were considered adherent if PDC was ≥ 80%, a commonly accepted threshold in chronic disease adherence research. This approach was adopted because caregiver report represented the only feasible method for estimating treatment continuity in conflict-affected settings lacking pharmacy infrastructure and prescription records.

text: In the absence of pharmacy refill data, adherence and treatment gaps were assessed through caregiver interviews and clinical documentation. Caregivers were asked about periods without medication availability, interruptions in treatment, inability to refill or obtain ASMs, dose-rationing practices, and the approximate duration of missed treatment periods. Adherence was assessed using caregiver-reported medication availability over the preceding 90 days using an adapted PDC measure. Treatment gaps were defined as interruptions in ASM therapy lasting ≥ 30 days, a threshold selected to identify interruptions likely to affect seizure control. The audit evaluated treatment continuity and did not verify actual medication ingestion. Given the healthcare disruptions during the conflict, caregiver-reported medication possession represented the most feasible proxy measure for ASM exposure. Structured interviews focused on medication stock depletion, displacement, clinic closures, and barriers to pharmacy access.

text: The 90-day observation period was selected for both methodological and clinical reasons. A 3-month interval is commonly used in epilepsy follow-up and allows assessment of medium-term treatment continuity while minimizing recall bias. In conflict and displacement settings, longer observation periods increase the likelihood of incomplete reporting and recall errors due to disrupted healthcare records. The 90-day window was considered sufficient to identify clinically significant interruptions in ASM access and their association with seizure worsening, hospitalization, and status epilepticus during the conflict. This timeframe balanced feasibility, recall reliability, and clinical relevance within an unstable healthcare environment.

text: This retrospective clinical audit demonstrated a substantial burden of antiseizure medication (ASM) non-adherence among children with epilepsy receiving care during the armed conflict in central Sudan, affecting more than three quarters of the study population. In contrast, a pre-conflict study conducted in the same region reported good adherence in approximately three quarters (71.6%) of participants . Prolonged treatment gaps were more common than simple non-adherence and reflected major disruptions in continuity of epilepsy care, affecting nearly three quarters of patients. These findings are consistent with evidence from other low-resource and conflict-affected settings-a study from northwest Ethiopia conducted on adults- where health system instability exacerbates existing epilepsy treatment gaps . Caregivers frequently reported multiple barriers to medication access during the conflict; therefore, the percentages presented in the results were not mutually exclusive and exceeded the total number of participants (64). Medication stock-outs accounted for more than half of the reported barriers and have similarly been identified as a major cause of treatment interruption in a Kenyan study conducted on adults under non-conflict conditions, which investigated discontinuities in antiretroviral therapy (ART) and treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) caused by drug shortages . In the present audit, more than half of caregivers identified displacement and relocation as barriers to treatment continuity, whereas transport insecurity was the least frequently reported barrier. By comparison, a Sudanese study conducted during armed conflict reported lack of transportation (37.9%) as the leading barrier to medication continuation . In the current study, transport-related barriers accounted for approximately one quarter of cases, possibly reflecting differences in the study setting. Financial hardship and clinic closures were also frequently reported contributors to ASM discontinuation. The convergence of multiple conflict-related barriers suggests that non-adherence was driven predominantly by structural and health system factors rather than individual caregiver behavior. Similar findings have been reported in studies conducted in other resource-limited settings . Treatment gaps of 30 days or longer are clinically significant and likely contribute to epilepsy-related complications, including emergency presentations, hospital admissions, and episodes of status epilepticus. Increased seizure frequency was reported in more than half of participants, while over one quarter required hospital admission. Fewer than one fifth experienced status epilepticus. Comparable findings were reported in an Australian study examining self-discontinuation of ASMs, in which 51 patients (65%) experienced seizure recurrence and 43 (84%) subsequently resumed treatment. Additionally, 22 patients (28%) sustained seizure-related injuries following treatment discontinuation. text: This retrospective audit demonstrated that epilepsy treatment gaps and ASM non-adherence among Sudanese children during the current armed conflict were highly prevalent and affected a substantial proportion of children with epilepsy. The findings suggest that treatment interruption was driven predominantly by structural barriers rather than caregiver non-compliance. Definitive pre-conflict data on emergency department attendance and status epilepticus were unavailable in the study setting; therefore, direct attribution of these outcomes to the armed conflict could not be established. Protecting ASM supply chains should be prioritized in humanitarian response planning. Urgent context-specific interventions are required to maintain treatment continuity, and repeat audits are essential to evaluate the effectiveness of targeted clinic-level interventions in this setting.

text: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by an enduring predisposition to seizures, affecting approximately 50 million people worldwide . It is one of the most prevalent neurological conditions in pediatric populations. A recent systematic analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 reported 18.15 million prevalent cases of epilepsy in children and adolescents globally, with a prevalence rate of 688.43 per 100,000 population, underscoring the substantial burden this condition places on pediatric healthcare systems worldwide . Across Arab countries, epidemiological research on epilepsy remains limited. Nevertheless, available evidence indicates that the prevalence of epilepsy in the Arab region, including Palestine, is approximately 6.9 per 1,000 individuals . Epilepsy arises from multiple possible causes, including metabolic, genetic, structural, infectious, immune, and unknown origins, and individuals may have more than one contributing etiology . Beyond its neurological manifestations, epilepsy is frequently accompanied by a range of psychiatric and behavioral comorbidities that compound its clinical burden, particularly in pediatric populations . These include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorders, depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbances . These comorbidities are frequently underrecognized in clinical practice, especially in resource-limited settings where access to neuropsychiatric services is constrained. Moreover, a large proportion of people with epilepsy live in low- and middle-income countries, where restricted availability of diagnostic and therapeutic services leads to a substantial treatment gap. Many individuals in such settings remain undertreated or untreated due to shortages in healthcare infrastructure, limited availability of neurology and epilepsy-specific services, economic constraints, cultural beliefs, social stigma, and reliance on traditional treatments . The Palestinian healthcare system faces unique challenges, including limited resources, geographical fragmentation, restricted access to specialized care, and ongoing political instability . Healthcare facilities are distributed unevenly across the West Bank, with specialized pediatric neurology services concentrated in major cities. To our knowledge, there are currently no fellowship-trained pediatric epileptologists practicing in the West Bank. Pediatric neurology services are provided by a small number of general pediatric neurologists, and there are no dedicated pediatric epilepsy centers or epilepsy monitoring units in the territory. Consequently, children with epilepsy often receive initial care from general pediatricians rather than specialists. This makes it essential that pediatricians possess adequate knowledge about epilepsy to provide appropriate initial management, recognize complications, educate families, and make timely referrals when necessary. Several studies have examined epilepsy knowledge among healthcare providers globally , all highlighting variable levels of knowledge gaps in specific domains. A recent study by Abu Libdeh et al. assessed epilepsy knowledge among 168 pediatricians in Jordan. The study revealed important knowledge gaps, especially regarding comorbidities and long-term management. Given the similarities in healthcare systems, cultural contexts, and training backgrounds between Jordan and Palestine, adapting their validated questionnaire provided an excellent opportunity to assess Palestinian pediatricians’ knowledge and compare findings. text: The target population included all pediatric residents across all training years, general pediatricians, and pediatric subspecialists (excluding pediatric neurologists) currently practicing in the West Bank. A convenience sampling technique was mainly employed, which, while limiting generalizability to the broader population, is widely utilized in clinical settings where comprehensive sampling frames are unavailable and probability-based approaches are impractical . To enhance representativeness, multiple recruitment strategies were used, including direct visits to hospitals and clinics across diverse geographic regions of the West Bank, digital recruitment through professional social media groups, and snowball sampling through participant referrals.

text: Sample size was calculated using the OpenEpi online calculator for a cross-sectional prevalence study with a finite population. The following parameters were specified: an anticipated proportion of adequate knowledge of 50% (conservative estimate), a margin of error of 5%, a confidence level of 95%, and an estimated population size of 500 practicing pediatricians in the West Bank based on expert consultation. The minimum required sample size was calculated as 218 participants. The final sample of 246 respondents exceeded this requirement, providing adequate statistical power for this study.

text: This study used a questionnaire developed and validated by Abu Libdeh et al. in the Jordanian context. Permission was obtained from the original authors for adaptation to the Palestinian setting. Only minor contextual modifications were made, including adapting geographic references and practice settings to reflect our Palestinian healthcare structure. The questionnaire was administered in English via Google Forms. The instrument comprised six categories: demographics, causes of epilepsy (3 items), long-term management of epilepsy (5 items), comorbidities (6 items), quality of life (4 items), and first-aid management of seizures (7 items). Knowledge items (25 total) were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from “strongly agree” to “strongly disagree”. Prior to data collection, a pilot study was conducted among 15 pediatricians (residents, general pediatricians, and subspecialists) not included in the final sample, who provided feedback on item clarity, relevance to Palestinian practice, and feasibility of completion. In our sample, the adapted questionnaire demonstrated acceptable internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.707 for the full scale.

text: Consistent with the methodology of Abu Libdeh et al. , questionnaire responses were classified as correct if the response was one of the two Likert-scale choices in agreement with the correct answer, or incorrect if the respondent chose “neutral” or one of the two choices not in agreement with the correct answer. A binary variable (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) was computed for each of the 25 knowledge items, and composite scores were calculated for each domain and for the total questionnaire. The normality of knowledge score distributions was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. All scores significantly deviated from normality (p < 0.05), confirmed by visual inspection of histograms and Q-Q plots. Therefore, non-parametric tests were used for all group comparisons. Descriptive statistics were computed using frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, while medians and interquartile ranges were computed for continuous variables. For inferential analysis, Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to compare knowledge scores across three or more groups, with Dwass-Steel-Critchlow-Fligner (DSCF) post-hoc pairwise comparisons where appropriate. Mann-Whitney U tests were used for two-group comparisons. All tests were two-tailed, and statistical significance was set at α = 0.05. Analyses were performed using Jamovi Software (version 2.3).

text: Table 3 presents the correct response rate for each of the 25 individual knowledge items. Within the etiology domain, 87% of respondents correctly identified that epilepsy is not a contagious disease, but only 52% correctly disagreed that epilepsy is caused by stress. In the long-term management domain, 80.5% appropriately rejected the notion that anti-seizure medications can be immediately withdrawn upon achieving seizure freedom, and 80.1% recognized that some children with epilepsy benefit from special diets. The comorbidities domain revealed some gaps, as only 46.3% of respondents recognized that hyperactivity is more common in children with epilepsy (CWE), and awareness of the risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) was present in only 62.6%. First-aid management items had uniformly high correct response rates, with the notable exceptions of “do not stand away from the patient” (50.8%) and “do not put a metallic object in their hand” (78.5%).
