text: Identifying patients with an underlying antibody-associated etiology remains a significant challenge in clinical practice. Broad neuronal antibody testing in individuals with low pretest probability is not recommended, as it may lead to the detection of antibodies with uncertain clinical significance, inappropriate initiation of immunotherapy, and unnecessary increase in healthcare costs. Thus, antibody testing should be reserved for individuals with clinical features suggestive of AAE and a reasonable likelihood of benefiting from immunotherapy. 13 16 In recent years, multiple clinical scoring systems have been developed to guide antibody testing and, in some cases, empirical immunotherapy. Dubey et al. 24 introduced the Antibody Prevalence in Epilepsy (APE) score after analyzing clinical, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and CSF data from patients with new-onset or established epilepsy of unknown etiology. A score ≥ 4 showed high sensitivity (82.6%) and specificity (82.0%) for neuronal-antibody positivity. 24 To improve performance in patients with encephalopathy, memory loss, or neuropsychiatric symptoms, the same group 25 subsequently proposed the Antibody Prevalence in Epilepsy and Encephalopathy (APE2) score, in which a cutoff ≥ 4 yielded a sensitivity of 99% and a specificity of 93% for the presence of neuronal antibodies. While the APE and APE2 scores share similarities, the APE2 score has an expanded maximum of 18 points (versus 15 for the APE), due to refined criteria such as separating faciobrachial dystonic seizures from facial dyskinesias and incorporating additional MRI findings. It also narrows the relevance of malignancies to those diagnosed within 5 years. Both scores are primarily suited to the identification of acute symptomatic seizures due to autoimmune encephalitis, rather than AAE. 17 In 2021, De Bruijn et al. 23 developed the Antibody Contributing to Focal Epilepsy Signs and Symptoms (ACES) score based on a multicenter cohort of patients with focal epilepsy of unknown etiology, excluding those with signs of encephalitis. The study included individuals with epilepsy duration between 2 and 18 years. A multivariate analysis identified six predictive variables: history of autoimmune disease, behavioral changes, cognitive symptoms, speech disturbance, autonomic symptoms, and mesial temporal-lobe hyperintensities on MRI. An ACES score ≥ 2 demonstrated 100% of sensitivity (95%CI = 81.4–100) and 84.9% of specificity (95%CI = 67.9–100). Although all antibody-positive patients were captured with this threshold, 14% of those meeting this criterion had negative antibody panels, reinforcing that the score is better suited for screening rather than diagnosis. Notably, nearly 70% of antibody-positive patients would have been missed using the APE2 score alone, underscoring the importance of tailored tools for chronic epilepsy scenarios. 23 Also in 2021, the Antibody Prevalence in Epilepsy before Surgery (APES) score was introduced 19 to identify candidates for antibody testing during preoperative evaluation in drug-resistant focal epilepsy of unknown etiology. This is especially relevant given the poorer postoperative outcomes observed in antibody-positive patients. Adapted from the APE2 score, the APES score includes additional variables such as positron-emission tomography and computed tomography (PET-CT) abnormalities, focal neurological signs at seizure onset, and personal or family history of autoimmunity. This is especially relevant given the poorer postoperative outcomes observed in antibody-positive patients. Adapted from the APE2 score, the APES score includes additional variables such as positron-emission tomography and computed tomography (PET-CT) abnormalities, focal neurological signs at seizure onset, and personal or family history of autoimmunity. Cerebrospinal fluid data were excluded, given that lumbar puncture is not routinely performed in preoperative protocols. A cutoff ≥ 4 showed improved sensitivity (100% versus 71.4%) with comparable specificity (44.3% versus 49.4%) relative to the APE2 score. Among individuals with complete datasets ( n = 60), the predictive accuracy remained consistent. 19 However, the score still requires external validation before routine clinical implementation. Another scoring tool proposed in 2021 is the Antibody in Drug-Resistant Temporal-Lobe Epilepsy (ARTE) score, 26 aimed at identifying antibody-positive individuals among patients with pharmacoresistant TLE of unknown cause. The study assessed 27 adults with disease duration > 12 months. Clinical variables were compared between antibody-positive and -negative patients to derive the score. A cutoff ≥ 1 yielded 100% of sensitivity and 46.1% of specificity, while ≥ 3 increased the specificity to 100% but reduced the sensitivity to 35.7%. 26 The small sample size limits generalizability and highlights the need for validation in independent cohorts. Table 2 outlines the criteria for each scoring system, whereas Table 3 provides a direct comparison of them. In 2022, the ‘Obvious’ indications for Neural antibody testing in Epilepsy or Seizures (ONES checklist) was developed 27 through a literature review and subsequently evaluated for sensitivity and specificity in comparison with the APE2/ACES reflex score. This retrospective analysis included 96 patients who underwent neural antibody testing for epilepsy or seizures of unknown etiology. The APE2/ACES reflex score was defined as either an APE2 score ≥ 4, or an APE2 score ≤ 3 combined with an ACES score ≥ 2. The median interval from seizure onset to neural antibody testing was of 2 (range: 0–41) years, with 38% of the patients tested within 1 year of seizure onset. No significant difference in sensitivity or specificity was observed between the ONES checklist and the APE2/ACES reflex score. 27 However, as discussed regarding the APE and APE2 scores, the ONES checklist is more appropriate for acute presentations in which autoimmune encephalitis is suspected, and it may have limited applicability in chronic epilepsy without encephalitic features. Table 4 presents the ONES checklist, which adopts a distinct approach by emphasizing clinical features suggestive of neural antibody positivity that might otherwise go unrecognized by clinicians. Once appropriate candidates are identified, either through clinical assessment or validated screening tools (selected according to whether the presentation is acute or chronic, as illustrated in Figure 2 ), the next challenge is determining which antibodies to test for. Because the clinical phenotype rarely suggests a specific antibody, a broad, parallel testing approach is preferred to avoid delays and costs associated with sequential testing. 28 Simultaneous testing of the serum and CSF is also recommended, as certain antibodies may be compartment-specific; for instance, NMDAR antibodies may be negative in serum, while LGI1 antibodies may be absent in CSF. 10 28 29 False positives can occur, particularly in commercial panels, and they must be interpreted in the context of the clinical scenario. Indeed, in some cases, more than one neuronal autoantibody may be identified. 11 Conversely, some patients with classic autoimmune phenotypes may test negative for all known antibodies, reinforcing the need for diagnostic criteria that integrate clinical and laboratory features, as already occurs in rheumatology. 17 The testing methodology depends on the antibody type. Antibodies against intracellular antigens can be detected using Western blot, line assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), fixed tissue-based assay (TBA), cell-based assay (CBA), or radioimmunoassay (RIA). Antibodies targeting surface antigens are typically assessed using immunohistochemistry, RIA, non-fixed or post-fixed TBA, and CBA—the latter being the most widely-adopted method. Non-fixed or post-fixed TBA involves rodent brain-tissue incubation followed by microscopy or immunofluorescence, and it is used for antibody discovery and CBA screening. 11 12 15 30 For anti-GAD65 antibodies specifically, commercial tests include ELISA, RIA, TBA, and line immunoassays. The ELISA and RIA are highly-sensitive, but they may detect low-titer antibodies that lack clinical significance; only high-titer anti-GAD65 antibodies are considered relevant in autoimmune neurological syndromes. 12 Testing the serum and CSF is advisable, as some patients show intrathecal synthesis despite low or undetectable serum levels. 31 Confirmatory testing using multiple techniques, such as combining CBA and immunofluorescence, enhances diagnostic accuracy, especially since different CBA methods (live versus fixed cells) can vary in sensitivity and specificity. 17 19 For intracellular antibodies, the preferred strategy includes fixed TBA and line assay, with the latter often showing higher sensitivity compared with indirect immunohistochemistry. 12 In Brazil, for example, the 2024 Consensus on Autoimmune Encephalitis 32 recommends a combined approach using CBA and TBA, along with paired serum and CSF analyses, for patients meeting the criteria for possible autoimmune encephalitis. Therefore, antibody interpretation must integrate clinical phenotype, disease chronology, antibody titer, and compartment (serum versus CSF), rather than relying solely on seropositivity.

text: In AAE patients, EEG remains a useful tool to evaluate encephalopathy, epileptiform discharges, and seizure activity. However, there are no EEG patterns specific enough to reliably identify AAE outside the context of autoimmune encephalitis. 33 The ‘extreme delta brush’ pattern, for example, is considered characteristic of anti-NMDAR encephalitis, but it is not typically observed in other antibody-associated epilepsies. On the other hand, VEEG monitoring is particularly informative. Subtle clinical manifestations may go unnoticed by patients, resulting in an underestimation of seizure frequency; VEEG provides a more accurate assessment of seizure burden, and it is also valuable for monitoring treatment response to immunotherapy and ASMs. 1 22 Brain MRI remains a cornerstone in the evaluation of epilepsy, supported by well-established guidelines by the ILAE. Repeat imaging using the harmonized neuroimaging of epilepsy structural sequences (HARNESS)-MRI protocol—which includes high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) T1-weighted, 3D fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and two-dimensional (2D) coronal T2-weighted sequences—is recommended in cases in which previous MRI is unavailable or suboptimal. Importantly, neuroimaging findings should be interpreted in conjunction with electroclinical data, especially in the context of unexplained seizure worsening, rapid cognitive decline, or new-onset neuropsychiatric symptoms. 34 Positron emission tomography and computed tomography with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), which assesses regional cerebral glucose metabolism, can offer additional diagnostic information. This technique is widely used in the evaluation of brain tumors and inflammatory disorders. 35 In AAE, most available data focus on cases of autoimmune encephalitis or acute symptomatic seizures. For the early detection of inflammatory brain involvement, PET-CT has been proposed as a modality more sensitive than MRI. 35 36 Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) may be elevated in infectious or systemic inflammatory states. While nonspecific, some diagnostic protocols 37 include these markers as part of the workup, particularly to screen for systemic autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Several systemic autoantibodies have also been investigated in epilepsy. In a 2015 observational study 38 involving 319 patients without known autoimmune disease, the presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-β2-glycoprotein 1, anticardiolipin IgG, antimicrosomal antibodies, and antithyroglobulin was evaluated. At least one autoantibody was detected in 23.5% of the participants, with the following prevalences: anticardiolipin (9.4%), antimicrosomal (7.5%), ANA (5.6%), anti-β2-glycoprotein (5.6%), and antithyroglobulin (3.25%). Regarding the role of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, a study 39 comparing the prevalence of antithyroid antibodies in 42 patients with adult-onset TLE, stratified by known and unknown etiology, found a higher frequency of anti-TPO positivity among patients with unknown etiology. Furthermore, late-onset TLE associated with antithyroid antibodies tended to occur in middle-aged women and was frequently accompanied by cognitive decline and other autoimmune disorders, including anti-GAD65 positivity. 39 However, anti-TPO antibodies are relatively common in the general population (particularly among women), and their presence may represent an epiphenomenon rather than a direct pathogenic mechanism. Thus, although these findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the controversial role of anti-TPO antibodies in steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT), anti-TPO positivity alone should not be considered evidence of AAE. text: higher frequency of anti-TPO positivity among patients with unknown etiology. Furthermore, late-onset TLE associated with antithyroid antibodies tended to occur in middle-aged women and was frequently accompanied by cognitive decline and other autoimmune disorders, including anti-GAD65 positivity. 39 However, anti-TPO antibodies are relatively common in the general population (particularly among women), and their presence may represent an epiphenomenon rather than a direct pathogenic mechanism. Thus, although these findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the controversial role of anti-TPO antibodies in steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT), anti-TPO positivity alone should not be considered evidence of AAE. These data reinforce the importance of a comprehensive and clinically-contextualized autoimmune evaluation in selected patients. Complement-system analysis has emerged for the identification neuroinflammation. Activation of the complement within the CNS is increasingly recognized as a contributor to tissue injury in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases. In animal and human studies, dysregulation of the classical complement pathway has been associated with poor seizure control. A study 40 comparing 157 patients with epilepsy to 54 healthy controls, for instance, found significantly-elevated plasma complement component 4 (C4) levels among individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy, suggesting a role for complement activation in pharmacoresistance. In epilepsy, CSF analysis is typically nonspecific, but it can offer valuable insights in certain contexts. Pleocytosis is rare following seizures, although it may occur when lumbar puncture is performed within hours to days after a seizure. When present, further testing should be performed to exclude infectious or immune etiologies such as meningitis or encephalitis. In contrast, elevated CSF protein levels are more frequently observed—reported in 10 to 61% of the patients, depending on the series—and they are believed to reflect blood-brain barrier dysfunction rather than a specific etiologic factor. 29 Establishing a clear protein cutoff to distinguish inflammatory from postictal changes is difficult due to variability in methodology and inconsistent exclusion of confounding conditions across studies. Oligoclonal bands (OCBs) are rare in epilepsy patients (reported in 0–10% of the patients), but, when present, they may suggest an underlying autoimmune mechanism. These bands are most frequently observed in cases of anti-NMDAR, anti-GAD65, and anti-GABAB receptor encephalitis. Some authors 29 advocate that the presence of an inflammatory CSF profile —defined by pleocytosis and OCB positivity—should prompt investigation for immune epilepsy, even in the absence of detectable neural autoantibodies. More recently, research has focused on cytokine profiling as a potential biomarker strategy. A study comparing patients with drug-resistant epilepsy and positive neuronal autoantibodies to those without antibodies found significant differences in CSF levels of interleukin-13 (IL-13), RANTES (also known as chemokine ligand-5, CCL5), and vascular endothelial growth fator (VEGF). Although promising, these findings require replication in larger, prospective cohorts before being incorporated into the routine clinical practice.

text: A 2018 systematic review 42 demonstrated that the efficacy of ASMs in AAE is limited. Only ∼ 10% of the patients achieved seizure freedom with ASM monotherapy, and fewer than 15% experienced a reduction greater than 50% in seizure frequency. These findings underscore the need to consider adjunctive immunotherapy in selected patients. 30 Regarding immunotherapy, a case series 43 evaluated 81 patients without clinical features suggestive of limbic encephalitis (although a subgroup presented with psychiatric symptoms, movement disorders, cognitive impairment, or coexisting autoimmune disease), with a mean disease duration exceeding 6 years. Among antibody-positive patients who received immunotherapy, 75% (9/12) achieved a reduction greater than 50% in seizure frequency, and 50% became seizure-free. In 2016, Bakpa et al. 15 published a review including 34 studies (involving 1,451 patients), reporting clinical improvement in 81% of the patients following immunotherapy, with 67% achieving seizure control within 10 months. However, most included studies involved patients with associated encephalopathy, suggesting that cases of autoimmune encephalitis may have been incorporated, thereby limiting the precision and generalizability of these estimates to isolated AAE. Diagnostic delay is another factor influencing treatment response. In a cohort of 86 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy of unknown etiology, 19 the mean interval between seizure onset and comprehensive presurgical evaluation, including assessment for immune-mediated causes, was of 14.2 years. Such delay may contribute to reduced responsiveness to immunotherapy due to the development of irreversible structural or network alterations. More invasive and costly interventions typically reserved for drug-resistant epilepsy, such as epilepsy surgery and neurostimulation devices, appear to be less effective in patients with immune-mediated etiologies. A retrospective multicenter study 44 demonstrated that seizure outcomes following temporal-lobe surgery in patients with neuronal antibodies were inferior to those observed in other clinical contexts. Given the limited efficacy of the usual therapeutic approaches, once an immune etiology is reasonably established, a trial of immunotherapy should be considered. However, treatment response depends on the timing of the intervention and the type of autoantibody involved. In cases associated with intracellular antibodies, such as anti-GAD65, complete seizure resolution is uncommon. 10 Importantly, the evidence supporting immunotherapy in chronic AAE remains largely derived from observational cohorts and retrospective series, frequently including patients with encephalitic features. Randomized controlled trials are lacking, and response rates may reflect early treatment of active inflammation rather than reversal of established epileptogenic networks. Once structural or network remodeling becomes consolidated, seizure persistence may no longer represent ongoing immune activity. In general, during the induction phase, the first-line therapies include intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), and plasma exchange (PLEX). The second-line therapies typically include rituximab and cyclophosphamide. In the maintenance phase, the options include gradual tapering of first-line agents, continuation of second-line therapy, or the addition of an alternative immunotherapy, such as mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine. 45 Empirical immunotherapy should be reserved for patients with high pretest probability of immune etiology and objective supportive features (such as inflammatory CSF profile, high-titer neuronal antibodies, compatible MRI findings). text: Epilepsy care worldwide is characterized by significant disparities, particularly in low- and middle-income regions such as Latin America, where access to essential diagnostic tools—including EEG, MRI, and ASMs—remains limited. 46 To guide the rational adoption of new diagnostic technologies, Schaafsma et al. 47 proposed a hierarchical framework that evaluates test characteristics (such as sensitivity and specificity), diagnostic yield (that is, improvement in the accurate classification of disease versus non-disease), clinical impact, and cost-effectiveness. When assessed using this framework, autoantibody testing in selected patients with epilepsy demonstrates meaningful clinical usefulness. Autoantibody testing is fundamental for the diagnosis of autoimmune conditions, including AAE. Early identification of an immune-mediated etiology may enable the timely initiation of immunotherapy and potentially mitigate cognitive decline and contribute to improved long-term outcomes, especially in patients undergoing a preoperative evaluation. Nonetheless, financial and systemic barriers frequently limit the availability of antibody testing in resource-constrained settings. These include high test costs, insufficient laboratory infrastructure, and limited coverage by public or private health systems. To address these barriers, it is imperative to foster the development of cost-effective testing platforms, invest in local laboratory capacity, encourage public–private collaborations, and multicentric consortia. Such strategies could enable earlier and more accurate diagnoses, ultimately improving care for patients with suspected AAE across diverse healthcare systems. Recognizing and addressing these diagnostic and structural challenges will be critical to advance equitable, evidence-based care for epilepsy patients with potential autoimmune etiologies. Autoimmune-associated epilepsy remains a diagnostically-challenging entity at the intersection between epileptology and neuroimmunology. A structured, probability-based approach integrating clinical phenotype, validated screening tools, using comprehensive autoantibodies panels in CSF and serum tested by appropriate techniques, and contextual antibody interpretation is essential to avoid underdiagnosis and overtreatment.

text: The underutilization of epilepsy surgery now represents a public health crisis, even as neuromodulation and other minimally destructive approaches broaden surgical candidacy and begin to reshape the field’s therapeutic paradigms . Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where access to specialist care is limited . Despite the availability of more than 30 antiseizure medications, approximately one-third of patients do not achieve adequate seizure control with pharmacotherapy alone . For many of these patients, surgical resection or thermal ablation offers the best chance of seizure freedom. Yet a substantial subset are not candidates for these approaches because the seizure onset zone lies within or near eloquent cortex, is multifocal or poorly localized, or has already been treated unsuccessfully . For this population, chronic neuromodulation offers a nondestructive, reversible, and adjustable alternative. Three modalities are currently in clinical use for epilepsy: vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which delivers intermittent open-loop cervical stimulation; anterior nucleus of the thalamus DBS (ANT-DBS), which delivers scheduled bilateral thalamic stimulation; and responsive neurostimulation (RNS), which delivers stimulation contingent on detected electrocorticographic (ECoG) activity at or near the epileptogenic zone [, , , , , ]. Across separate long-term studies, the reported median seizure reduction at three years has been approximately 44% for VNS , approximately 40% for ANT-DBS in the European MORE registry , and approximately 82% for the RNS System in its postapproval study . Of these, the RNS occupies a unique position: it is the only FDA-approved device that records from and stimulates at the seizure focus itself, makes autonomous real-time stimulation decisions based on those recordings, and stores the underlying raw electrographic data for retrospective physician review . This architecture, with sensing, processing, and stimulation co-localized at the pathological source, is what distinguishes closed-loop from open-loop neuromodulation and what makes the RNS the most instructive clinical model for understanding adaptive brain stimulation . The lessons learned from the RNS are increasingly relevant to adaptive DBS systems developed primarily for movement disorders. In parallel, DBS hardware has advanced in areas such as current steering, directional leads, chronic local field potential recording, and embedded control algorithms [3,, , , ]. These systems were not designed specifically for epilepsy, with the earlier Activa PC + S work in epilepsy models as a notable exception, but they now raise many of the same engineering questions . This convergence is especially relevant as network-level epilepsy targets such as the anterior nucleus, centromedian nucleus, and pulvinar of the thalamus gain increasing clinical interest . text: In this review, we compare four implantable systems: the RNS System (NeuroPace, Mountain View, CA), the Percept PC (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN), the G106RS (PINS Medical, Beijing, China), and the AlphaDBS System (Newronika, Milan, Italy). We performed a review of all available published literature describing the technical capabilities of these devices. These four systems were selected because each is an implantable closed-loop or sensing-enabled device that has received marketing approval in at least one jurisdiction for chronic use: the RNS System (FDA 2013), the Percept PC (Conformite Europeenne [CE] mark and FDA approval, 2020), the AlphaDBS System (CE 2021), and the G106RS (marketed in China). Investigational-only research platforms that also support concurrent sensing and stimulation, such as the Medtronic Summit RC + S and the Picostim-DyNeuMo, were therefore excluded from the primary device comparison and are instead considered among future directions. We focus on sensing architecture, biomarker strategy, artifact management, data handling, and degree of closed-loop autonomy. text: The Responsive Neurostimulation System, approved by the FDA in 2013, was the first commercially available closed-loop intracranial neurostimulation device . It is indicated for adults aged 18 years and older with medically refractory focal epilepsy arising from no more than two epileptogenic foci, including patients whose seizure onset zones cannot be safely resected because they involve eloquent cortex . More recent evidence suggests a broader network-level role for the platform, including the randomized NAUTILUS trial of bilateral centromedian thalamic responsive stimulation for idiopathic generalized epilepsy and multiple thalamic case series in multifocal epilepsy [21,22,, , ]. The system continuously monitors electrocorticographic activity through implanted depth or subdural electrodes and delivers brief responsive stimulation when prespecified ictal patterns are detected, with the goal of interrupting seizure activity before it propagates or generalizes . Electrode placement near the seizure onset zone, with recording and stimulating contacts positioned within or immediately adjacent to the seizure onset zone, enables recording with high spatial and temporal resolution; because electrocorticographic activity is a spatially local signal, effective detection generally requires contacts within the onset zone [8,, , ]. Depth and subdural strip leads each contain four platinum-iridium contacts, and although only two leads can be connected to the neurostimulator at a given time, additional leads may be implanted and retained for future selection if initial targets prove suboptimal . Contacts can be configured for sensing, stimulation, or both, using bipolar or referential recording montages and multiple cathode-anode stimulation arrangements . This design requires robust stimulation-artifact management, but it also preserves close spatial correspondence between the recorded biomarker and the delivered therapy . Whether stimulation is most effective when delivered at the seizure focus itself, immediately adjacent to it, or within downstream propagation pathways remains an open question, and the chronic recording capability of the RNS is well suited to help address it . Long-term clinical follow-up has shown progressive improvement in seizure outcomes. Median seizure frequency reduction was 44% at one year in the pivotal trial and 53% at two years . In longer-term follow-up, reported median seizure reduction increased to 58% at three years, 66% at five years, 69% at seven years, and 75% at nine years . This sustained improvement is a defining clinical observation associated with the platform and may reflect, at least in part, continued refinement of detection and stimulation parameters over time . Direct head-to-head randomized comparisons of brain-responsive neurostimulation with anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation or vagus nerve stimulation are lacking, but the available long-term evidence consistently favors responsive neurostimulation across both focal and generalized epilepsies. In drug-resistant focal epilepsy, vagus nerve stimulation produces median seizure reductions of approximately 35% , and anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation improves from roughly 33% at two years to 55% at five years in long-term registry follow-up , whereas brain-responsive neurostimulation improves from approximately 62% at six months to 82% at three years and sustains median reductions of about 75% through nine years, with many patients achieving extended seizure-free intervals . text: anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation or vagus nerve stimulation are lacking, but the available long-term evidence consistently favors responsive neurostimulation across both focal and generalized epilepsies. In drug-resistant focal epilepsy, vagus nerve stimulation produces median seizure reductions of approximately 35% , and anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation improves from roughly 33% at two years to 55% at five years in long-term registry follow-up , whereas brain-responsive neurostimulation improves from approximately 62% at six months to 82% at three years and sustains median reductions of about 75% through nine years, with many patients achieving extended seizure-free intervals . In idiopathic generalized epilepsy, pooled analyses report median reductions near 48% for vagus nerve stimulation and 65% for thalamic deep brain stimulation , while responsive stimulation of the centromedian nucleus produced a 76.8% median reduction at 18 months, a 62.5% responder rate, and rendered 40% of patients free of generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the first randomized controlled trial conducted in this population . These cross-study comparisons cannot substitute for randomized head-to-head data and are influenced by differences in patient populations, stimulation targets, and follow-up duration; nonetheless, they position brain-responsive neurostimulation at the higher end of the efficacy range among currently available implantable neurostimulation options. A related assumption warrants scrutiny. It is sometimes argued that certain seizure networks are so difficult to treat that they require the continuous stimulation delivered by DBS rather than detection-triggered intermittent therapy. No published data support this claim. No trial has identified a circuit phenotype or patient subgroup in which continuous stimulation outperforms responsive stimulation, and no head-to-head comparison of the two strategies within any proposed subgroup has been conducted. The premise is further undermined by the design of thalamic DBS itself: in the SANTE trial and its long-term follow-up, stimulation was delivered on an intermittent duty cycle of 1 min on and 5 min off, so even “continuous” DBS is in practice scheduled intermittent stimulation delivered without regard to brain state . Conversely, responsive stimulation achieves its outcomes with a strikingly small stimulation dose, with typical RNS patients receiving brief detection-triggered stimulations totaling only a few minutes per day while attaining the long-term seizure reductions described above . The available evidence therefore suggests that when and where stimulation is delivered matters more than how much, and it provides no empirical basis for the claim that some seizure circuits need continuous stimulation. Stimulation is delivered as current-controlled, charge-balanced biphasic pulses . The device uses a single digital-to-analog converter output pair, one anodic and one cathodic, to generate each stimulation burst. When multiple contacts share a polarity, current divides across those contacts according to impedance rather than being independently specified at each electrode . Responsive therapy can be organized as sequential therapies triggered after detector events, and programming spans detector selection, pattern-specific thresholds, stimulation pathway configuration, amplitude, pulse width, frequency, burst duration, therapy order, and daily therapy limits . When multiple contacts share a polarity, current divides across those contacts according to impedance rather than being independently specified at each electrode . Responsive therapy can be organized as sequential therapies triggered after detector events, and programming spans detector selection, pattern-specific thresholds, stimulation pathway configuration, amplitude, pulse width, frequency, burst duration, therapy order, and daily therapy limits . Programmable parameters include pulse frequency from 1 to 333 Hz, pulse width from 40 to 1000 μs, amplitude from 0.5 to 12 mA, and burst duration from 10 to 5000 ms . Charge density per phase must remain below 30 μC/cm2 per electrode . The RNS implantable pulse generator is skull mounted and connects to the leads through a titanium case measuring 60 × 28 × 7.7 mm, weighing 17.2 g, and occupying 11 cm3 . Onboard storage retains approximately 30 channel-minutes of ECoG (about 7.5 min when all four channels are recorded simultaneously) in programmable segments of 30–240 s sampled at 250 Hz, with the oldest recordings overwritten unless reserved . Importantly, the device stores raw ECoG waveform snippets surrounding detected events rather than only derived spectral summaries . It also records multiple event classes and summary histories that shape interpretation of device behavior, including long episodes, saturation events, magnet-triggered recordings, scheduled recordings, therapy counts, and daily Neurostimulator History metrics . This makes the RNS distinctive among currently deployed clinical systems in providing waveform-level retrospective review of detection-linked events for programming and algorithm refinement, even though broader device behavior still must be inferred from sparse event-linked samples rather than continuous recordings . Average battery life is approximately 8.4 years . Detection algorithms are physician programmed and can incorporate measures such as spectral power, line length, area under the curve, and bandpass features . Their optimization remains labor intensive and is often empirical. The RNS programming workflow therefore depends not only on stored ECoG review but also on interpretation of device metadata, including therapy delivery rates, detector-specific event counts, long-episode behavior, and magnet-correlated events . Because the device stores only peri-event recordings rather than continuous data, retrospective review is limited to episodes that triggered detection or were otherwise captured by storage rules, which constrains assessment of false positives, missed events, and the broader electrophysiological context in which detections occurred . text: limitations of the platform warrant emphasis alongside its strengths: only two leads and four sensing channels can be active at once; stimulation is delivered from a single current source without independent per-contact steering; the 250 Hz sampling rate constrains access to higher-frequency oscillations; and detection settings are deliberately biased toward high sensitivity, so the majority of detections are never independently verified against the stored electrographic record. Detection counts in some cases therefore could correlate only weakly with true seizure frequency, and detection programming remains labor intensive and empirical . Nonetheless, this device recently became the first to employ an AI tool, termed “ECoG-Assistant,” that reliably detects electrographic seizure patterns in recordings stored on the Patient Data Management System (PDMS) . Beyond focal epilepsy, the RNS has also been used off label in other settings, including responsive thalamic stimulation for Tourette syndrome and centromedian thalamic stimulation in idiopathic generalized epilepsy . The Scheduled Therapy mode introduced in the RNS 320 also permits stimulation during programmed time windows or recurring intervals independent of detection, allowing the platform to approximate continuous or cyclical open-loop stimulation while preserving chronic sensing and event-triggered recording capabilities when clinically appropriate .

text: The Percept PC is a DBS platform approved by the FDA in 2020, and CE marked in Europe the same year, for the treatment of Parkinson’s disease, essential tremor, dystonia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder . Its initial approval covered conventional DBS delivery together with the BrainSense sensing platform, which enables chronic recording of local field potentials during active stimulation [17,, , ]. The device has become one of the most important commercial platforms for adaptive DBS development because it combines widely used DBS hardware with chronic sensing capability . BrainSense technology supports two distinct recording modes. BrainSense Timeline records local field potential power continuously during stimulation delivery, providing a longitudinal view of spectral activity over days to months . BrainSense Survey, by contrast, records local field potential data with stimulation paused and samples across contact pairs to characterize the spectral landscape before programming . These modes serve different purposes and should not be conflated: Timeline reflects neural activity during therapeutic stimulation, whereas Survey characterizes the unstimulated baseline . Stimulation is delivered in constant-current mode through 16 independent current sources, one per available contact . This multiple independent current control architecture enables current steering and directional field shaping when paired with SenSight directional leads and is also compatible with Medtronic leads 3387, 3389, and 3391 . Amplitude is programmable in 0.05 mA steps up to 12.5 mA, pulse width from 20 to 450 μs, and frequency from 3 to 250 Hz . Its sensing architecture imposes important constraints. During concurrent sensing and stimulation, the recording contacts must flank the stimulating cathode, and sensing and stimulation cannot occur on the same contact; when stimulation is off, by contrast, local field potentials can be surveyed across other bipolar contact pairs, so the adjacency requirement applies specifically to simultaneous sensing and stimulation rather than to sensing in general . This limits flexibility when the best recording site is not the best stimulation site. Stimulation-artifact rejection relies on hardware blanking and is generally adequate for routine clinical use, although residual artifact can persist at higher stimulation amplitudes and frequencies . Sampling is limited to 250 Hz in both BrainSense Survey and LFP streaming modes . Because sensing is digitized at approximately 250 Hz, chronic BrainSense recording is also subject to sense-stimulation interactions that depend on the stimulation frequency: at lower stimulation frequencies the stimulation fundamental and its harmonics fall within the sensed band, whereas at higher frequencies the artifact is aliased to a mirror frequency. Low-frequency stimulation in particular can therefore degrade or preclude reliable chronic sensing, an interlock that constrains adaptive strategies requiring low-rate stimulation . This is sufficient for beta-band biomarkers but restricts evaluation of higher-frequency signals, including stimulation-entrained gamma oscillations, which may provide useful information about therapeutic engagement in some patient groups . Broader-band systems such as the AlphaDBS and G106RS address this limitation at the hardware level, although clinical validation of gamma-driven adaptive control remains early . Low-frequency stimulation in particular can therefore degrade or preclude reliable chronic sensing, an interlock that constrains adaptive strategies requiring low-rate stimulation . This is sufficient for beta-band biomarkers but restricts evaluation of higher-frequency signals, including stimulation-entrained gamma oscillations, which may provide useful information about therapeutic engagement in some patient groups . Broader-band systems such as the AlphaDBS and G106RS address this limitation at the hardware level, although clinical validation of gamma-driven adaptive control remains early . The Percept PC pulse generator has dimensions of 68 × 55 × 11 mm, a volume of 34.9 cm3, and a mass of 61 g . The sensing noise floor is below 300 nV/√Hz, with an input range of 0.55–400 μV rms . Longitudinal storage is available for up to 60 days of trend data, but those data consist of narrow-band power values rather than raw waveforms [17,, , , ]. The device is conditionally compatible with 3 T magnetic resonance imaging and uses a hybrid silver vanadium oxide primary cell [17,, , , ]. The Percept platform is also available in a rechargeable version, the Percept RC (CE marked in 2023 and FDA approved in January 2024), which shares the BrainSense sensing architecture but provides a longer rated service life at the cost of periodic recharging. The two versions share the same BrainSense sensing and BrainSense Timeline storage capabilities (the Percept PC retains up to approximately 60 days of trend data); the principal difference of the RC is its rechargeable power source and longer rated service life rather than its sensing or storage architecture . Both the Percept PC and Percept RC are labeled MR conditional for full-body imaging at 1.5 T and 3 T under specified conditions . Recent clinical studies have suggested that adaptive stimulation using the Percept platform can improve outcomes relative to conventional continuous DBS in selected Parkinson’s disease cohorts. In a blinded randomized feasibility study, chronic adaptive DBS produced greater improvement in several motor outcomes than conventional continuous stimulation . In the ADAPT-PD study, long-term personalized adaptive DBS met its primary noninferiority goal relative to conventional DBS, with post hoc analyses suggesting increased on-time and reduced total electrical energy delivered in selected adaptive modes . These results are encouraging, but they should be interpreted in the context of a system whose sensing flexibility and data storage design remain more constrained than those of platforms that permit sensing on any contact during stimulation, broader-band recording, and retention of raw multichannel waveforms, capabilities exemplified by the target-site waveform capture of the RNS and the artifact-tolerant any-contact sensing of the AlphaDBS .

text: The AlphaDBS System is a fully implantable closed-loop DBS platform that received CE marking for conventional DBS and neural sensing in 2021 . It is being evaluated in a pilot multicenter randomized crossover trial comparing adaptive DBS with conventional DBS in Parkinson’s disease . The system was designed to address two longstanding limitations of earlier bidirectional devices: inadequate artifact rejection during simultaneous sensing and stimulation, and dependence on external processors for execution of the control algorithm . The pulse generator has a volume of 20.96 cm3 and weighs 32.70 g, making it compact relative to many existing rechargeable DBS devices . The system supports 16 independent current-controlled stimulation channels and accepts Medtronic lead extensions . Stimulation is delivered as capacitively coupled, actively charge-balanced asymmetric biphasic pulses, with amplitude from 0 to 5 mA, pulse width from 40 to 250 μs, and frequency from 40 to 200 Hz . The platform can operate in either conventional or adaptive mode . In adaptive mode, stimulation amplitude is adjusted in real time using an embedded proportional feedback algorithm based on subthalamic beta-band local field potential power between 10 and 35 Hz . This proportional control approach builds on earlier clinical demonstrations of beta-driven adaptive stimulation by the same group, including an 8-h adaptive DBS study in Parkinson disease . The algorithm runs entirely on chip and continuously updates output within clinician-defined therapeutic limits . This distinguishes the AlphaDBS from systems in which chronic sensing is available but autonomous control remains more constrained in the commercial configuration . A central technical feature of the AlphaDBS is its stimulation-artifact-management architecture, termed FilterDBS, which derives from earlier work on analog suppression of stimulation artifact in local field potential recordings . Stimulation-artifact suppression occurs at the analog chip level before digitization and does not rely on blanking windows, symmetric electrode constraints, or backend digital filtering . As a result, sensing can be performed on any contact, including contacts actively delivering stimulation . Two differential sensing channels can be multiplexed across any of the eight contacts per lead, with analog-to-digital conversion at 512 Hz . In an initial three-patient pilot cohort, signal quality at the beta peak was high, wireless data loss was low, and no cardiac artifact was reported . Data handling occurs in two modes. In streaming mode, raw local field potentials are transmitted on demand to the physician programmer . In embedded mode, the device logs compressed spectral features to onboard memory, including beta-band power every minute, full spectra from 5 to 35 Hz every 10 min, and stimulation amplitude every 10 min . These data are transferred during recharging and then relayed through a smartphone-based pipeline . The rechargeable battery retains most of its capacity over repeated cycles, and firmware can be updated over the air . Current limitations include a sensing bandwidth that remains optimized for beta-band control rather than for broader high-frequency biomarker exploration and a control law that remains relatively simple . text: The G106RS, developed by Beijing PINS Medical Equipment Co., Ltd., is a rechargeable DBS system with integrated local field potential sensing. The device is designed for bilateral stimulation of deep brain targets in movement disorders and supports both conventional stimulation and sensing-assisted operation . In the English-language peer-reviewed literature the device is characterized primarily within a device-technology review rather than in dedicated primary technical or clinical studies, and published clinical evidence remains limited relative to that for the RNS and Percept PC . The implantable pulse generator measures 55 × 52 × 10 mm and weighs 38 g. Stimulation is voltage controlled, with an output range of 0–10 V, pulse widths of 30–450 μs, and frequencies of 2–250 Hz. The platform has been described as supporting multichannel local field potential acquisition with broader sampling capability than the Percept PC, transmitting up to eight channels of local field potential data at a reported 1000 Hz sampling rate, which is broader than the Percept PC and potentially useful for studying gamma-band and other higher-frequency biomarkers . However, the published evidence base remains nascent, and peer-reviewed technical characterization of artifact rejection, onboard storage, and embedded closed-loop algorithms remains limited. Several device parameters attributed to the manufacturer, including stimulation-off and stimulation-on sampling rates and onboard storage behavior, have not been independently validated in peer-reviewed studies and should be regarded as provisional. For that reason, the G106RS is best viewed as an emerging bidirectional platform with promising sensing capability rather than as a fully characterized clinical standard.

text: Across systems, the largest practical differences arise less from nominal stimulation ranges than from sensing architecture (Table 1). The RNS and AlphaDBS rank highest in contact flexibility and autonomy, but they do so through different design philosophies: the RNS emphasizes target-site waveform capture in epilepsy, whereas the AlphaDBS emphasizes artifact-resistant embedded adaptive control in DBS. The Percept PC is strongest in current-source sophistication and now supports commercially available adaptive operation, but its sensing flexibility and raw-data retention remain more limited. The G106RS appears promising as a broader-band sensing platform, yet many of its core technical characteristics remain insufficiently characterized in peer-reviewed clinical literature. The RNS provides one of the clearest examples of target-site sensing linked directly to responsive stimulation in a commercially deployed device . Two features are especially instructive for adaptive DBS systems: recording from the pathological tissue itself and storing raw waveform data rather than only derived features . The first lesson is the importance of biomarker specificity. In the RNS, stimulation is driven by ictal ECoG patterns recorded from or near the seizure onset zone . This provides a biomarker that is spatially close to the pathological source and often more directly tied to the clinical event than the broader physiological signals used in current DBS systems. That specificity defines the platform’s usefulness as both a therapeutic and observational device . By contrast, most adaptive DBS systems rely on broader biomarkers, particularly beta-band power, recorded under stricter hardware constraints [17,18,, , ]. In the Percept PC, sensing during stimulation requires the recording contacts to flank the stimulating cathode, the sensing bandwidth is limited to 250 Hz, and stored data are derived power envelopes rather than raw local field potential traces . These design choices limit retrospective review of algorithm decisions, reduce flexibility for biomarker discovery, and make it harder to evaluate false positives or missed detections without a device upgrade . For epilepsy specifically, the sensing evidence for these DBS platforms is largely extrapolated from movement disorders; direct epilepsy sensing data are so far limited to thalamic local field potential recordings at network targets such as the anterior and centromedian nuclei, and it is the chronic sensing capability, rather than the stimulation hardware, that most requires epilepsy-specific validation . Stimulation-entrained gamma oscillations have emerged as a promising biomarker for DBS optimization in some patient groups . The 250 Hz sensing ceiling shared by the Percept PC and the RNS limits systematic development of gamma-based control strategies on either platform . Broader-band systems such as the AlphaDBS and G106RS address that limitation in hardware, although clinical validation of gamma-driven adaptive DBS remains early . The RNS also illustrates the value of preserving spatial correspondence between sensing and stimulation. Any of the four contacts per lead can be assigned to sensing or stimulation, and sensing and stimulation can occur on the same contacts . Broader-band systems such as the AlphaDBS and G106RS address that limitation in hardware, although clinical validation of gamma-driven adaptive DBS remains early . The RNS also illustrates the value of preserving spatial correspondence between sensing and stimulation. Any of the four contacts per lead can be assigned to sensing or stimulation, and sensing and stimulation can occur on the same contacts . This requires careful artifact suppression, but it also ensures that the measured biomarker and therapeutic field remain closely aligned . DBS systems that constrain sensing contacts relative to stimulation contacts may sacrifice some of that correspondence . Finally, the RNS highlights the importance of algorithm transparency. Although its storage is limited to detected-event segments rather than continuous recordings, it still preserves raw waveforms that allow clinicians to inspect what the device actually recorded at the time of stimulation . Future closed-loop systems would benefit from extending this principle toward more continuous raw-signal storage. Without waveform-level review, retrospective validation of device behavior remains incomplete . DBS platforms offer several engineering advances that could inform future development of the RNS. One is lead design. Standard NeuroPace depth and cortical strip leads contain four cylindrical contacts and no directional capability . By contrast, DBS has progressively moved toward eight-contact leads, including segmented directional electrodes that enable current steering and more selective shaping of the electric field [, , , , , ]. Incorporating a higher number of contacts or directional designs into responsive epilepsy stimulation could improve both recording specificity and stimulation precision, to the extent that knowledge about anatomical target engagement continues to improve [, , , , , ]. A second lesson is current-source architecture. Contemporary DBS platforms such as the Percept PC and AlphaDBS provide independent current-controlled outputs across contacts . The RNS uses a single current source, so current divides passively across parallel cathodes according to impedance . Independent per-contact current control would allow more precise field shaping and could support more flexible adaptive stimulation strategies . DBS programming has also developed more formal approaches for estimating the volume of tissue activated by combining lead geometry, anatomy, and stimulation settings . RNS programming remains more empirical and is often guided by detected event rates and patient-reported outcomes . As understanding of circuit-level targets in epilepsy improves, volume-of-tissue-activated-informed programming may help make responsive stimulation more systematic and less resource intensive . On data management, DBS platforms have often offered longer trend storage than the RNS, but storage quantity is less important than storage content. The RNS stores raw ECoG snippets, which are often more informative than longer archives of narrow-band power alone . An ideal future design would combine the strengths of both approaches by supporting broader longitudinal storage while preserving raw multichannel waveform data .

text: Optimizing device settings in DBS and RNS remains one of the most resource-intensive aspects of closed-loop neuromodulation [3,16,, , ]. Establishing stable settings often requires repeated programming visits over several months . Even for a standard four-contact lead, the number of possible contact configurations is large, and each can be combined with many amplitudes, pulse widths, and frequency settings . The parameter space expands further with eight-contact leads, directional electrodes, independent current sources, and adaptive control features [17,, , , , , ,82]. Manual exploration of this space is inherently limited [16,, , ]. The principal clinical risks of suboptimal programming are under-stimulation, which leaves the intended target insufficiently modulated, and over-stimulation, which spreads current into neighboring structures and produces cognitive, psychiatric, or motor side effects . Current strategies to reduce these risks include volume-of-tissue-activated modeling, local field potential-guided contact selection, and iterative adjustment based on clinical assessment and patient-reported outcomes . Closed-loop systems reduce part of this burden by linking stimulation to a physiological signal, but they also introduce new optimization challenges. Detection thresholds, control laws, biomarker definitions, and stimulation bounds all require initial configuration and ongoing revision . Experience with the RNS suggests that continued refinement of detection settings can yield meaningful clinical benefit even years after implantation . Analogous long-term refinement is likely to play a central role in adaptive DBS as chronic sensing and algorithm design continue to improve .

text: Several converging technical and biological challenges are likely to shape the next generation of closed-loop neuromodulation. The first is biomarker validation. Closed-loop control is only as reliable as the electrophysiological signal on which it depends, and in epilepsy the biomarkers used to drive therapy remain incompletely validated. Chronic ambulatory recordings have shown that interictal epileptiform activity, detection surrogates such as line length and bandpass spectral power, and circadian and multiday cycles of seizure risk can be tracked over years, but their specificity for the ictal state and their stability across sleep, medication changes, and behavioral state are still being defined . Device-derived detection counts are deliberately biased toward high sensitivity and often correlate only weakly with independently verified seizures, which complicates their use as endpoints; analyses linking chronic responsive-stimulation neurophysiology to seizure control illustrate both the promise and the present limits of epilepsy biomarkers for guiding therapy . Establishing markers that are measurable over time, specific to the clinical state of interest, and robust to physiological confounding therefore remains a central prerequisite for reliable closed-loop control in epilepsy . The second is sensing bandwidth. The 250 Hz ceiling shared by the RNS and Percept PC is adequate for current dominant biomarkers but restricts systematic study of higher-frequency signals, including gamma activity and stimulation-entrained oscillations . Platforms with broader bandwidth, including the G106RS and, to a lesser extent, the AlphaDBS, may be better suited for evaluating next-generation biomarkers . Future epilepsy systems would also benefit from supporting four simultaneously active leads rather than two, which would better enable network-level circuit assessment and therapy across bilateral cortical and thalamic nodes by allowing seizure onset, propagation, and control sites to be sampled and modulated in parallel . The third is onboard computation. Current implantable algorithms remain deliberately simple, typically threshold detectors or proportional feedback controllers, because of constraints in power consumption, memory, and timing . As implantable processing improves, more complex classifiers, multifeature detection systems, and model-based control strategies may become feasible. Progress in this area will depend not only on hardware advances but also on a better mechanistic understanding of how neural signals and stimulation parameters map to clinical state . A fourth challenge is circuit-level biology. The progressive improvement observed with long-term brain-responsive neurostimulation suggests that chronic stimulation may drive functional reorganization of epileptic networks over time . Longitudinal analyses support this view: chronic responsive neurostimulation is associated with progressive, treatment-related changes in network excitability and interictal activity that accrue over months to years and track with clinical improvement . The cellular and network mechanisms underlying this reorganization remain incompletely understood, and better mechanistic insight could help guide stimulation paradigms toward more durable therapeutic effects . Emerging investigational platforms also point toward a broader future for closed-loop neuromodulation in epilepsy. In the United Kingdom, the Picostim-DyNeuMo platform is now being evaluated in the Children’s Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation for Epilepsy Trial (CADET) Pilot for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, highlighting interest in cranially mounted adaptive stimulation for severe pediatric generalized epilepsies . Closed-loop neuromodulation has advanced from experimental concept to established clinical practice in selected disorders . The systems reviewed here reflect different engineering priorities (Fig. 2A). The RNS emphasizes target-site sensing and waveform-level transparency in epilepsy . The Percept PC combines chronic sensing with flexible current steering across a broad DBS indication base . The G106RS offers broader-band sensing within a still-limited published literature. The AlphaDBS demonstrates that simultaneous sensing, stimulation, and embedded adaptive control can be integrated within a compact implantable platform . Across devices, the most important differences arise less from nominal stimulation parameter ranges than from sensing architecture. Contact flexibility, artifact suppression, bandwidth, and the nature of stored data all shape what biomarkers can be used, how algorithms can be refined, and how transparently device behavior can be reviewed over time . Devices that can record from clinically relevant contacts during stimulation, across a broad frequency range, while preserving raw waveform information are likely to provide the strongest foundation for future adaptive therapy . Further progress will require better biomarkers, broader and cleaner sensing, more capable onboard computation, and a deeper mechanistic understanding of how chronic stimulation reshapes neural circuits . Open-loop and network-targeted strategies will remain important, especially in generalized or multifocal disorders, but the broader direction of the field points toward systems that measure brain state continuously and adjust therapy accordingly . As that transition continues, the boundary between epilepsy neurostimulation and adaptive DBS is likely to become increasingly porous .

text: Epilepsy is one of the most prevalent neurological disorders, affecting 50 million people worldwide. Genetic studies have identified over 1,000 genes that cause monogenic epilepsies (1), enabling a diagnosis for 30%–50% of individuals with epilepsy (2–5). Hence, more than 50% of individuals with a presumed genetic cause of epilepsy are awaiting a genetic diagnosis (5, 6). This diagnostic gap is unlikely to be resolved solely by improving the detection and interpretation of variants on the basis of monogenic inheritance (7, 8). It is likely that combinations of some variants in specific genes play an important role in undiagnosed epilepsies. In addition, antiepileptic drugs are ineffective in more than 30% of individuals with epilepsy (9). This underscores the need to dissect the underlying molecular mechanisms to improve diagnostics and therapeutic interventions. One of the main factors that limits our understanding of epilepsy at a mechanistic level is the involvement of numerous genes. Although ion channels and synaptic proteins that directly regulate neuronal activity are key contributors, the mechanisms underlying numerous epilepsy-associated genes remain poorly understood. Elucidating the molecular pathways responsible for these disorders and establishing the pathogenicity of variants in these genes will improve diagnosis and treatment for many unsolved and/or refractory cases. Among the molecular pathways that remain poorly understood in epilepsy, actin dynamics have emerged as a potential contributor, and increasing evidence shows that variants in actin regulatory genes are associated with seizures (10, 11). Actin dynamics are essential for numerous cellular functions, including neuronal activity (10, 11). Actin dynamics involve the conversion of globular actin (G-actin) to filamentous actin (F-actin) or the reverse process, and it is tightly regulated by Rho GTPases. Plasma membrane receptors respond to extracellular signals to modulate the activity of Rho GTPases through the activation of Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) (12). This GEF-GTPase activation promotes actin dynamics together with actin-binding proteins (12), which can either increase or reduce actin polymerization (13, 14). An important GEF in the CNS is TIAM Rac1 associated GEF 1 (TIAM1). TIAM1 is highly enriched in neurons, where it regulates actin dynamics by activating Rac GTPase activity (15, 16). Notably, we recently showed that biallelic loss-of-function (LoF) variants in TIAM1 cause developmental epilepsy (16). To investigate whether and how disruption of actin dynamics causes seizures, we utilized fly and human cell models for TIAM1-associated disease. We discovered an “actin/mitochondria/glutamate (AMG) pathway,” wherein actin polymerization defects lead to increased mitochondrial fission in glutamatergic neurons. This is associated with elevated ROS production. These defects lead to increased glutamatergic transmission and can be suppressed by inhibiting mitochondrial fission with mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) or by reducing ROS with N-acetyl-l-cysteine amide (NACA). We also assessed whether other epilepsy-associated genes affecting this pathway may have similar effects. Interestingly, many transheterozygous mutant combinations of genes that affect the AMG pathway exhibit synergistic or additive effects leading to obvious seizures in flies, suggesting that digenic variants in the AMG pathway genes can combine to cause seizures. text: By querying the literature (1, 17) and the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database (18), we identified approximately 50 human genes that are involved in actin regulation and epilepsy among approximately 1,000 genes associated with epilepsy (Supplemental Figure 1A and Supplemental Table 1; supplemental material available online with this article; https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI198696DS1). Many of these correspond to downstream effectors of Rho GEFs and actin-binding proteins. Flies can be used to study the mechanisms underlying epilepsy. Mutations in fly orthologs of human genes that are associated with seizures often cause behavioral phenotypes consistent with human seizures, including mechanical stress–induced hyperactivation and paralysis (bang sensitivity) and/or heat stress–induced seizures and paralysis (heat sensitivity) (19–21). This hyperactivation of neurons has been confirmed, using electrophysiological studies, in some fly mutants that have seizures (22, 23). Furthermore, antiepileptic drugs used in humans often ameliorate these seizure-like phenotypes in flies (24–26). We previously identified individuals with variants in TIAM1 who exhibited developmental delay and epilepsy (16) and showed that lack of sif (still life, the fly TIAM1 ortholog) in neurons leads to seizure-like phenotypes, including bang and heat sensitivity (16). Since TIAM1 plays an important role in actin dynamics (15, 27) (Supplemental Figure 1B), we explored the phenotypes associated with loss of sif in fly neurons. We validated the notion that ubiquitous expression of a UAS-sif RNA interference (RNAi) (~88% knockdown efficiency) can induce severe phenotypes (Figure 1, A–C) that are very similar to those observed in sif-mutant animals (16). We next determined which neuronal cell populations require sif by selectively inducing expression of the UAS-sif RNAi in specific neuronal cell subtypes using established Galactose-responsive transcription factor (GAL4) drivers (Table 1). Interestingly, the sif RNAi in cholinergic neurons caused the most severe climbing defects (Figure 1A). However, sif RNAi in glutamatergic neurons caused the most severe bang sensitivity and heat sensitivity, but milder climbing defects when compared with the cholinergic sif RNAi (Figure 1, A–C). In contrast, knockdown of sif in either GABAergic neurons or dopaminergic neurons did not induce these phenotypes. These data indicate that sif was required in glutamatergic neurons and cholinergic neurons for proper neuronal activity. Given that glutamatergic and cholinergic transmissions can be excitatory in both humans and Drosophila, whereas GABAergic transmission is primarily inhibitory (28, 29), the above observations indicate that sif loss may lead to an increase in excitatory synaptic transmission. Since glutamatergic sif RNAi causes the most severe seizure-like phenotypes, we further assessed the sensitivity of glutamatergic neurons to sif loss. We first considered whether loss of sif could genetically interact with genes required in the glutamatergic network — Eaat2 and Nmdar1 (Figure 1D). Loss of EAAT2, a glutamate transporter that is required for glutamate clearance, causes developmental epilepsy due to an accumulation of glutamate in the synaptic cleft (30). Interestingly, transheterozygous (GeneALoF/+ GeneBLoF/+) flies carrying 1 copy of a strong LoF allele for sif and Eaat2 exhibit more severe bang sensitivity when compared with the single heterozygous flies (Figure 1E, detailed genotypes are provided in Supplemental Table 2).

text: To assess whether the activity of glutamatergic neurons is increased upon sif loss, we generated VGlut-GAL4>CaLexA flies. CaLexA induces a calcium-dependent nuclear import of LexA, which is stimulated by Ca2+-regulated dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) (32). It includes 2 components: UAS-mLexA-VP16-NFAT and lexAop-rCD2-GFP. In the presence of VGlut-GAL4 and increased Ca2+ activities, GFP will be expressed and localized to the membrane of glutamatergic neurons. As a result, sif RNAi flies showed a significant increase in GFP intensity in the CNS, including the brain lobes and the ventral nerve cord (VNC), when compared with the control RNAi (Supplemental Figure 2, A and B). These data indicate that sif loss in glutamatergic neurons led to increased neuronal activity. Given that synaptic transmission at the fly neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is mediated by glutamate and an increase in synaptic transmission at larval NMJs has previously been shown to cause crawling defects (22, 23, 33), we evaluated crawling behavior of sif-mutant larvae. Control third instar larvae crawled approximately 3 cm in a minute (Figure 2A). In contrast, sif-mutant third instar larvae only crawled approximately 0.8 cm in a minute. The sifT2A-GAL4 is a severe LoF allele (16) and produces GAL4 under the endogenous sif regulatory elements, which allows expression of the UAS cDNA in the proper spatial and temporal pattern of sif to assess the rescue effect (16). We observed that the crawling defects were fully rescued by expressing WT sif cDNA in the mutant background (Figure 2A, sif rescue), demonstrating that this phenotype was due to sif loss. These data suggest a defect in either muscle function, synaptic transmission, or both during larval development. To determine if there are morphological defects at the larval NMJ, we stained the NMJs with HRP, a neuronal membrane marker (34), and syt EGFP, a synaptic vesicle marker (35). We did not observe obvious changes in fluorescence of HRP or syt EGFP when compared with controls (Supplemental Figure 3, A–E). Hence, sif did not obviously affect the neuronal morphology or distribution of synaptic vesicles in third instar larvae. To assess the electrophysiological properties of NMJs, we performed intracellular recordings of third instar muscles. Consistent with a previous study (36), we did not observe obvious differences in the average amplitude and frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic potentials (mEPSPs) in sif mutants when the axons were severed (Supplemental Figure 4, A–C). We therefore recorded without severing the axons of glutamatergic motor neurons from the CNS. In control animals, approximately 30% of the muscles showed patterned EPSPs in a 2-minute recording period (Figure 2, B and C). These periodic contractions were induced by the CNS pattern generator, which drives muscle contractions (37, 38). In contrast, 80% of the sif-mutant larvae exhibited large, nonperiodic bursts of EPSPs in a 2-minute recording (Figure 2, B and C). Hence, the frequency and amplitude of EPSPs were significantly increased in sif-mutant muscles when compared with controls (Figure 2, D–G). In control animals, approximately 30% of the muscles showed patterned EPSPs in a 2-minute recording period (Figure 2, B and C). These periodic contractions were induced by the CNS pattern generator, which drives muscle contractions (37, 38). In contrast, 80% of the sif-mutant larvae exhibited large, nonperiodic bursts of EPSPs in a 2-minute recording (Figure 2, B and C). Hence, the frequency and amplitude of EPSPs were significantly increased in sif-mutant muscles when compared with controls (Figure 2, D–G). Note that the increase in glutamatergic transmission was significantly rescued by expression of sif cDNA (Figure 2, D–G). In summary, our data indicate that loss of sif increased glutamatergic transmission without altering NMJ morphology.

text: To determine whether the seizure-like phenotypes of sif mutants are due to a disruption in actin dynamics, we assessed dominant interactions between sif and other actin regulatory genes. As a GEF, TIAM1/Sif regulates actin remodeling by activating the Rho GTPase RAC1. The downstream effectors of Rho GTPases regulate actin filaments together with the actin-binding proteins that promote actin polymerization, including profilin (fly Chickadee, Chic) and actin related protein 2/3 complex (ARP2/3) (Figure 3A). We assessed chic01320/+ (a LoF allele) flies and observed that they had mild bang sensitivity, whereas Arp3EP3640/+ (a LoF allele) single-heterozygous flies did not show obvious bang sensitivity (Figure 3B). However, transheterozygous animals that carried a single LoF allele of sif and chic exhibited a severe bang-sensitive phenotype (Figure 3B). Similarly, sif and Arp3 transheterozygous flies were also bang sensitive (Figure 3B). These phenotypes were also observed using another LoF of the chic221 allele and the Arp3515FC allele (Supplemental Figure 5A). We also tested cofilin (fly Twinstar, Tsr), a protein that disassembles actin filaments (13) (Figure 3A). Neither tsrT2A-GAL4/+ (a LoF allele) flies nor the sifT2A-GAL4/+ tsrT2A-GAL4/+ transheterozygous flies displayed obvious bang sensitivity (Figure 3B). These data indicate that the loss of sif affected bang sensitivity by reducing actin polymerization and that other proteins required for proper actin polymerization also play a critical role in seizures. We next aimed to visualize the defects in actin filaments in neurons using an established reporter, Lifeact-RFP (39, 40). Lifeact is a 17 amino acid peptide that binds to 2 consecutive actin subunits on the F-actin filament in cells and tissues (40), and its intensity is proportional to the amount and length of F-actin present (41). Knockdown of sif in motor neurons leads to an accumulation of small “actin patches” in cell bodies. These resemble actin patches in yeast (42) and correspond to short actin filaments. Interestingly, we also observed this phenotype when we knocked down chic (Figure 3, C and D). Since profilin (Chic) is known to promote actin polymerization, these actin patches likely reflect a reduction in actin polymerization levels. Hence, these data provide compelling evidence that loss of sif affects actin polymerization as previously shown in mammalian cells (27).
section: Sif loss promotes seizures by affecting actin polymerization.

text: Numerous genes encoding proteins that regulate actin dynamics are associated with developmental epilepsy. GEF proteins regulate the actin cytoskeleton by activating Rho GTPases like RAC1 and RAC3, and variants in these genes have been associated with seizures in humans (43, 44). In addition, although mice that lack Rac1 or Rac3 do not exhibit seizures, double-homozygous-KO mice exhibit spontaneous seizures (45). We therefore performed genetic interaction studies using 2 fly Rac alleles: Rac1J11 (a LoF allele) and Rac2KG05681 (a LoF allele), and 1 LoF chic allele. Both Rac1J11 and Rac2KG05681 synergized with chic01320, and the transheterozygous flies were bang sensitive (Supplemental Figure 5B, Supplemental Video 1). These data are consistent with seizures resulting from a disruption to a GEF/RAC GTPase pathway that reduces actin polymerization. We next assessed whether loss of 1 copy of 2 different genes that promote actin polymerization can similarly affect seizure sensitivity. WASHC4 (fly SWIP) encodes a subunit of the WASH complex that promotes actin polymerization (46), and FLNA (fly cher) encodes an actin cross-linking protein filamin A, which stabilizes polymerized actin filaments (Figure 3A). Pathogenic LoF variants in both WASHC4 and FLNA have been associated with seizures in humans (1, 46, 47). Both SWIPCR70302/+ chic01320/+ and cherMiMIC/+ chic01320/+ flies exhibit increased bang sensitivity when compared with chic01320/+ flies (Supplemental Figure 5B and Supplemental Videos 2 and 3). In contrast, single-heterozygous loss of SWIP or cher alone does not cause obvious bang sensitivity. These data further indicate that disruptions in actin polymerization are associated with increased bang sensitivity and that digenic loss of genes regulating actin polymerization increases seizure susceptibility. To determine if the actin regulatory proteins cause seizures by affecting glutamatergic transmission, similar to loss of TIAM1/sif, we performed genetic interaction studies with genes encoding proteins that are known to affect glutamate uptake at the fly NMJs. The previously tested mutations — Rac1J11, Rac2KG05681b, SWIPCR70302, and cherMIMIC alleles — all caused an obvious increase in bang sensitivity when combined with a single Eaat2T2A-GAL4 LoF allele (Supplemental Figure 5C). Together, these data provide evidence that seizures can be caused by reduced actin polymerization levels in glutamatergic neurons.
section: Actin polymerization defects promote seizures in flies.
