text: an earlier published case, vinpocetine was used in an 8‐year‐old boy with a GABRG2 (c.254 T > A p.[Ile85Lys]); however, functional characterization of this variant was not performed at the time. 15 Subsequent functional analysis demonstrated that this variant did not impair receptor function, 7 suggesting this variant may not be the cause of the epilepsy. Other randomized, blinded, or open‐label studies have evaluated vinpocetine as adjunctive therapy in unselected epilepsy cohorts to decrease seizure frequency 9 , 11 or improve cognitive outcomes. 12 Although a decreased frequency of generalized tonic–clonic seizures was reported after vinpocetine, no significant increase in cognitive abilities was observed. In unselected epilepsy cohorts lacking functionally confirmed GABAA receptor LoF variants, vinpocetine did not improve neuropsychiatric comorbidities or cognitive function. 9 , 12 Broader clinical benefits beyond seizure reduction thus appear more likely when vinpocetine is administered to patients with a verified LoF GABAA receptor variant. The included patients harbored variants in genes encoding GABAA receptors. Two patients (#3, #8) carried paralogous variants (GABRB3 p.[Tyr302Cys] and GABRB2 p.[Tyr301Cys]), which showed a two‐ to threefold reduction in vinpocetine potency compared to WT receptors. Both variants decreased the maximum GABA‐evoked current caused by a reduction in GABA maximum open probability; thus, GABA alone was unable to elicit maximal receptor response even at high concentrations. Despite reduced potencies, vinpocetine enhanced the functional response of these two variant receptors. When coapplied with GABA, vinpocetine increased the inhibitory current beyond that achievable with GABA alone, this increase in modulatory efficacies compensate for its reduced potencies. The pharmacological profile of vinpocetine on these two paralogous variants may account for the favorable response observed. In our cohort, two patients (#2, #4) carried the same variant (GABRA1, p.[Gly251Asp]). One improved in adaptive behavior and executive function, whereas the other discontinued vinpocetine due to AEs. Several factors may influence the response to vinpocetine, including concomitant medications and bioavailability, which may be 60%–100% higher when taken with food. 22 Thus, interpersonal differences make it difficult to predict the outcome. The study has limitations. Data were collected retrospectively, and neither patients nor caregivers were blinded to the intervention. A randomized, placebo‐controlled clinical trial is necessary to confirm the results. The sample was small, which did not allow calculation of significance. Additionally, patients treated abroad obtained vinpocetine from nutritional supplement shops, introducing potential issues with the quality and dosages used. Adherence to this supplementary treatment was assumed to be constant, as caregivers were responsible for the medication.

text: This retrospective observational study presents comprehensive data on patients with GABAA receptor LoF variants treated with vinpocetine as a precision medicine. The findings suggest that vinpocetine can reduce seizure frequency, improve SWI, and enhance nonseizure outcome measures. Electrophysiological data support that vinpocetine can restore function in patients with GABAA receptor LoF variants, indicating a potential compensatory mechanism. However, variability in dosing and product quality in patients treated abroad highlights the need to standardize preparations. Our results support that vinpocetine may be a promising targeted therapy for patients with GABAA receptor LoF variants, especially when treatment is individualized and closely monitored. Controlled clinical trials are needed to validate these findings and establish optimal treatment protocols.

text: Epilepsy is a disorder with multiple etiologies, including genetic and structural causes, that affects more than 50 million people worldwide. 1 Among these, focal seizures are the most common type, accounting for 61% of all epilepsy patients. 2 Antiseizure medications (ASMs) represent the mainstay of treatment, with approximately two thirds of patients achieving long‐term remission after ASM initiation, whereas one third progress to drug‐resistant epilepsy (DRE). 3 , 4 The course of epilepsy is dynamically variable, with seizure control status influenced by time, therapeutic interventions, and baseline characteristics; some patients may even alternate between drug‐responsive and drug‐resistant states. 5 Prolonged follow‐up periods are therefore critical for distinguishing persistent remission from unstable fluctuating disease courses. 6 , 7 Clarifying the factors affecting long‐term prognosis and developing targeted interventions is thus of great significance for optimizing clinical epilepsy management. Previous studies have identified multiple independent prognostic predictors for epilepsy, including abnormal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, epileptiform electroencephalographic (EEG) discharges, and other clinical factors. 8 , 9 , 10 In recent years, the impact of sleep‐related factors on epilepsy prognosis has gradually gained attention, but existing research has mostly been limited to early outcomes or first seizures. 11 , 12 No study has systematically explored the associations between baseline seizure timing and drug responsiveness. Given the complex interaction between sleep and epilepsy, this prospective cohort study aimed to determine the long‐term prognosis of newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients receiving standardized ASM therapy, and to clarify whether baseline seizure timing serves as an independent prognostic factor for this population.

text: Starting from September 2015, we consecutively recruited newly diagnosed patients with focal epilepsy from the specialized epilepsy clinic of the Department of Neurology in our hospital and conducted prospective follow‐up for the enrolled patients. Inclusion criteria included the following: (1) a definite diagnosis of focal epilepsy made by neurologists in accordance with the diagnostic and classification criteria for epilepsy issued by the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) in 2017 13 ; for patients enrolled prior to the release of these criteria, retrospective reclassification was conducted based on their complete preserved medical records to ensure uniform diagnostic standards; and (2) no prior treatment with any ASMs. Exclusion criteria included the following: (1) symptomatic epilepsy caused by active or progressive central nervous system (CNS) diseases; specific etiologies included active CNS infections, progressive CNS neoplasms, active autoimmune or inflammatory diseases (e.g., acute phase of anti‐N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate receptor encephalitis, active multiple sclerosis), progressive neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer disease, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy), and acute phase cerebral injuries; (2) comorbidity with severe and unstable systemic diseases (e.g., severe heart, liver, or renal failure); (3) active mental disorders, referring primarily to psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, acute phase of bipolar affective disorder) or mental status accompanied by severe behavioral disturbances; and (4) patients judged by investigators to be unable to cooperate with long‐term follow‐up or neurological function assessment; the operational definition was an inability to comprehend medical advice or maintain a continuous and accurate seizure log. It should be specifically noted that patients with mild to moderate cognitive impairment were included if they had reliable caregivers who could ensure medication adherence and assist with seizure documentation. To evaluate the long‐term prognosis of newly diagnosed patients with focal epilepsy, only those with a follow‐up duration of 36 months were included in this analysis.

text: For baseline data collection, clinical baseline data were systematically collected via a standardized form prior to ASM initiation. This comprehensive assessment recorded the following: demographic data (gender, age at onset, age at treatment initiation), past and personal history (perinatal and birth history, history of febrile seizures, family history of epilepsy), epileptic seizure characteristics (seizure type, aura, seizure timing, history of cluster seizures, history of status epilepticus, and pretreatment seizure burden), comorbidities and accompanying symptoms (headache, sleep problems), and auxiliary examination results (EEG, brain MRI appearance, etc.). For follow‐up and outcome monitoring, after enrollment, patients were followed up every 3–6 months, and the ASM treatment regimen was adjusted in a timely manner according to the patients' epileptic seizure status and adverse drug reactions. All patients were required to complete a follow‐up record form during each follow‐up, which detailed the seizure frequency during the follow‐up period, ASM type, adverse drug reactions, and other relevant information. For patients who were unable to attend in‐person outpatient visits, telephone follow‐up was adopted to inquire about the relevant situation from the patients themselves or their family members and complete the follow‐up records.

text: Seizure freedom was defined as being seizure‐free for at least 12 months, or for 3 times the longest pretreatment seizure‐free interval (whichever was longer). If no preexisting pretreatment seizure‐free interval was available, 12 months was set as the minimum duration for seizure freedom. Time to seizure freedom was measured as the interval from medication initiation to the point of attaining seizure freedom. Seizure relapse was defined as the recurrence of epileptic seizures in patients after they had achieved seizure freedom. Time to relapse refers to the time interval from the first achievement of seizure freedom to the first relapse. Immediate responders refers to patients who remained seizure‐free from the initiation of treatment and subsequently met the 12‐month or threefold pretreatment interval criteria at their earliest possible assessment milestone. Sustained seizure freedom refers to patients who did not relapse from treatment initiation through the entire follow‐up period. Drug‐responsive epilepsy refers to achieving seizure freedom after receiving appropriate (medication must be suitable for the patient's seizure type) and adequate (each ASM administered at 50% of the defined daily dose for a sufficiently long duration 14 ) ASM monotherapy or combination therapy. DRE refers to failure to achieve seizure freedom after receiving two or more appropriate and adequate ASM regimens. Undetermined prognosis refers to an intermediate clinical state at the end of follow‐up that could be classified as neither drug‐responsive nor DRE. The specific diagnostic criteria were as follows: insufficient observation duration: patients had achieved a period of seizure freedom at the last follow‐up, but the duration failed to reach 12 months or 3 times the longest pretreatment interictal interval; insufficient ASM exposure: patients experienced treatment failure with only the first appropriate ASM regimen and had not completed the evaluation of a second appropriate and adequate ASM regimen, thus not meeting the diagnostic criteria for DRE by definition; fluctuating treatment response: patients had achieved seizure freedom during follow‐up but relapsed before the final assessment (1–2 spontaneous seizures with regular medication adherence). 15 For cluster seizures, there is currently no standardized definition in epilepsy. The definition adopted in this study is “two or more epileptic seizures occurring within a 24‐h period.” 16 Treatment delay was defined as the time interval from the first occurrence of epileptic seizures to a confirmed diagnosis and the initiation of standardized treatment. Regarding seizure types, according to the 2017 ILAE Classification of Epileptic Seizures 13 and reflecting prognostic significance, patients were categorized hierarchically based on the most severe seizure type experienced: (1) focal to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures (FBTCS), (2) focal impaired awareness seizures (FIAS), and (3) focal aware seizures (FAS). For patients with multiple seizure types, the highest severity category (FBTCS > FIAS > FAS) was assigned for analysis. For patients with multiple seizure types, the highest severity category (FBTCS > FIAS > FAS) was assigned for analysis. Regarding seizure timing, according to the timing of epileptic seizures before treatment, patients were divided into two categories: (1) sleep‐exclusive seizures: epileptic seizures occurred only during sleep, with no seizure records during wakefulness; and (2) wake‐related seizures: epileptic seizures were not limited to sleep, including two scenarios: seizures occurring both during sleep and wakefulness, or seizures occurring only during wakefulness with no records of sleep‐period seizures. Sleep problems refers to persistent sleep abnormalities self‐reported by patients during the enrollment interview, including sleep onset disorder, sleep maintenance disorder, early awakening, poor sleep quality, and lack of restorative feeling after morning awakening.

text: Statistical analysis of the data was performed using the statistical software SPSS version 26.0. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to verify whether the measurement data conformed to a normal distribution. Measurement data with normal distribution were expressed as mean ± SD, whereas those with nonnormal distribution were presented as median (interquartile range [IQR]). Categorical variables were described as frequency (percentage). Kaplan–Meier method was used to generate survival curves for evaluating the incidence of DRE, the probability of achieving the first episode of seizure freedom, and the probability of seizure relapse. The log‐rank test was applied for intergroup comparisons. To evaluate potential selection bias, the chi‐squared test or Fisher exact test was used to compare the categorical variables of baseline information between the included analysis group and the excluded group, as well as between the determined prognosis group and undetermined prognosis group. The Mann–Whitney U‐test was employed for the comparison of continuous variables. A Cox proportional hazards regression model was used to analyze the effects of baseline factors on drug responsiveness. To identify relevant independent influencing factors, variables with statistical significance in univariate analysis were included in the multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression model for further analysis and forcibly adjusted for baseline characteristics that showed significant differences between the determined and undetermined groups (e.g., treatment delay and febrile seizures) as covariates to mitigate potential attrition bias. Finally, a sensitivity analysis was performed by including the undetermined group in the comparator (n = 563) to test the robustness of the findings under the conservative “worst‐case” assumption that all undetermined cases remained non‐DRE. The results were presented as hazard ratios (HRs) with their corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI). All results were considered statistically significant when p < .05.

text: The participant recruitment and exclusion process is illustrated in Figure 1. From September 2015 to September 2025, a total of 1147 patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy were screened; 296 patients were ineligible, and 68 did not provide informed consent. Finally, a total of 783 newly diagnosed patients with focal epilepsy were recruited in this study, including 446 male patients (57.0%), and the median follow‐up duration was 36.0 (IQR = 20.0–64.0) months. The median age at epilepsy onset was 26.0 (IQR = 16.0–46.0) years, and the median age at treatment initiation was 29.0 (IQR = 18.0–48.0) years. Among them, 28.1% (220/783) were excluded from the primary analytical cohort. Of these excluded patients, 28.2% (62/220) were excluded due to loss to follow‐up and 71.8% (158/220) were excluded owing to insufficient follow‐up duration. There were no statistically significant differences in baseline characteristics such as demographic data and clinical features between patients included in the analysis and those excluded (all p > .05; Table S1). A total of 563 patients completed at least 36 months of follow‐up and were included in the long‐term prognosis analysis (Table 1), with a median follow‐up duration of 48.0 (IQR = 36.0–78.0) months. According to the pretreatment seizure interval, 73.4% (413/563) required at least 12 months of seizure freedom to be judged as achieving seizure freedom, and 26.6% (150/563) required more than 12 months (three times their longest pretreatment interseizure interval).

Among these initial responders, 53.2% (194/365) were immediate responders who attained seizure freedom at the earliest assessment milestone. Notably, 33.4% (122/365) exhibited sustained seizure freedom from treatment initiation (Table S2).

text: A Sankey diagram illustrates the dynamic clinical course during treatment in Figure 3. Among the 365 patients who achieved seizure freedom, 64.1% (234/365) did not experience seizure relapse after achieving seizure freedom (including five late‐responders who initially met drug‐resistant criteria before reaching seizure freedom). Conversely, 35.9% (131/365) experienced at least one seizure relapse following their initial period of freedom (Figure 2B). The outcomes for patients with relapse were heterogeneous; 36.6% (48/131) regained seizure freedom during subsequent treatment and were reclassified as drug‐responsive epilepsy; 31.3% (41/131) developed drug resistance and were categorized as DRE, although four of these individuals subsequently achieved terminal seizure freedom; and 32.1% (42/131) had an undetermined prognosis.

text: During the study period, a total of 25.4% (143/563) developed drug resistance at some point in their clinical course (Figure 2C), although 6.3% (9/143) achieved seizure freedom in subsequent treatment. Because the proportion of DRE patients in this cohort was less than 50%, it was impossible to estimate the median time to DRE onset. At the end of follow‐up, 50.8% (286/563) were identified as having drug‐responsive epilepsy, 23.8% (134/563) were diagnosed with DRE, and 25.4% (143/563) were classified as having undetermined prognosis (Figure 3). Among patients with drug‐responsive epilepsy, 63.6% (182/286) achieved seizure freedom with monotherapy, 25.2% (72/286) reached seizure freedom with two ASMs, and 11.2% (32/286) attained seizure freedom with three or more ASMs. Among patients with undetermined prognosis, 95.8% (137/143) had only received one adequate course of ASM treatment; 4.2% (6/143) had a long maximum seizure‐free interval before treatment, making it impossible to determine their drug responsiveness at the end of follow‐up.

text: Among the 420 patients with determined prognosis, comparative analysis was conducted between 143 patients who developed DRE during treatment and 277 patients with purely drug‐responsive epilepsy; univariate analysis revealed that baseline factors including pretreatment seizure burden, seizure timing, history of cluster seizures, history of status epilepticus, brain MRI findings, and sleep problems were potentially associated with the development of drug resistance (p < .05; Table S4). Multivariate analysis was additionally adjusted by forcibly incorporating the imbalanced variables between the determined prognosis group and undetermined prognosis group (treatment delay and febrile seizures; Table S3). Multivariate analysis revealed that patients with wake‐related seizures had a 1.743‐fold risk of developing DRE compared with those with sleep‐exclusive seizures (95% CI = 1.101–2.760, p = .018; Figure 4); patients with a history of cluster seizures had a 2.630‐fold risk relative to those without such a history (95% CI = 1.845–3.749, p < .001), patients with a history of status epilepticus had a 2.126‐fold risk compared with those without such a history (95% CI = 1.394–3.242, p < .001), and patients with sleep problems had a 1.740‐fold risk relative to those without sleep problems (95% CI = 1.178–2.572, p = .005; Figure 5). To validate the robustness of our findings, we performed a sensitivity analysis (Table S5). All 143 patients with undetermined prognosis were assigned to the non‐drug‐resistant group, with the same covariates as the main analysis (Figure S1). The results confirmed that the risk effects of the core predictors were highly consistent; the HR for seizure timing (HR = 1.764, p = .015) was nearly identical to that in the main analysis (HR = 1.743, p = .018). In addition, a history of cluster seizures, a history of status epilepticus, and sleep problems all maintained significant statistical associations (p < .05), with effect directions consistent with the main analysis. Notably, abnormal brain MRI reached statistical significance in the sensitivity analysis model (HR = 1.484, p = .029), whereas it showed marginal significance in the main analysis (HR = 1.420, p = .054).

text: At the end of follow‐up, 50.8% of patients were drug‐responsive, 23.8% had DRE, and 25.4% had undetermined prognosis. Of drug‐responsive patients, 63.6% achieved seizure freedom with monotherapy, 25.2% with two ASMs, and 11.2% with three or more ASMs. Among patients with a determined prognosis, approximately one third (134/420) developed DRE, whereas among drug‐responsive patients, approximately two thirds (63.6%) achieved a responsive outcome using monotherapy. This distribution is highly consistent with previous studies, 7 , 17 , 18 with minor differences potentially attributable to variations in seizure freedom definitions and study populations. For example, in the present study, the proportion of patients who achieved final seizure freedom with monotherapy was 63.6%, which was lower than the 71.8% reported under the same assessment criteria in the Supporting Information of the study by Chen et al. 4 This discrepancy may be attributed to differences in the composition of epilepsy subtypes between the study populations. The study by Chen et al. enrolled patients without restrictions on epileptic seizure types, with generalized epilepsy accounting for 21.5% of the enrolled cohort, and the seizure freedom rate of this subtype (65.0%) was higher than that of focal epilepsy (60.8%). Such a more inclusive population composition, coupled with a higher proportion of subtypes with high responsiveness to monotherapy, may have contributed to the elevated overall success rate of seizure freedom achieved with monotherapy. At the same time, our study observed that the seizure‐free rate in patients showed a gradual decreasing trend as the number of ASM treatment regimens increased, and this pattern was highly consistent with the findings of Chen et al., indicating that most patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy have a favorable response to initial treatment. Multiple other studies have confirmed that treatment responses in epilepsy patients are mostly concentrated in the early treatment phase; as the number of treatment regimen adjustments increases, the additional seizure control benefits provided by subsequent medications decrease significantly, 3 , 7 , 19 which further confirms the importance of optimizing initial treatment. By identifying independent predictors of DRE based on pretreatment baseline clinical features, this study complements the existing body of knowledge in the field. These findings hold the potential to assist clinicians in preliminarily assessing the risk of drug resistance before ASM initiation and may inform the development of individualized ASM treatment strategies to capitalize on the critical early therapeutic window. Prioritizing early treatment optimization helps avoid the progressive attenuation of seizure control benefits caused by repeated subsequent treatment regimen adjustments and ultimately maximizes the probability of achieving sustained long‐term seizure freedom. Among patients with undetermined prognosis, 95.8% had received only one course of adequate ASM treatment; 4.2% had a long maximum seizure‐free interval before treatment, making it impossible to determine their drug responsiveness at the end of follow‐up. In addition, 29.4% of patients in this group had achieved seizure freedom but relapsed before the end of follow‐up, further increasing the complexity of prognostic judgment. text: of seizure control benefits caused by repeated subsequent treatment regimen adjustments and ultimately maximizes the probability of achieving sustained long‐term seizure freedom. Among patients with undetermined prognosis, 95.8% had received only one course of adequate ASM treatment; 4.2% had a long maximum seizure‐free interval before treatment, making it impossible to determine their drug responsiveness at the end of follow‐up. In addition, 29.4% of patients in this group had achieved seizure freedom but relapsed before the end of follow‐up, further increasing the complexity of prognostic judgment. For patients with inadequate treatment, the use of monotherapy may relate to clinical management strategies for low‐frequency seizures. Some patients with low seizure frequency are maintained on their original regimen for observation in clinical practice instead of receiving immediate add‐on or switch therapy. This results in their treatment course failing to meet the prognostic evaluation criterion of two adequate treatment regimens. This observation raises an important clinical question regarding the management of patients who remain under the cover of an undetermined prognosis. The high percentage of patients receiving only one course of treatment underscores the importance of a better targeted approach to epilepsy management. Rather than adopting a passive observational stance, clinicians should—much like chess players calculating the best move at each point in the game—draw upon their professional knowledge and clinical experience to select the most appropriate ASM regimen for a given patient, and refine the regimen based on their gestalt of the patient's response to each treatment adjustment. 20 On the other hand, the maximum follow‐up duration in this study was 10 years. This period may still be insufficient to reliably assess long‐term drug responsiveness in patients with prolonged pretreatment seizure‐free intervals. Future studies should extend follow‐up durations to better distinguish between natural disease course and actual treatment response. This will reduce the proportion of patients with undetermined prognosis and improve the reliability of epilepsy prognosis classification.

text: In this 10‐year prospective study, we observed that 64.8% of patients achieved seizure freedom at least once, with a median time to first remission of 27.0 months. Among the initial responders, more than half (53.2%) of patients were immediate responders, achieving seizure freedom at the first assessment point. Notably, one third (33.4%) of initial responders exhibited sustained seizure freedom from the start of treatment. However, up to 35.9% of patients experienced relapse after achieving seizure freedom. Notably, among patients with relapse, 36.6% regained seizure freedom and were reclassified as drug‐responsive, whereas 31.3% of relapsed patients were ultimately classified as having DRE. The above results were generally consistent with the trends of multiple long‐term follow‐up studies. The Brodie team conducted a series of classic longitudinal cohort studies in patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy. They first reported a single‐center cohort of patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy in 2000, 3 and subsequently performed long‐term follow‐up analyses with multiple dimensions. Later in 2006, they published a midterm follow‐up analysis based on this cohort, which enrolled 558 patients with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. The results showed that during follow‐up, 61.5% of patients with focal epilepsy achieved 12‐month seizure freedom, with an overall relapse rate of 21%, and 40% of the patients with relapse progressed to DRE. 19 Subsequent analysis after expanding this cohort and completing long‐term follow‐up revealed that the 12‐month seizure freedom rate of patients with focal epilepsy was 62.5% at the last follow‐up, with minimal change in the seizure freedom rate. 4 Another cohort study involving 448 newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients reported that 59.6% of patients achieved seizure freedom during follow‐up, with a median time to first seizure freedom of 12.1 months and a 16.5% relapse rate among the cohort. 17 Evidence from a study has found that most patients achieve long‐term seizure freedom from the initiation of treatment. 21 Together with the findings of the aforementioned study, the results of the present study confirm that newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients have an overall favorable prognosis and that most are highly responsive to initial treatment; however, the fluctuating nature of the disease course and the risk of relapse cannot be ignored, and relapse serves as an important clinical marker for identifying potential DRE. A total of 143 patients (25.4%) developed drug resistance during treatment and were diagnosed with DRE, whereas nine patients (6.3%) achieved first‐time seizure freedom during subsequent treatment and were reclassified as drug‐responsive epilepsy. Brodie et al. also proposed that some patients require a relatively long treatment cycle to enter the first remission period. 7 The observed transitions between remission‐refractory and refractory‐remission states in the present study further confirm the fluctuating nature of the epilepsy disease course. 5 Our evidence also suggests that, although DRE remains a persistent and difficult‐to‐treat condition for the majority of patients, drug‐resistant status is not immutable. Brodie et al. also proposed that some patients require a relatively long treatment cycle to enter the first remission period. 7 The observed transitions between remission‐refractory and refractory‐remission states in the present study further confirm the fluctuating nature of the epilepsy disease course. 5 Our evidence also suggests that, although DRE remains a persistent and difficult‐to‐treat condition for the majority of patients, drug‐resistant status is not immutable. In the DRE cohort of the present study, although only 6.3% of patients ultimately achieved complete seizure control, DRE should not be regarded as an irreversible clinical end‐stage. As demonstrated by research, a meaningful proportion of patients may still benefit from later line therapies, with 6.7% of patients attaining seizure freedom even with the seventh ASM trial. 4 , 22 This small but significant subset of successful transitions suggests that, for some patients, the emergence of drug resistance may reflect a need for more refined treatment optimization. Therefore, for high‐risk patients, the treatment strategy should maintain a dual focus of optimizing initial therapy to maximize early response, while continuing to pursue sequential optimization of subsequent treatments, ensuring that no potential opportunity for seizure control is prematurely abandoned.

text: Multivariate regression analysis identified wake‐related seizures, a history of cluster seizures, a history of status epilepticus, and sleep problems at baseline as independent risk factors for the development of DRE in newly diagnosed patients with focal epilepsy. The sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of the main findings. Notably, abnormal brain MRI reached statistical significance in the sensitivity analysis model (HR = 1.484, p = .029), whereas it was only marginally significant in the main analysis (p = .054). Given that the HR values were highly consistent between the two models (1.484 vs. 1.420), we consider that the marginally significant p‐value in the main analysis may be attributable to insufficient statistical power due to the limited sample size, suggesting that this variable remains a potential independent predictor of DRE. Crucially, this study is the first to clarify the predictive value of baseline seizure timing (wake‐related seizures) for the long‐term prognosis of newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients, providing a valuable supplement for clinical implementation of precise risk stratification. The analysis results showed that patients with wake‐related seizures at baseline had poorer prognosis, with their risk of developing DRE significantly increased by 74.3%. This result echoes the findings of D'Alessandro et al., namely that pure sleep epilepsy is typically associated with better drug responsiveness. 23 In addition, a study by Licchetta et al. demonstrated that the occurrence of seizures during wakefulness is significantly associated with a poorer prognosis. 24 This research evidence from different epilepsy subtypes further highlights the value of baseline seizure timing in the prognostic assessment of newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. However, a potential methodological limitation should be considered. Given that patients whose first epileptic seizure occurs during sleep are highly likely to have subsequent seizures confined to the sleep phase, and that the probability of seizures occurring during wakefulness gradually decreases as the disease course progresses, 25 it is possible that some sleep‐exclusive seizures in the present study were unrecognized by patients or caregivers, particularly if the patients presented with subtle seizure manifestations. 11 Such underrecognition could lead to an overestimation of seizure‐free rates in the subgroup classified as having sleep‐exclusive seizures, thereby potentially exaggerating the prognostic contrast with the wake‐related seizure group. Future studies incorporating objective seizure detection methods, such as long‐term video‐EEG monitoring, may help clarify whether this bias influences the observed association. The associations between prognostic factors such as history of cluster seizures, history of status epilepticus, and abnormal brain MRI findings observed in the present study and epilepsy prognosis have been verified in multiple studies. 26 , 27 , 28 In terms of neuroimaging, studies have shown that patients with brain structural abnormalities have a 1.5–2.8‐fold higher risk of developing drug resistance than those with normal brain structure. 3 , 29 , 30 Among patients with drug‐resistant focal epilepsy requiring surgical treatment, the most common brain structural abnormality is hippocampal sclerosis, followed by intracranial tumors and malformations of cortical development. 31 These structural lesions may contribute to the formation of abnormal neural networks. text: and abnormal brain MRI findings observed in the present study and epilepsy prognosis have been verified in multiple studies. 26 , 27 , 28 In terms of neuroimaging, studies have shown that patients with brain structural abnormalities have a 1.5–2.8‐fold higher risk of developing drug resistance than those with normal brain structure. 3 , 29 , 30 Among patients with drug‐resistant focal epilepsy requiring surgical treatment, the most common brain structural abnormality is hippocampal sclerosis, followed by intracranial tumors and malformations of cortical development. 31 These structural lesions may contribute to the formation of abnormal neural networks. Such networks not only bypass the inhibitory effects of the endogenous antiepileptic system but also prevent traditional ASMs from accessing their targets, ultimately leading to DRE. 32 In terms of clinical manifestations, studies have shown that seizure clusters are often associated with higher seizure frequency, an increased risk of drug resistance, and a lower likelihood of achieving seizure remission. 33 From an electrophysiological perspective, the occurrence of seizure clusters typically indicates that the epileptogenic focus in the brain exhibits extremely high synchronized discharge intensity and a low tendency toward spontaneous remission. 34 In addition, a history of status epilepticus, as a severe seizure phenotype, typically indicates a severe imbalance of inhibitory mechanisms within the brain. Previous studies have indicated that the proportion of patients who achieved long‐term seizure freedom during follow‐up was significantly lower in those with a history of status epilepticus than in the general population. 35 Moreover, the difficulty of achieving seizure freedom increases exponentially with the number of status epilepticus episodes. 36 Of particular note, the predictive value of baseline sleep problems for DRE may be closely related to the complex bidirectional relationship between sleep and epilepsy. 37 Sleep problems can exacerbate existing problems faced by many epilepsy patients, as they may aggravate or induce epileptic seizures; conversely, epileptic seizures and ASM can further worsen sleep problems, 38 and the longer the course of epilepsy, the poorer the sleep quality. 39 A study by Byars et al. found that up to half of children with newly diagnosed epilepsy had sleep problems at the time of diagnosis, which is far higher than the proportion in our study (13.9%); this discrepancy may be attributed to heterogeneity in the study populations. In addition, Byars et al.'s study also confirmed that sleep problems exert a significant impact on children with newly diagnosed epilepsy, and this conclusion further validates the importance of baseline sleep problems for epilepsy prognosis. 40 Our study results also remind clinicians that they should attach great importance to the assessment and early intervention of sleep problems, so as to help prevent and minimize the impact of patients' sleep problems on epilepsy conditions. This study has several limitations. Although the core outcome measures were collected prospectively, certain baseline historical information (e.g., birth history) relied on retrospective recall by patients and their families. This may have introduced a degree of recall bias, particularly in elderly patients or those with a longer disease duration.

text: This study elucidates the inherent complexity and dynamic nature of prognostic assessment in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. Through systematic longitudinal observation, we demonstrate that long‐term epilepsy outcomes are not fixed but rather evolve dynamically between drug‐responsive and drug‐resistant states. Baseline clinical features, particularly seizure timing (wake‐related seizures) as an independent prognostic factor identified in this study, provide a preliminary empirical basis for early risk stratification. At the initiation of treatment, early identification of patients with high‐risk prognostic features allows for more proactive management strategies, including earlier referral for presurgical evaluation. However, the presence of a substantial proportion of patients with undetermined prognosis underscores the inherent limitations of relying solely on static baseline indicators for prediction. Furthermore, our findings highlight the need for clinicians to adopt a longitudinal perspective in follow‐up, fully recognizing the variability of treatment response. For patients with suboptimal initial treatment response, outcomes should not be prematurely deemed as failures; instead, continued optimization of therapeutic strategies is warranted, as drug resistance may be reversible in a subset of patients. Nevertheless, once a definitive diagnosis of DRE is established, presurgical evaluation should be prioritized over indefinite sequential trials of additional ASMs, to optimize the long‐term prognosis of patients.

text: More than one quarter of people with epilepsy may become pregnant. 1 , 2 The complex relationship between sex steroid hormones and seizures causes unique challenges in people with epilepsy. 3 These relationships can be bidirectional as hormones can affect some antiseizure medications (ASMs) and seizures, and ASMs and seizures may have an impact on hormones. 3 , 4 , 5 In women with epilepsy (WWE), pregnancy becomes a vulnerable time where extra caution needs to be taken, including more intensive monitoring and possible modification of ASMs. 6 When planning pregnancy, people with epilepsy can be reassured that seizure freedom for at least 9 months preconception is highly predictive of seizure freedom during pregnancy. 7 , 8 The postpartum phase is a particularly vulnerable period due to sleep disruption, stress, changing hormones, and ASM concentrations, often leading to the need for rapid and complex dosing regimen changes. 6 , 9 , 10 Newborn safety is also of great concern. 11 Due to fear of recurrent seizures, many people with epilepsy are fearful of holding their newborn or parenting without another adult present. No studies have used data from prospective seizure diaries to inform counseling about postpartum seizure precautions based on seizures experienced before delivery. Our primary goal was to use prospectively collected seizure diaries from a well‐controlled observational study to guide data‐informed counseling about postpartum seizures. By reanalyzing seizure diaries from the Maternal Outcomes and Neurodevelopmental Effects of Antiepileptic Drugs (MONEAD) study, we evaluated whether characteristics of seizure freedom and seizure frequency before delivery were associated with postpartum seizure freedom and seizure frequency. Additionally, for women with who were not seizure‐free, we used a data‐driven approach to estimate the typical variability in seizure frequency to give more information about what a meaningful change in their own seizure frequency would be, thus helping to provide knowledge for the postpartum period.

text: Pregnant WWE, aged 14–45 years, enrolled at ≤20 weeks gestational age (GA) in the longitudinal, prospective MONEAD cohort study were included in this analysis. 7 Exclusion criteria included women with a GA > 20 weeks at enrollment, exposure to non‐ASM teratogens, the detection of major congenital malformations, or a history of genetic disorder, intelligence quotient < 70, and major medical illness. 7 Participants with functional neurologic disorder were also excluded. MONEAD also included control groups of nonpregnant WWE and healthy pregnant women, who were not included in this analysis. All participants consented for enrollment in MONEAD. This reanalysis of MONEAD data was approved with a waiver of additional consent by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board (STUDY24020010). MONEAD recorded information about the participant's seizure types and epilepsy syndrome, as well as demographic and other clinical data. At the first visit of the study, demographic information was obtained, which included detailed epilepsy histories. Participants were asked about age at onset, seizure type, and prior imaging. The site investigators classified seizures and epilepsy syndromes based on the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke criteria. Participants' seizures were classified according to the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE)'s 2010 classification of seizures and epilepsy and categorized as focal, generalized, or unspecified onset (Table S1). A semiology core committee for epilepsy classification consisting of expert epileptologists validated the seizure types in participants. Other than epilepsy and seizure information, MONEAD recorded information about age, self‐identified race, ethnicity, breastfeeding, ASM type(s) and dose, maternal outcomes, and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Treatment regimens, including dosing, were managed by each participant's medical team and were not altered for the study. Seizure frequency was recorded prospectively with an electronic daily seizure and medication diary from the date of enrollment through 9 months postpartum (Figure 1). Study visits occurred approximately every 3 months after enrollment, including a birth visit, to verify diary entries and for other study protocol procedures. 7 In addition to prospective seizure diaries, women provided retrospective seizure diaries from enrollment back to conception, as well as preconception. Women reported their historical epilepsy type(s), how many seizures occurred from conception to enrollment, and how many seizures occurred in the 9 months prior to pregnancy. The retrospective data during pregnancy (from conception until enrollment) was only used in analyses involving looking at the preconception state. This analysis focuses on seizure frequency reported during the phases recorded either prospectively or retrospectively. For analysis, we separated prospective phases as (1) postpartum including peripartum (delivery to 9 months), (2) postpartum excluding peripartum (6 weeks postpartum to 9 months), and (3) pregnancy (enrollment [up to 20 weeks GA] through birth). Retrospective phases included (4) early pregnancy (conception through enrollment) and (5) preconception (9 months prior to conception).

text: Due to the clinical importance of seizure freedom, our first analysis focused on seizure freedom and did not evaluate numerical seizure frequency. Seizure freedom was defined as total absence of all seizure types during each prospective or retrospective phase. All analyses included the peripartum period unless its exclusion is explicitly stated. Using logistic regression, we evaluated the association between postpartum seizure freedom and characteristics of seizures prior to the postpartum period. To build upon prior work, we evaluated associations with seizure freedom during pregnancy based upon prospective diaries, then evaluated the potential association of long‐term seizure freedom by including retrospective pregnancy and preconception diaries. The study used terminology from the 2017 ILAE Classification of Seizure Types. To further characterize these associations, we also evaluated the impact of seizure type and seizures that were focal versus generalized onset. Convulsive seizures included focal to bilateral tonic–clonic (FBTC), generalized tonic–clonic (GTC), and unclassified epilepsy type with convulsions. For this article, we have translated that terminology to the 2025 classification of epileptic seizures. 12 We defined “convulsive” seizures as focal, generalized, or unclassified seizures with an observable motor component that corresponds to either elementary or complex motor phenomena as defined in the 2025 classification. As a sensitivity analysis, we evaluated whether these associations differed when postpartum excluded the peripartum phase (birth to 6 weeks postdelivery). We summarize these associations by reporting odds ratios (ORs), Cohen kappa, and predictive statistics of predictive value, sensitivity, and specificity. The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of predictive statistics were calculated using binomial exact intervals. For all analyses, we considered a p‐value less than .05 to be significant. Due to the limited number of potential associated factors, we did not use cross‐validation or other techniques to address potential overfitting.

text: In participants with recurrent seizures during pregnancy (excluding those who were seizure‐free), we also evaluated the median percent reduction in seizure frequency from pregnancy to the postpartum phase. In addition, we evaluated associations between the average and variability (SD) of seizure frequency during both pregnancy and postpartum to investigate what degree of percent reduction in seizure frequency may be statistically meaningful. 13 , 14 , 15 In participants with any type of seizure during their prospective pregnancy seizure diary, we evaluated whether a higher seizure frequency was associated with a different median percent reduction in seizure frequency from pregnancy to postpartum. Consistent with statistical models of seizure frequency change in clinical trials, the percent reduction in seizure frequency was 100% minus postpartum seizure frequency divided by prospective pregnancy seizure frequency. 16 Due to nonlinearities and potential outliers in percent reduction of seizure frequency, we used rank regression to associate the rank of percent reduction in seizure frequency with the log of seizure frequency in pregnancy. In addition to median seizure frequency, the variability of seizure frequency allows clinicians to interpret what a statistically meaningful change in seizure frequency may be. Based on previous work from other seizure diary studies (NeuroVista, Seizure Tracker, and Human Epilepsy Project), 13 , 17 we evaluated whether there was a linear association between the log of average seizure frequency and the log of the SD of seizure frequency. Using log–log multivariable regression, we evaluated whether that log–log association was different postpartum compared to prospective pregnancy. We also used Wald post hoc statistics to compare the slope of the log–log regression to the value observed in other seizure diary studies, .7, and the Poisson distribution, .5.

text: MONEAD enrolled 351 pregnant WWE who provided postpartum seizure diary data. Twenty patients were excluded from analysis due to fetal death, voluntary abortion, or withdrawal from the study prior to delivery. This analysis included 331 pregnant WWE (see Figure 2 for STROBE [Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology] flowchart). text: Overall, 60.7% (199/331) participants were seizure‐free during pregnancy and 61.0% (202/331) were seizure‐free postpartum. WWE who were seizure‐free during pregnancy were more likely to be seizure‐free postpartum (OR = 6.78, 95% CI = 4.15–11.1, p < .0001). The predictive value of seizure freedom during pregnancy based on postpartum seizure freedom was 78% (95% CI = 72%–84%). Conversely, 35% of participants who had seizures in pregnancy were seizure‐free postpartum (95% CI = 27%–43%). Results excluding the peripartum phase from delivery to 6 weeks were similar and are summarized in Table S2. In our evaluation of long‐term seizure freedom, postpartum seizure freedom also was associated with preconception seizure freedom (OR = 5.84, 95% CI = 3.57–9.58, p < .0001; Figure 3), conditionally independent of pregnancy seizure freedom (Figure 3). For participants who were seizure‐free during the 9‐month preconception period (irrespective of seizure status in pregnancy), 80.6% were seizure‐free postpartum (95% CI = 75%–87%). In contrast, only 41.6% of participants who had seizures during the 9 months preconception were seizure‐free postpartum (95% CI = 34%–49%; irrespective of seizures in pregnancy). Long‐term seizure freedom during both 9 months preconception and pregnancy was associated with 85% seizure freedom postpartum (95% CI = 78–91%), whereas seizure occurrence during both pregnancy and preconception had a 36% probability of seizure freedom postpartum (95% CI = 28–44%). Of those who had seizures in pregnancy, 20% were seizure‐free in preconception. The logistic regression analysis revealed that although seizure freedom in both pregnancy and preconception were associated with postpartum seizure freedom, there was no synergistic supra‐additive association of long‐term seizure freedom during both pregnancy and preconception (interaction OR = 1.40, 95% CI = .42–4.70, p = .59; Table S3a). These associations were not significantly different when evaluated for each seizure type (difference between generalized and any seizure type, OR = .97, 95% CI = .43–2.21, p = .95). For participants with generalized seizures, 68% were seizure‐free in pregnancy and 61% were seizure‐free postpartum. Among participants with generalized seizures, there was no significant additive association of GTC seizures in pregnancy with any (or convulsive) seizure occurrence postpartum (OR = .8, 95% CI = .2–3.5, p = .76), after accounting for the association above with occurrence of any seizure type (OR = 6.8, 95% CI = 4.0–11.8, p < .001). For participants with focal seizures, 56% were seizure‐free during pregnancy and 60% were seizure‐free during postpartum. Similarly, in participants with focal seizures, there was no significant additive association between convulsive seizures in pregnancy and any (or convulsive) seizure occurrence postpartum (OR = .9, 95% CI = .3–2.7, p = .87), after accounting for the association above with occurrence of any seizure type (OR = 5.1, 95% CI = 2.5–10.6, p < .001). We investigated whether convulsions during pregnancy affected seizure freedom postpartum. Convulsions included FBTC seizures, GTC seizures, and convulsive seizures with unclassified onset. text: In participants with seizures during pregnancy, the median postpartum reduction in seizure frequency was 77% (interquartile range = −100 to −30.7%; Figure 4). Of the 132 participants with seizures in pregnancy, 18% had an increase in seizure frequency, 12% had a decrease of less than 50%, 35% had postpartum seizures with a 50% or greater decrease, and 35% participants were seizure‐free. Higher seizure frequency in pregnancy was not associated with greater percent reductions in postpartum seizure frequency (p = 0.59). In our evaluation of the variability of seizure frequency, there was a strong log–log linear association between average and SD of seizure frequency during both pregnancy and the postpartum period (Figure 5). When using daily seizure frequency diaries, the slope of that association was .58 (95% CI = .49–.67; p greater than .5 [slope of theoretical Poisson], <.01; p less than .7 [slope of nonclinical trial seizure diaries], <.01). When using fortnightly seizure frequency diaries, the slope was .66 (95% CI = .63–.69; p greater than .5, <.01; p less than .7, <.01). Those associations did not significantly change in the postpartum period compared to the pregnancy period. For example, when a participant had monthly seizures during pregnancy, the expected 95% CI of their monthly seizure frequency could range from 0 to 2 seizures per month. Alternatively, participants with daily seizures had an expected 95% CI of monthly seizure frequency ranging from weekly seizures to 4.5 seizures per day.

text: Overall, our data demonstrated that seizure freedom during pregnancy had a robust association with seizure freedom during the postpartum period. Even when participants had seizures during pregnancy, they could have improvements postpartum, because 35% were seizure‐free postpartum and the median reduction in seizure frequency was 77%. When continued seizures were present, our analysis of variability can be used to determine what constituted a statistically meaningful change in seizure frequency. These results can be used to directly counsel patients about seizure precautions and prognosis after delivery based on their seizure control during pregnancy. These results can reassure WWE who were seizure‐free by informing them that the likelihood of seizures occurring when taking care of their infant is low, although not zero. Our prior publication from the MONEAD cohort demonstrated that 61% of participants were seizure‐free postpartum. 7 These results show that 78% of participants who were seizure‐free during pregnancy maintained that seizure freedom postpartum. Furthermore, 85% of participants who were seizure‐free long term during both preconception and pregnancy maintained seizure freedom postpartum. In new parents with long‐term recurrent seizures during both pregnancy and preconception, it is appropriate to discuss a postpartum care plan with patients so that both baby and mother can receive the necessary support during this time of change. Because 15% of this population of participants did have seizures, and approximately half of this percentage had convulsive seizures, it remains appropriate to discuss seizure precautions and emphasize medication adherence and other measures to address potential seizures, as discussed on the Epilepsy & Pregnancy Medical Consortium website. 18 Our study focused on the presence or absence of seizures overall, not the seizure type. Prior studies reported that focal seizures were more likely to worsen during pregnancy compared to generalized onset seizures. 19 , 20 Our detailed evaluation of the potential influence of epilepsy type and seizure type demonstrated that changes were similar irrespective of the presence generalized or focal onset seizures, or if their seizures included impaired consciousness or convulsions. Convulsions are of particular importance, as seizures with convulsions are one of the strongest risk factors for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy and other severe consequences of recurrent seizures. 21 , 22 To assist in counseling of patients with seizures during pregnancy separately from patients who were seizure‐free, we investigated the change in seizure frequency from pregnancy to postpartum. There was a median reduction of 77% in seizures from pregnancy to postpartum, indicating those with seizures in pregnancy were likely to have seizure reduction postpartum. These results indicated that seizure frequency did improve over time, which could have been an effect of changing ASM regimens and doses in response to seizures, natural variability in seizure frequency, and increased willingness to change ASM type or dose when the regimen no longer needed to be balanced against risk to the fetus. Additionally, there may be alterations in seizure risk corresponding to hormonal fluctuations occurring between pregnancy, peripartum, and the postpartum period. text: to postpartum, indicating those with seizures in pregnancy were likely to have seizure reduction postpartum. These results indicated that seizure frequency did improve over time, which could have been an effect of changing ASM regimens and doses in response to seizures, natural variability in seizure frequency, and increased willingness to change ASM type or dose when the regimen no longer needed to be balanced against risk to the fetus. Additionally, there may be alterations in seizure risk corresponding to hormonal fluctuations occurring between pregnancy, peripartum, and the postpartum period. Therefore, even if patients had seizures in pregnancy, the clinical care provided throughout MONEAD was associated with continual improvement in seizure frequency. These reported seizure frequency change numbers focused on participants who had recurrent seizures in pregnancy and therefore differed from previous reporting of MONEAD, the latter of which also included participants who were seizure‐free during pregnancy. 8 When a change in seizure frequency occurs during pregnancy and postpartum, our estimates of the variability of seizure frequency can evaluate whether numerical changes reflect a real worsening or improvement in seizure frequency. Especially in these high‐risk periods where ASM modifications can happen quickly in response to a small number of seizures, clinicians need to both accurately and quickly gauge whether seizures have increased, decreased, or stayed the same. Based on similar results, Chiang and colleagues demonstrated that clinicians' accuracy in assessing whether underlying seizure frequency had changed was 75%, including both over‐ and underinterpretation of numerical differences. 23 By incorporating this understanding of seizure frequency variability, clinical decision support tools improved clinicians' accuracy 88%. In addition to that numerical assessment, clinical decisions to change treatments also consider changes in teratogenic risk of dose changes, seizure type (e.g., tonic–clonic versus focal preserved consciousness), time of day (e.g., nocturnal vs. daytime), and the influence of seizures on quality of life. 24 , 25 The slope of the association between the average and SD of seizure frequency was similar to that seen in placebo‐controlled randomized clinical trials and was lower than the other long‐term seizure diary studies of the Human Epilepsy Project, Seizure Tracker, and intracranial monitoring with NeuroVista. 13 The slope of these associations was higher than the Poisson distribution, which reflected “overdispersion” where there was more variation in seizure count than expected. The similarity of the slope of MONEAD to the clinical trials, both of which had slopes reflecting lower overdispersion than the nonclinical trial diaries, may have been driven by multiple factors. 15 , 17 Although ASM dose changes can address recurrent seizures, one goal of ASM management in pregnancy is to maintain ASM concentrations that are comparable to predetermined optimal concentrations within a patient to avoid concentrations known to be inadequate. 8 , 10 In contrast, Human Epilepsy Project, Seizure Tracker, and NeuroVista participants may have changed their ASMs and other treatments more frequently or they may have been less diligent about accurately counting seizures, especially for higher seizure frequencies. text: nonclinical trial diaries, may have been driven by multiple factors. 15 , 17 Although ASM dose changes can address recurrent seizures, one goal of ASM management in pregnancy is to maintain ASM concentrations that are comparable to predetermined optimal concentrations within a patient to avoid concentrations known to be inadequate. 8 , 10 In contrast, Human Epilepsy Project, Seizure Tracker, and NeuroVista participants may have changed their ASMs and other treatments more frequently or they may have been less diligent about accurately counting seizures, especially for higher seizure frequencies. Although “overdispersion” in seizure count can be caused by unaccounted for modifications of ASM and inaccuracies in seizure counting, it also can be caused by other systematic patterns in seizures such as catamenial and other multiday seizure cycles. Our approach using MONEAD data to evaluate how seizure information prior to delivery can inform counseling of postpartum seizure control has important limitations. In a sensitivity analysis, we demonstrated that these conclusions did not change when the postpartum period included or excluded the first 6 weeks after delivery, as this is a sensitive time of hormonal change. As is common in studies of patient‐reported diaries, it was challenging to determine nonadherence to diary when patients reported seizure freedom. The participants in MONEAD were followed and managed by local subspecialty experts in epilepsy during pregnancy, which likely included counseling about sleep hygiene, partner support, medication adherence, active monitoring of serum ASM levels, and multiple modifications of ASM doses throughout the study, and therefore, patients may have experienced a lower change in seizure frequency than a more generalized population. 8 , 10 Participants in MONEAD were 83% White and 71% college educated; therefore, subsequent studies are needed to understand these patterns in more diverse populations with broader ranges of socioeconomic status and clinical providers. Although this discussion emphasizes how seizures during pregnancy predicted postpartum seizure control based on prospective seizure diaries, preconception seizures also provided valuable information, even though they were temporally separated and based on retrospective seizure diaries.

text: Seizure freedom in pregnancy and preconception was a reliable indicator of postpartum seizure freedom. That association was observed irrespective of the type of epilepsy or type of seizure. In participants who were not seizure‐free during pregnancy, continued subspecialty care was associated with a 35% seizure freedom rate and, if not seizure‐free during pregnancy, 77% median seizure frequency reduction. These results could be used to provide individualized counseling to pregnant patients about what they could expect for seizure frequency postpartum based on how many seizures they had during and before pregnancy.

text: Epilepsy is one of the most common chronic neurological disorders, and despite advances in anti‐seizure therapy and adequate treatment, about one‐third of patients with epilepsy remain drug resistant. 1 For these individuals, epilepsy surgery represents a key therapeutic option. Recent studies have suggested incorporating genetic testing into the presurgical workup. However, most available data derive from pediatric cohorts 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 or convenience samples of patients already selected for clinical genetic testing. 6 , 7 , 8 Consequently, unbiased evaluation of adult presurgical cohorts is needed to clarify whether indication for genetic testing should be expanded to all surgical candidates. Few studies have systematically examined postsurgical outcomes in patients with genetic epilepsies, and reported results vary widely, likely depending on the underlying gene. 9 Interpretation is further limited by selection bias, cancellation of surgery after a genetic diagnosis, and the predominance of pediatric series. Small series of patients with pathogenic variants in the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway suggest favorable surgical outcomes, 8 , 9 , 10 yet sample sizes remain too small for firm conclusions. Overall, it remains unknown how often routine presurgical genetic testing in adults identifies clinically relevant variants or influences surgical decision‐making and outcome prediction. Hence, genetic testing is not routinely incorporated into the presurgical workup in many adult epilepsy centers. With this study, we aimed to determine the diagnostic yield of genetic testing in patients undergoing presurgical evaluation for epilepsy.

metadata.title: Low diagnostic yield of presurgical genetic testing in adult patients with epilepsy.

text: All consenting outpatients and inpatients with epilepsy at Foothills Medical Centre, Calgary, were prospectively recruited from 2019 to 2023. From this cohort we selected patients who had been admitted to one of our seizure monitoring units for presurgical evaluation, either before or after recruitment (n = 151). The aim of the admission was to devise a resective or ablative surgical approach. If this was not possible, neuromodulation was considered. Patients admitted purely for non‐surgical purposes were excluded. Eighty‐eight patients with focal epilepsy, genetic generalized epilepsy, and developmental and epileptic encephalopathy received exome sequencing as part of the Epi25 collaborative. 11 An additional 27 patients underwent exome sequencing within the Rational antiepileptic drug selection by combining gene network and ICT analysis (RAISE‐GENIC) consortium based on being responders or non‐responders to anti‐seizure medication (ASM) independent of epilepsy type. 12 Hence, among all pre‐surgical patients, 115 of 151 (76%) underwent research exome sequencing. Of the remaining 36 patients who did not undergo research exome sequencing, 3 had clinical genetic testing (2 targeted gene panels, and 1 chromosomal microarray). The final diagnosis was determined based on the results of the presurgical evaluation. Exome sequencing reads were aligned to the human genome build GRCh38/UCSC hg38, and variant calling was performed using the integrated Dynamic Read Analysis for GENomics (DRAGEN) platform (version 4.2). Variant annotation and filtering were conducted with the Geneyx Analysis platform (version 6.1). Data were stored in Variant Call Format (VCF) at the University of Calgary and processed using a validated pipeline applied in clinical diagnostics. A curated epilepsy gene panel was applied to the exome backbone, comprising 765 Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM)‐listed epilepsy‐associated genes. Variants with <10 supporting reads, a minor allele frequency >.01% in gnomAD v4.1, or classified as benign/likely benign in ClinVar (2024–12) were excluded. Additional filters included predicted inheritance patterns, in silico predictor scores, and overlap with relevant Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms. Variants were classified according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines, 13 and previously reported likely pathogenic/pathogenic variants were flagged. Diagnostic yield was determined for all likely pathogenic and pathogenic variants and was defined as the percentage of patients harboring ≥1 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant(s) (per ACMG criteria) among all patients who received genetic testing. Associations between identified monogenic etiologies and postsurgical outcomes were assessed based on clinical outcome and seizure frequency.

A small percentage had been admitted for presurgical evaluation but was eventually confirmed to have generalized epilepsy (8/115, 7%) or combined generalized and focal epilepsy (1/115, .9%). Of those tested, 55% (63/115) had nonlesional epilepsy. Structural epilepsy was present in 52 of 115 (45%), with hippocampal sclerosis being the most frequent structural cause (21/115, 18%) followed by focal cortical dysplasia (7/115, 6%) and other malformations of cortical development (6/115, 5%). An acquired etiology due to traumatic or non‐traumatic intracranial hemorrhage or lesion, perinatal postischemic or hypoxic lesion, vascular malformation, or immune‐mediated lesion was present in 10 of 115 patients (9%). Other lesions accounted for the remaining 10 lesional cases (9%). Exome sequencing with gene panel analysis identified four pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants and three variants of uncertain significance (VUSs). Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were detected in established epilepsy genes, including nonsense variants in DEPDC5 (c.2512C>T; p.R838*) and NPRL2 (c.121C>T; p.Q41*), a frameshift variant in PRRT2 (c.649dup; p.R217Pfs*8), as well as a splice donor loss in KCNT2 (c.1783+2T>A). Pathogenicity scores were high (Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) 34–37; Muttaster 1; SpliceAI 0.99), and population frequencies were absent or extremely low in gnomAD v4.1. In addition to classic loss‐of‐function variants, missense variants of uncertain significance were observed, including RELN (c.2690A>G; p.D897G), RORB (c.1196A>C; p.N399T), and a further NPRL2 variant (c.473A>C; p.K158T), with CADD scores from 21.2 to 26.6 and REVEL scores up to .91 (Table 2). All identified variants met stringent read depth and population exclusion criteria. Overall, the diagnostic yield for (likely) pathogenic variants using exome sequencing was 3.5% (4/115). EEG recordings captured interictal epileptiform discharges over the left anterior temporal and right posterior head regions. However, as no seizures were captured, seizure lateralization remained uncertain. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) did not show an epileptogenic lesion. She had a nonspecific lesion at the right cervicomedullary junction. There was no evidence of intellectual disability or a familial history of epilepsy. text: We used exome sequencing to investigate a cohort of 115 patients, who had been admitted to the seizure monitoring unit for presurgical workup, and identified (likely) pathogenic variants in 4 of 115 (3.5%). Our results demonstrate a low yield of genetic testing in adult patients undergoing presurgical workup if no other criteria for genetic testing such as positive family history or presence of intellectual disability are applied. Prior studies in adult presurgical cohorts reported a higher yield of genetic testing. A recent U.S. study reported pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 23 (10%) of 233 adult patients tested. 6 However, this study only reported on the subset of cases who had received genetic testing based on clinical indications. The size of the total cohort was not specified. A Dutch study from 2019 reported on a mixed cohort including 57% adults and 43% children who had undergone genetic testing, with a (likely) pathogenic variant identified in 40 (12%) of 325 tested patients. 8 Only 14% of the total presurgical cohort had received genetic testing. It is highly likely that the patients undergoing genetic testing were enriched for features that typically trigger clinical genetic testing, such as intellectual disability or family history, 15 , 16 which substantially increased the yield in these studies. Furthermore, the selection of patients for inclusion may have affected the results. We included patients admitted for presurgical workup independent of the final epilepsy diagnosis, resulting in the inclusion of some patients with generalized epilepsies. The Dutch study only included patients discussed in their presurgical case conference, 8 where patients not considered for surgery based on the video‐EEG monitoring results were presumably not presented. When including only patients with confirmed focal epilepsy and excluding acquired etiologies (such as trauma, stroke, infection, or immune cause), the yield would be 4.2% (4/96) in our cohort. Previous studies in pediatric patients also reported substantially higher yield between 17.5%–42%, 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 which is likely related to the high percentage of patients with additional developmental delay, such as developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. These often have a genetic etiology, thus increasing the yield of genetic testing. 15 , 16 In our adult cohort, only 28/115 patients (24%) would have met criteria for clinical genetic testing (nonacquired cause and presence of intellectual disability or family history for epilepsy) with a yield of 3.6% (1/28). Our cohort was not selected for features that would trigger clinical genetic testing and, therefore, better represents the real‐world situation for patients admitted to a seizure monitoring unit for presurgical workup. There is some potential for bias in our cohort, as not all patients admitted for presurgical video‐EEG monitoring fulfilled the inclusion criteria of the Epi25 collaborative and Rational antiepileptic drug selection by combining gene network and ICT analysis (RAISE‐GENIC) consortium. Nevertheless, 76% of our cohort underwent research exome sequencing. For focal epilepsies, the Epi25 cohort is enriched for nonlesional cases and hippocampal sclerosis. text: that would trigger clinical genetic testing and, therefore, better represents the real‐world situation for patients admitted to a seizure monitoring unit for presurgical workup. There is some potential for bias in our cohort, as not all patients admitted for presurgical video‐EEG monitoring fulfilled the inclusion criteria of the Epi25 collaborative and Rational antiepileptic drug selection by combining gene network and ICT analysis (RAISE‐GENIC) consortium. Nevertheless, 76% of our cohort underwent research exome sequencing. For focal epilepsies, the Epi25 cohort is enriched for nonlesional cases and hippocampal sclerosis. Some genetic variants are associated with other structural lesions, such as GATOR1 variants in focal cortical dysplasia. 17 A lower prevalence of patients with structural lesions other than hippocampal sclerosis (Table 1) may have reduced the yield in our study. When patients with and without genetic testing were compared in our cohort, there was a trend for a more frequent structural cause in the untested patients (64% vs 45%, p = .051; Table 1). The only characteristic that reached statistical significance was the presence of a vascular malformation, which was more prevalent in the untested subgroup (p = .029, Table 1). Nevertheless, our cohort included 12 patients (11%) with malformations of cortical development including focal cortical dysplasia, which is comparable to typical adult cohorts undergoing presurgical evaluation. 18 Therefore, we conclude that our results are representative for typical adult cohorts admitted for presurgical evaluation but may be an estimate at the lower end of the spectrum.

text: Pathogenic variants in the cohort were identified in the DEPDC5, NPRL2, KCNT2, and PRRT2 genes. DEPDC5 and NPRL2 pathogenic variants lead to enhanced mTORC1 signaling and underlie familial focal epilepsy with variable foci including a spectrum of focal epilepsies, often associated with focal cortical dysplasia or hemimegalencephaly. 17 , 19 Both patients included in our cohort had nonlesional focal epilepsy. This is consistent with the phenotypic spectrum of DEPDC5 and NPRL2 and confirms that such variants can also occur in epilepsies without MRI‐detected lesions. However, it remains unclear if small dysplastic lesions may be present that could not be identified on MRI. KCNT2 variants represent a rare cause of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by variable developmental delay, epilepsy, and neurological deficits. 20 Loss‐of‐function variants in KCNT2, as observed in our patient, have been described to be associated with a milder phenotype with less severe developmental delay and focal epilepsy as opposed to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. 20 Hence, the phenotype observed in our patient was on the mild end of the spectrum with absence of developmental delay. Variants in PRRT2 are associated with self‐limited familial infantile epilepsy. 21 The phenotype of our patient with the PRRT2 variant (mesial temporal sclerosis with amygdala enlargement) is atypical for this gene but this patient had a strong family history consistent with self‐limited familial infantile epilepsy. Later epilepsy onset has rarely been described in patients with PRRT2 pathogenic variants. 22 , 23 It remains unclear if the adult‐onset seizures in our patient are part of the phenotypic spectrum of PRRT2 or occurred independently of the genetic variant. Of interest, only one of the four patients with pathogenic variants in our cohort showed features that would have triggered clinical genetic testing (positive family history of epilepsy in first‐degree relatives). The other three had no intellectual disability, developmental delay, or family history of epilepsy. Conversely, of the 111 patients without a pathogenic variant, 35 had features that would have triggered clinical genetic testing (positive family history of epilepsy, intellectual disability). This suggests that relying on typical clinical indications for genetic testing may miss patients with a genetic cause for their epilepsy and does not increase yield (1/36, 2.8%). VUSs were found in NPRL2, RELN, and RORB. The missense variant in NPRL2 remained a VUS as it was unknown if it resulted in a loss of function and segregation data was not available. The RELN variant was not considered as pathogenic as it was heterozygous and the typical mode of inheritance for RELN is recessive. There is weak evidence that heterozygous variants may be linked to autosomal dominant lateral temporal lobe epilepsy and generalized epilepsy. 24 , 25 Pathogenic RORB variants have been described in photosensitive generalized and occipital lobe epilepsies, 26 which was not consistent with the patient's phenotype. Only the patient with the KCNT2 variant underwent epilepsy surgery and had a good outcome. It is unlikely that the decision to proceed with surgery would have been changed if the variant had been known presurgically.
