text: Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) is an epileptic syndrome representing 15%–20% of people with epilepsy (a subtype of genetic generalized epilepsy [GGE]), encompassing childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy (JAE), juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), and generalized tonic–clonic seizures alone. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 GGE accounts for 23%–43% of new onset epilepsy in children and adolescents. 5 , 6 , 7 The mean age at onset varies depending of combination of absence, myoclonic, myoclonic–tonic–clonic and generalized tonic–clonic (GTC). 7 These types of seizures may present forced head and eyes deviation or version. 3 , 7 , 8 Eighty percent of them respond to the appropriate treatment. 9 The electroencephalogram (EEG) typically shows 2.5–5.5‐Hz generalized spike–wave (GSW)/generalized polyspike–wave (GPSW) elicited by hyperventilation, sleep, or awakening with or without photoparoxysmal response and may have fragmentation. 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 Absence seizures progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures were reported as “the double generalization phenomenon in juvenile absence epilepsy” 13 or “absence‐to‐bilateral‐tonic‐clonic seizure as a generalized seizure type.” 14 Some of these patients may have focal features during the progression to a GTC seizure, a phenomenon referred to as generalized onset seizures with focal evolution (GOFE), 15 which was first described in 2009 by Williamson. 16 The incidence and prevalence of this seizure type is unknown. Continuous video‐EEG monitoring is the gold standard diagnostic tool. Quantitative EEG (QEEG) processes, transforms, and analyzes the digital EEG signals using complex mathematical algorithms, giving information about specific frequency bands, signal complexity, simplistic analysis of connectivity, and network analysis. 17 , 18 Following the International League Against Epilepsy seizure classification and QEEG analysis, we hypothesize that absence seizures may lead to focal evolution before progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures. The primary objective of this study was to characterize the electrographic abnormalities and possible network underlying this transition from an absence to a bilateral tonic–clonic seizure in patients with generalized epilepsy.

metadata.title: Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?
metadata.authors: Toro-Perez J|Sell E|Doja A|Suller-Marti A|Muir K|Healy S|Bulusu S|Whiting S|Caraballo R
metadata.parent_title: Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized? - INTRODUCTION
metadata.breadcrumb: Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?

text: We conducted a retrospective chart review of all patients with GGE admitted to the epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) of a provincial pediatric epilepsy center during May 2014 to May 2024. The study protocol was approved by the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario Research Ethics Board (REB protocol no: 22/56X, ROMEO file no: 20221223). We analyzed clinical history, EMU EEG recordings, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and genetic tests to identify patients with both absence and generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Inclusion criteria included the following: absence seizures progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures, normal brain MRI, and 48–72 h of video‐EEG recording. Exclusion criteria included the following: patients with severe developmental epileptic encephalopathy. EMU EEGs were recorded with XLTEK EMU‐40 with a sampling rate of 1024 Hz and a bandpass filter of .3 and 70 Hz. EEG data were reviewed with NeuroWorks software version 9.1. Selected EMU EEGs underwent QEEG analysis using Persyst software (version P13). The specific algorithms used for analysis were as follows: EEG view in longitudinal bipolar montage and EEG view in Laplacian montage with artifact reduction on and both EEG and trends in spike/seizure detection view for morphology, voltage, and quantification. Three certified epileptologists (J.T.‐P., S.W., R.C.) reviewed the EEGs using the following criteria. To identify GOFE progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure, a regular 10–20 system EEG view in longitudinal bipolar montage was used. The parameters utilized in this study were as follows: 1‐Hz low‐frequency filter (LFF), 70‐Hz high‐frequency filter (HFF), 60‐Hz notch, 10‐μV/mm sensitivity, and 30‐mm/s time base (TB). To corroborate the seizure and its focal evolution (defined by a generalized to focal transition), recording was reviewed in EEG view in Laplacian montage using Persyst analysis with artifact reduction on, 1‐Hz LFF, 70‐Hz HFF, 60‐Hz notch, 10‐μV/mm sensitivity, and 30‐mm/s TB. To evaluate the neuronal network involved in GOFE to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure, a split screen containing both the EEG view (same to corroborate seizure and 15‐s duration) and the trend view windows showing spike/seizure detection allowed us to adjust settings. The types of discharge were displayed using a color‐coded scheme: green bar for generalized spike detection (0–3 per second), dark red bar for right hemisphere spike detection (0–3 per second), dark blue bar for left hemisphere spike detection (0–3 per second), dark red bar for right hemisphere spike rate threshold (≥3 per 10 s), dark blue bar for left hemisphere spike rate threshold (≥3 per 10 s), and light red bar for seizure probability.

text: Six hundred twenty‐seven patients were admitted to the EMU during May 2014 to May 2024; 66 of them had a diagnosis of GGE. All of them had absence and GTC seizures. Seven patients, all females, had GOFE and were included. Eight seizures were recorded (two seizures from Patient #2), and the interrater reliability was .81–1. Three patients had JAE, two had JME, and two had GGE. One of the patients with JAE had a 15q11.2 interstitial loss, whereas the patients with GGE had pathogenic variants in SLC13A5 and CFTR (ΔF508 and L206W). We included the patient with SLC13A5 due to the absence of severe psychomotor delay as well as because her EEG did not support an ongoing epileptic encephalopathy, which was in keeping with a milder phenotype. The mean age at seizure onset was 7.5 years (range = 1–12, SD ±5.0139), at epilepsy syndrome diagnosis was 8.14 years (range = 1–13, SD ±5.1455), and at GOFE diagnosis was 13.04 years (range = 4–16.5, SD ±4.2338; see Table S1). With respect to the seizure types, all had absence and GTC seizures; four reported myoclonic seizures and one focal motor seizures (SLC13A5). Perinatal history was unremarkable. Six of them had normal neurodevelopment (one had mild motor delay). Comorbidities reported were depression (2/7), suicidal ideation (2/7), anxiety (1/7), functional neurological disorder (1/7), migraine (1/7), cystic fibrosis (1), and asthma (1/7). The EMU video‐EEG recording showed a normal background with appropriate posterior dominant rhythm in six of seven and runs of generalized 5–6‐Hz theta activity with normal posterior dominant rhythm in one (SLC13A5). Intermittent photic stimulation elicited photo paroxysmal response in four patients and triggered a GOFE in one at 12 Hz. Hyperventilation triggered absence seizures in six patients, absence status epilepticus in one, and myoclonic seizures in one. With respect to the epileptiform activity: Interictally: In all, there was activation of 2.5–3.5‐Hz GSW/GPSW as well as fragments of those discharges.Ictally: A total of eight seizures were recorded showing GOFE progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure. The mean duration of absence was 7.13 s (range = 3.5–13.5, SD ±4.0598), of focal evolution was 15.25 s (range = 4–23, SD ±6.0886), and of progression to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure was 58.21 s (range = 8.5–78, SD ±23.7799). Electrographically, there were 2.5–3.5‐Hz GSW/GPSW with high voltage that was higher over the bilateral frontal regions. All absence seizures had sudden onset, seven had sudden offset, and one had gradual offset. Subsequently, all of them were followed by different patterns of focal evolution (Table 1). The first focal evolution (T1) was seen in the lateral frontal region (three on the right [F4] and one on the left [F3]), in the occipital region (one on the right [O2], one on the left [O1] and one bilateral [O1‐O2]), and in the frontal–central region (one on the right frontal and one on the left central region [F4‐C3]; see Figure S1). text: offset. Subsequently, all of them were followed by different patterns of focal evolution (Table 1). The first focal evolution (T1) was seen in the lateral frontal region (three on the right [F4] and one on the left [F3]), in the occipital region (one on the right [O2], one on the left [O1] and one bilateral [O1‐O2]), and in the frontal–central region (one on the right frontal and one on the left central region [F4‐C3]; see Figure S1). The second focal evolution (T2) was seen mainly in the right inferior frontal (F8), right central (C4), left parietal (P3), and central midline regions (Table 1). Afterward, this activity evolved to bilateral tonic–clonic progression. Clinically, all of them had complete or partial behavioral arrest in association with 2.5–4‐Hz GSW/GPSW. Different nonmotor and motor signs were seen throughout focal evolution (T1, T2, T3). The main nonmotor signs were impaired awareness (4/8) and changes in the facial expression (1/8), whereas the main motor signs were forced head deviation (7/8) and forced eye deviation (3/8). During the early phase of the bilateral tonic–clonic progression, lateralization was seen as the following: fencing posture (2/7), sign of four (2/7), and body version to one side (2/7; Table 1).Postictally, seven seizures showed generalized postictal suppression. Clinically, all patients were confused and sleeping afterward. QEEG was done in Laplacian montage and permitted the analysis of brain activity excluding artifacts. The color of the bars were as follows: green (representing generalized discharges), blue (representing left hemisphere discharges), and red (representing right hemisphere discharges). Each image showed the absence seizure in a green bar representing GSW/GPSW > 3 Hz. During the focal evolution, the spike detection tool was activated in dark red on the right hemisphere and in dark blue on the left hemisphere according to T1, T2, T3, T4. Posteriorly, evolution was noticed; spike detection was analyzed in 10‐s intervals, showing increasing amplitude on the involved hemisphere before the bilateral tonic–clonic progression (a light red bar indicated seizure detection). This activity was in keeping with a GOFE (Figure 1; see also Figures S2–S8).

text: GOFE is an electroclinical pattern in which generalized onset epileptic activity, manifesting as an absence seizure, evolves into focal discharges during the same ictal event, often followed by bilateral tonic–clonic activity. This electroclinical pattern has been described in patients with GGE. In a group of patients with GGE, the distinction between generalized and focal epileptiform activity can be blurred, with features that fall in between these two extremes, and in some cases, there may be an overlap. 15 , 16 , 19 These seizure patterns pose a diagnostic dilemma and are a challenge for even the most experienced epileptologists. The cohort of patients with GOFE studied in our institution were all females; this is a meaningful finding. We have no explanation for this, however, including our cases, 60% are females, 28% males, and 12% unknown (see Table S2). More work is needed to determine why females may be more at risk of this pattern. Clinically and electrographically, our patients showed features similar to those reported in the first description of this seizure type (2009), which included six patients with IGE showing generalized onset seizures with focal EEG and clinical evolution. 16 Another study in Nashville (2016) reported nine patients with generalized epilepsy who showed semiology concerning for focal seizures, with video‐EEG monitoring confirming GOFE. 19 Recently, GOFE was reported in three patients in Strasbourg (2022), highlighting that GOFE shares many features with GGE and that its recognition is clinically important to avoid misdiagnosis of focal epilepsy and consequently the inappropriate use of narrow spectrum antiseizure medications. 20 Recently, another study reported that focal electroclinical features are commonly seen in generalized seizures, whereas GOFE represents a largely unknown ictal variation in GGE, bearing a risk of misclassification (see Table S2). 21 In some cases, the prominent focal signs could lead to intensive video‐EEG monitoring as part of a presurgical evaluation even including stereo‐EEG. 15 , 19 , 22 Recognizing this seizure type implies treatment reassessment including the use of broad spectrum antiseizure medication such as valproic acid alone or in association with lamotrigine. 22 Additionally, some specific single gene genetic conditions as SLC13A5 have different seizure types, including absence seizures with the main electrographic patterns including 3‐Hz generalized spike and wave showing features of IGE. 23 Three theories were proposed to explain this seizure type. 24 The first is focal cerebral dysfunction or a focal/lateralized weakness of seizure initiation–termination mechanisms. 16 The second is a focal ictal transformation of an IGE seizure variant due to a coexistent focal epilepsy (not seizures), which may require more complex management. 24 The third proposes that existing hyperexcitable cortical areas or systems may continue firing independently after the diffuse/generalized corticothalamic oscillations are inhibited. 25 Furthermore, a review of generalized absence seizures described the presence of different motor clinical manifestations, even with the same electrographic pattern, which could be related to the broad neuronal network involved in the seizure generation and seizure propagation, implying thalamocortical fibers. 26 This statement is reinforced by functional brain MRI studies,

metadata.breadcrumb: Layer 3 > Epilepsy > DISCUSSION > Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?

text: The second is a focal ictal transformation of an IGE seizure variant due to a coexistent focal epilepsy (not seizures), which may require more complex management. 24 The third proposes that existing hyperexcitable cortical areas or systems may continue firing independently after the diffuse/generalized corticothalamic oscillations are inhibited. 25 Furthermore, a review of generalized absence seizures described the presence of different motor clinical manifestations, even with the same electrographic pattern, which could be related to the broad neuronal network involved in the seizure generation and seizure propagation, implying thalamocortical fibers. 26 This statement is reinforced by functional brain MRI studies, which reported the involvement of the thalamus, caudate nuclei, and default mode areas during generalized spike–wave paroxysms and absence seizures. Moreover, they confirm high synchronization activity in the thalamocortical network by demonstration of blood oxygen level‐dependent (BOLD) activation in the thalamus, the frontomesial cortex, and the cerebellum, and BOLD deactivation in default mode areas. 27 , 28 In our cohort of patient, we found a considerable right‐lateralized frontal predominance. Woermann et al. analyzed a voxel‐based morphometry of 35 patients with IGE, reporting subtle changes in the frontal lobe by MRI. 29 Seneviratne et al. reported volume reduction or increase in the frontal and thalamic cortical areas in a voxel‐based morphometry study. 28 Kim et al. reported small volume of cortical gray matter in the right frontal lobe as well as regional smaller volume in the rostral and middle frontal, right lateral orbitofrontal, right precentral, right superior and middle temporal regions. Also, small volume was noticed in the left middle and inferior temporal regions. 30 The reason the right frontal lobe has more predisposition or impairment in patients with IGE remains unclear. Is there an anatomical predisposition or is this a consequence of the continuous thalamocortical network activation? Deep evaluation of the seizures with QEEG analysis, specifically using the spectrogram, increases the accuracy of the diagnosis in different seizure types due to sensitivity of 72% to identify seizures and sensitivity of 94% to determine focality of the seizures. 18 QEEG analysis with Persyst software uses deep learning and artificial neuronal networks to identify and classify interictal and ictal epileptiform discharges. Spike detection and seizure detection views are the most accurate tools to monitor background activity, screen for artifacts, analyze waveform morphology, and map voltage field spread. 18 One study investigated under QEEG structured data segmentation including frequency bands, cortical regions, and hemispheric localization for the accurate diagnosis of pediatric epilepsy. 31 In our cohort, the analysis described was applied and confirmed our diagnosis of GOFE. The presence of the green bar (spike detection generalized) time lock with absence seizure suddenly stopped and led to focal evolution in the red bar (right hemisphere) or blue bar (left hemisphere) to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure (red bar in seizure probability and black bars in spike detection in all foci; Figure 1). Subsequently, we confidently halted any further evaluation.

metadata.breadcrumb: Layer 3 > Epilepsy > DISCUSSION > Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?

text: In our cohort of patients with GOFE, QEEG analysis accurately showed that after absence seizure there is focal activation of the frontal (mainly right) and occipital cortices with evolution to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure. We hypothesize that GOFE could involve the activation of the thalamus and the cortex via the thalamocortical network based in the QEEG analysis and the literature evidence of functional MRI in absence seizures. A detailed history, appropriate diagnostic tools such as video‐EEG recording of seizures, and awareness of all diagnostic possibilities can help avoid misdiagnosing GOFE as focal epilepsy, defining appropriate treatment, and may prevent unnecessary presurgical evaluations. Additional study of more patients to confirm findings is required.

text: Although findings from this study suggest that GOFE may be a seizure type in patients with GGE, this cannot be definitively concluded due to the small number of patients (all female) included in a single‐center retrospective study, which limits generalizability. In addition, the variability in seizures recorded across patients, the lack of a GGE control group, and QEEG software restrictions (such as the use of Laplacian montage in some seizures with first focal activations at occipital electrodes [O1, O2]) could contribute to the limitations of this study. Further studies are needed to validate and expand on these findings. In the future, researchers could consider high‐density EEG with standardized or exact low‐resolution electromagnetic tomography source reconstruction, which could help to address the spatial resolution problem. Also, effective connectivity measures such as Granger causality or directed transfer function would add propagation directionality beyond spike density asymmetry. In addition, EEG functional MRI would allow direct testing of the thalamocortical hypothesis. Is well known that patients with GGE do not undergo to stereo‐EEG; however, the use of this invasive study could be individualized in specific types of patients with GGE.

text: This is the first reported series of GOFE cases in which all patients were female and in which all EEG recordings were systematically analyzed using QEEG. QEEG applies specific mathematical algorithms, including spectral analysis focused on power density, automated spike detection and localization, and neuronal network analysis, enabling objective assessment of the temporal relationships within EEG recordings and providing an unbiased characterization of neuronal activity. In addition, this series represents the second largest collection of recorded seizures documenting this uncommon and underrecognized seizure type. The systematic application of QEEG in this context may improve diagnostic accuracy for GOFE and help reduce misclassification as focal epilepsy.

text: Stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) provides precise seizure localization during presurgical evaluation for drug‐resistant epilepsy (DRE), a complex brain network disease. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 However, prior studies document a transient “implantation effect” defined as an acute reduction in clinical seizure frequency lasting up to 5–6 months following the placement of intracranial electrodes or neuromodulatory devices without active stimulation or resective surgery. 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 Electrode‐induced neurological and behavioral changes observed across various conditions are hypothesized to stem from acute inflammation, gliosis, and neural plasticity. 10 Although the exact mechanisms remain unclear, the implantation effect can critically confound invasive monitoring by suppressing seizures and impairing accurate seizure onset localization. Given the inherent risks of SEEG, including infection, hemorrhage, and neurological deficits, characterizing this phenomenon is vital. 11 Therefore, our study explored potential demographic and clinical predictors of the implantation effect in patients who underwent SEEG investigation with depth electrodes.

text: This retrospective analysis evaluated patients who underwent SEEG monitoring with depth electrodes between December 2018 and February 2020. Eligible participants were admitted to the Epilepsy Monitoring Unit (EMU) and met the following criteria: (1) provided informed consent; (2) completed follow‐ups at 1, 3, 6, or 12 months postdischarge; (3) received no subsequent therapeutic interventions (e.g., resective surgery, neuromodulation, or thermocoagulation); and (4) possessed documented postdischarge seizure frequency data. Demographic and clinical data were extracted from paper and electronic medical records. Documented variables included age, epilepsy history, baseline seizure frequency, cortical stimulation, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography findings, preoperative antiseizure medications (ASMs), the number of implanted electrodes, bilateral distributions of electrodes, total contacts per patient, and seizure frequency after SEEG investigation.

text: Patients were stratified into time‐specific cohorts based on the timing of their most recent seizure frequency record. To determine the seizure reduction rate for each patient, the most recent recorded seizure frequency was subtracted from the preimplantation baseline frequency and divided by the baseline value. The seizure reduction rate was categorized using a dichotomous parameter; patients achieving less than a 50% reduction were classified as nonresponders, whereas those achieving a reduction rate of 50% or more were categorized as responders. A secondary analysis comparing patients achieving complete seizure freedom and those who did not was also completed. Statistical analyses were performed using R (v4.2.2). Continuous variables were summarized as median (interquartile range [IQR]) and compared between cohorts using a t‐test or Mann–Whitney U‐test following normality verification via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies (%) and evaluated using chi‐squared or Fisher exact tests, applying the latter if >20% of expected cell counts were <5. 12 To control the type I error rate, a Bonferroni correction was applied, establishing an adjusted statistical significance threshold of α = .0012.

text: Fifty‐one of the 110 patients who underwent SEEG met the study's inclusion criteria. Seizure frequency data were clearly identified and extracted from follow‐up records for seven of the 51 patients at 1 month, 20 at 3 months, 12 at 6 months, and 12 at 12 months. The median age of the participants was 34.0 years (IQR = 25.0–46.0), with 57.4% of the participants being women (n = 27). All 51 patients were diagnosed with DRE. The median duration of EMU stay was 14 days (IQR = 10.5–17.0).

text: From the total included patients, data available for the 1‐month follow‐up group consisted of seven patients, of whom five patients (71.4% of the 1‐month follow‐up cases) were reported as responders. Responders at this juncture experienced a median seizure rate of .0 seizures per month (IQR = .0–6.0). At the 3‐month follow‐up, 20 patients were included, yielding a responder rate of 35.0% (seven responders). These responders demonstrated a median seizure frequency of .0 seizures per month (IQR = .0–6.0). At the 6‐month follow‐up, the responder rate was 33.3% (4 of 12 patients followed up with), with a median of .7 seizures per month (IQR = .3–2.0). The 12‐month follow‐up group comprised 12 patients, with six individuals (50.0% of those followed up with at 12 months) as responders. These responders displayed a median seizure rate of .7 seizures per month (IQR = .0–5.4; Figure 1, Table S1). No statistically significant differences were observed in demographic or clinical characteristics between responder and nonresponder groups at each follow‐up period, including cortical stimulation, MRI abnormalities, number of implanted electrodes and contacts, or number and type of ASMs (Table 1).

text: This study evaluates the clinical and demographic determinants of the implantation effect, providing a more comprehensive analysis in a larger patient cohort than existing literature. Our investigation revealed a 71.4% responder rate at 1 month, 35.0% at 3 months, 33.3% at 6 months, and 50.0% at 12 months postimplantation without subsequent therapeutic intervention. Additionally, complete seizure freedom was observed in 42.9% and 20.0% of patients at 1 and 3 months, respectively. These findings are consistent with previous studies reporting short‐term seizure reductions following intracranial electrode implantation. For instance, Percy et al. noted ≥50% seizure reduction in 36% of patients at 1 year, with a smaller proportion achieving seizure freedom. In our cohort, no specific clinical or demographic variables were identified as potential predictors of reduced seizure frequency postimplantation. 6 Several patients in our cohort who were classified as responders had documented uncontrolled seizures prior to SEEG admission. Similar observations have been made in previous studies and extend to those investigating deep brain stimulation and responsive neurostimulation where seizure frequency was noted after lead placement without stimulation (Table S3). 9 , 13 , 14 , 15 This reduction in seizure frequency is unlikely to be a spontaneous event. Surgical factors, particularly anesthetic use, have been implicated, with desflurane speculated to prolong seizure relief after electrode implantation. 8 However, sustained long‐term improvements suggest the implantation effect is unlikely to be attributable to anesthetics. 6 The role of ASMs in the implantation effect remains unclear. In our study, neither the type nor the overall load of preimplantation ASMs differed significantly between responders and nonresponders. However, dosage, adherence, and changes in ASM regimens were not tracked. This limitation is shared by previous studies, which often assessed only inpatient medication load or overlooked medication adjustments altogether. 6 , 8 , 9 Future research should account for specific dosages and regimen changes as potential factors influencing seizure reduction following depth electrode implantation. Given that clinical and demographic factors lack statistical significance here and in prior literature, 6 , 8 the precise timing of symptom reduction implicates electrode insertion as the primary driver of the implantation effect. We suspect this phenomenon is likely driven by electrode‐induced microlesions that disrupt seizure propagation networks within the epileptogenic zone. 7 , 16 , 17 At the molecular level, this disruption may be mediated by an acute inflammatory and neurophysiological cascade, including reactive astrogliosis, altered astrocyte–neuron signaling, gliotransmitter release, and localized neuroplastic axonal remodeling. 10 Crucially, because seizure reduction was independent of the total number of implanted electrodes, therapeutic modulation likely depends on the precise anatomical intersection of electrodes with critical network nodes rather than cumulative tissue trauma. Speculatively, this mechanism may also explain the lack of change in seizure frequency in some patients and increased seizure frequency in nonresponders. The former could indicate that electrodes missed critical epileptogenic networks, whereas the latter might arise from trauma‐induced reactive astrocytes releasing glutamate to elevate perielectrode neuronal excitability. 18 Ultimately, further research into these localized tissue–electrode interactions is required to elucidate the dual

text: neuroplastic axonal remodeling. 10 Crucially, because seizure reduction was independent of the total number of implanted electrodes, therapeutic modulation likely depends on the precise anatomical intersection of electrodes with critical network nodes rather than cumulative tissue trauma. Speculatively, this mechanism may also explain the lack of change in seizure frequency in some patients and increased seizure frequency in nonresponders. The former could indicate that electrodes missed critical epileptogenic networks, whereas the latter might arise from trauma‐induced reactive astrocytes releasing glutamate to elevate perielectrode neuronal excitability. 18 Ultimately, further research into these localized tissue–electrode interactions is required to elucidate the dual nature of this postimplantation network modulation. This study is primarily limited by its retrospective design, which resulted in small, variable follow‐up cohorts due to inconsistent medical record documentation. Because patients were captured at differing intervals, these fluctuating sample sizes limit the reliability of longitudinal seizure dynamics. Furthermore, long‐term findings must be interpreted with caution, as intermediary seizure activity was not captured. Finally, postdischarge medication adherence, dosages, and adjustments were not systematically tracked. These limitations underscore the necessity for prospective studies utilizing standardized protocols to rigorously quantify seizure frequency at fixed intervals and comprehensively monitor longitudinal medication compliance.

text: Our study provides valuable insights into the implantation effect following depth electrode insertion for SEEG monitoring, with responder rates ranging from approximately 71.4% at 1 month to 50% at 12 months postimplantation. Despite multiple patients reporting decreases in seizure frequency, no statistically significant clinical predictors of a ≥50% reduction in seizure frequency were identified. However, because responders exhibited uncontrolled seizures immediately prior to admission, spontaneous reduction is unlikely. Although our findings support the hypothesis that electrode‐induced microlesions disrupt epileptic networks, and that anatomical location is a key determinant of efficacy, these mechanisms remain speculative. Larger prospective studies integrating systematic electrode localization data are required to comprehensively elucidate the variables driving the implantation effect.

text: Epilepsy surgery is an established treatment for drug‐resistant focal epilepsy, with surgical success depending on accurate localization and resection of the presumed epileptogenic zone (p‐EZ). 1 , 2 The p‐EZ, however, is not a focal point but a spatially distributed cortical region capable of generating seizures. 3 Defining both its location and spatial extent remains a major challenge in presurgical evaluation, particularly in patients with non‐lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or discordant clinical and electrophysiological findings. 4 In this context, non‐invasive functional imaging techniques have become increasingly valuable for estimating cortical regions involved in epileptogenesis. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 Simultaneous electroencephalography/magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG) and EEG/functional MRI (EEG/fMRI) provide complementary information on epileptic activity. 10 , 11 EEG/fMRI offers whole brain coverage and high spatial resolution maps of blood oxygen level–dependent (BOLD) changes linked to epileptic discharges, 8 , 12 , 13 whereas MEG directly measures magnetic fields generated by these discharges, offering high temporal and good spatial resolution but low sensitivity to deep sources. 9 , 10 , 14 When combined with EEG, electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI) improves source localization accuracy by integrating both electrophysiological signals into a unified source model. 15 , 16 Both modalities have yielded promising results in identifying candidate regions for surgical resection, with several studies demonstrating good concordance between the most significant fMRI response or EMSI findings and intracerebral EEG findings. 7 , 10 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 Moreover, previous studies have reported that resection of the most significant fMRI response cluster is generally associated with good outcome, although not sufficient to ensure seizure freedom (with negative predictive values ranging from 0.63 to 100%). 19 , 21 For MSI, reported predictive values are similarly variable, with negative predictive values between 40 and 65% and positive predictive values between 60 and 83%, 9 , 20 likely reflecting methodological and cohort differences. Most previous studies have relied on qualitative evaluations or single‐point distance metrics between the localization peak (EEG/fMRI responses or EEG/MEG sources) and the surgical cavity, 9 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 overlooking the spatial extent of the p‐EZ. Given that incomplete resection of the p‐EZ may lead to persistent seizures, 3 , 4 assessing spatial overlap and dispersion relative to the surgical cavity may provide a more clinically meaningful evaluation. In the context of epilepsy surgery, when both modalities are available, their respective predictive value for postoperative outcome remains unclear. Should surgical planning prioritize regions identified by EEG/MEG, EEG/fMRI or by both modalities? Addressing this question requires analyzing both modalities in the same space. However, few studies have done so, 10 , 23 , 24 and most relied on qualitative or semi‐quantitative comparisons without a common anatomic reference, leaving their predictive performance unclear. text: We retrospectively identified patients with drug‐resistant unifocal epilepsy from the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) MEG database, who underwent both simultaneous EEG/MEG and EEG/fMRI as part of their presurgical evaluation between 2008 and 2019. Patients were included if they subsequently underwent open resective surgery and had at least 1 year of postoperative follow‐up. All patients had available preoperative and postoperative imaging. The study was approved by the institutional ethics board, and written informed consent was obtained. Of note, surgical planning was based on the overall electroclinical hypothesis integrating clinical, electrophysiological, and imaging data, including stereo‐electroencephalography when indicated, whereas EEG/MEG and EEG/fMRI results were considered at the discretion of the treating physicians. Patient selection is summarized in Figure 1.

text: Simultaneous EEG/MEG recordings, processing, and analysis were performed as described in previous studies. 10 , 25 , 26 Recordings were acquired using a 275‐gradiometer CTF MEG system (MISL, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada) and a 56‐channel EEG cap (Easy‐Cap, Herrsching, Germany). 25 , 26 Each session lasted ~1 h, divided into 10 runs of 6 min each. Interictal epileptic discharges (IEDs) were visually marked on MEG by a board‐certified epileptologist (C.A.), independently of EEG/fMRI results. The two runs containing the largest number of IEDs (or one run if the number exceeded 100 IEDs) were selected for analysis. 10 Source localization was performed using the coherent maximum entropy on the mean (cMEM) method, which is sensitive to the spatial extent of the underlying generators. 27 , 28 , 29 This framework enables a fusion approach for EMSI by combining EEG and MEG data into a single, unified source model. 15 , 16 EMSI was computed for each single marked IED, and a consensus map was generated by applying hierarchical clustering across all source maps, followed by averaging the maps within the cluster containing the largest number of IEDs. 10 This procedure improves the reliability of EMSI results across different IED types. 15 For patients with fewer than 10 IEDs, EMSI was computed using the averaged IED to balance consensus map reliability and source localizations signal‐to‐noise ratio. 10 The final consensus EMSI maps were analyzed at the first peak visible on either EEG or MEG data, since the first signal has been shown to have the highest concordance with intracerebral findings. 30

text: Simultaneous EEG/fMRI recordings, processing, and analysis were performed as described in previous studies. 17 , 21 Data were recorded using a 3 T MRI scanner with 25 MRI‐compatible EEG electrodes and were collected in runs of 6 min each, for a total of 6 to 15 runs per patient, acquired with patients at rest. Cleaned EEG data were reviewed by epileptologists (S.I. and M.T.), and IEDs were visually identified and grouped according to their morphology/shape and spatial distribution. Functional MRI data were analyzed using an event‐related design implemented in fMRIstat. 31 Each IED type was modeled as a separate regressor in a general linear model, using the onset and duration of all marked IEDs convolved with four predefined hemodynamic response functions peaking 3, 5, 7, and 9 s after the spike onset. 32 A statistical t‐map was generated for each IED type with noise modeled by nuisance regressors (e.g., motion and global averaged signal in the brain). A combined t‐map was then created by taking, at each voxel, the highest absolute t‐value from the 4 t‐maps created with each hemodynamic response function. This combined t‐map from each IED type was first thresholded (t > 3.1) and corrected for multiple testing using a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.05. 17 For subsequent analyses, only the fMRI cluster exhibiting the highest absolute t‐value (either activation: positive t or deactivation: negative t), corresponding to the most significant cluster, was considered for comparison with the surgical cavity. This cluster has been shown to best correlate with intracerebral findings (spike‐onset and seizure‐onset zones) 10 , 17 , 18 and to have surgical predictive value. 19 , 21 Although IED grouping in EEG/fMRI was based on scalp morphology and distribution, EMSI retained the largest source–space cluster after hierarchical clustering of individual IED maps. While these approaches may not isolate exactly the same IED subtype, both were intended to capture the dominant IED population in each patient.

text: To enable quantitative comparisons between EMSI map, the most significant fMRI cluster, and the surgical cavity, all modalities were co‐registered to a common cortical surface used for EMSI analysis (Figure 2). Postoperative imaging (MRI or computed tomography [CT]), the anatomic MRI acquired during EEG/fMRI, and the corresponding fMRI t‐map were co‐registered to the 3T anatomic MRI used for EMSI processing. For each patient, the surgical cavity was manually delineated in volume space using MRIcron 33 and smoothed using 5 mm kernel in Matlab (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) to account for potential co‐registration inaccuracies and postoperative brain distortion. 34 For fMRI analysis, in order to obtain a spatially contiguous pattern suitable for surface‐based interpolation and spatial comparison, we applied a voxel wise threshold of |t| > 3.1. Both the selected fMRI cluster of interest and the binary surgical cavity mask were projected onto the reference cortical surface. This projection followed a previously described method based on voronoï cells, which define anatomically informed interpolation kernels respecting sulco‐gyral morphology. 35 For each cortical vertex, the resulting fMRI response was averaged across the voxels comprising the corresponding voronoï cells. To quantitatively assess the spatial agreement between EMSI, the most significant fMRI cluster, and the surgical cavity considered as the gold‐standard together with surgical outcome, we computed three spatial metrics. (1) Area under the curve (AUC): the AUC of a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was derived by applying various thresholds on the EMSI maps, 36 using the surgical cavity voxels as reference. To reduce sampling bias caused by the large number of true‐negative voxels outside the surgical mask, AUC values were computed as the mean of two complementary measures: AUC_close (negative voxels, i.e., outside the cavity but near the cavity) and AUC_far (negative voxels distant from the cavity). Both measures were calculated using an equal number of voxels inside and outside the surgical cavity, with external voxels selected based on their proximity to the cavity boundary (30–35 mm). 10 , 36 Values above 0.70 were considered indicative of good spatial overlap. 10 (2) Distance localization error (DLE): the minimum Euclidean distance (in mm) between the maximum of each modality's map to the nearest voxel of the surgical cavity was calculated. 37 When the maximum localization was within the cavity, DLE = 0 mm. (3) Spatial dispersion (SD): spatial dispersion quantified the spatial spread (in mm) of each modality's response relative to the surgical cavity. It was calculated as the root mean square of the distance between each voxel and the closest resected voxel, weighted by the energy (squared value) of the source localization map at that voxel. 29 Because no statistical threshold can be directly applied to EMSI maps, these spatial metrics were computed without any threshold, as described previously. 14 Additional spatial metrics were estimated at the voxel‐level for each patient, precision (proportion of correctly localized voxels in the surgical cavity) and recall (proportion of the surgical cavity correctly identified by EEG/MEG or EEG/fMRI). text: It was calculated as the root mean square of the distance between each voxel and the closest resected voxel, weighted by the energy (squared value) of the source localization map at that voxel. 29 Because no statistical threshold can be directly applied to EMSI maps, these spatial metrics were computed without any threshold, as described previously. 14 Additional spatial metrics were estimated at the voxel‐level for each patient, precision (proportion of correctly localized voxels in the surgical cavity) and recall (proportion of the surgical cavity correctly identified by EEG/MEG or EEG/fMRI). For these analyses, voxels within the cavity were considered as ground truth, independently of postsurgical outcome. Precision and recall were derived from the same voxel‐wise overlap framework used for AUC computation (AUC_close and AUC_far). EMSI voxels were classified as active at 30% of the maximal EMSI value, whereas fMRI voxels were considered active when showing non‐zero values after interpolation onto the cortical surface.

text: We conducted non‐parametric tests. Patients were classified into good (Engel class I) and poor (Engel class II–IV) surgical outcome groups. Differences between outcome groups for AUC, DLE, and SD were assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test. The rank biserial correlation (rb) was used to represent effect size (ranges from −1 to + 1), with absolute cutoff values of 0.1–0.3, 0.3–0.5, and >0.5 interpreted as small, moderate, and large effects, respectively. Associations between spatial metrics were examined using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient ρ, with absolute values of 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 interpreted as small, moderate, and strong correlations, respectively. Analyses were restricted to patients with contributive findings for the corresponding modality, defined as >5 IEDs for EMSI and a significant fMRI response for EEG/fMRI. To assess the ability of each modality in predicting postoperative outcome at the patient‐level, patients were classified as true positive (TP), false positive (FP), true negative (TN), or false negative (FN) based on the spatial relationship between imaging results and surgical outcome, using the following two criteria: Combined spatial threshold: good spatial overlap (AUC > 0.70) 10 and resection of the maximum response (DLE = 0 mm) 37 ;Distance‐only threshold: DLE = 0 mm, consistent with prior studies relying only on the resection status of the maximum response. 9 , 19 , 21 A case was considered TP when the criterion was met in a patient with good outcome; all other combinations were classified as FP, TN, FN, accordingly. For example, for the combined spatial threshold (AUC > 0.70 and DLE = 0 mm), and using EEG/MEG, TP was defined as a patient with AUC > 0.70, DLE = 0 mm, and good outcome; FP met the same spatial criterion but had poor outcome; TN did not meet the spatial criterion (AUC ≤ 0.70 or DLE > 0 mm) and had poor outcome; and FN did not meet the spatial criterion but achieved a good outcome. For each modality and condition, we then computed sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). Finally, to determine whether spatial agreement between electrophysiological and hemodynamic responses improved predictive accuracy compared to individual modalities, analyses were restricted to patients with contributive results from both modalities, which were defined as concordant when both localizations were resected (DLE = 0) and discordant otherwise. All analyses were performed using the JASP statistical software (Version 0.95.1), 38 with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.

text: Twenty‐five patients (mean age of 27 ± 9 years, 12 female) with drug‐resistant focal epilepsy were included. Ten patients (40%) achieved a good surgical outcome, whereas 15 (60%) had persistent seizures at their last follow‐up. The cohort included both temporal (n = 9) and extratemporal (n = 16, including 4 patients with a presumed temporal plus epilepsy) cases. MRI was negative in 10 patients (40%). Table 1 summarizes the patient clinical and electrophysiological characteristics. A total of 1137 IEDs (range 9–215) were marked in EEG/MEG, of which 816 were included in the main cluster of the consensus map (cluster with the largest number of IEDs). In EEG/fMRI, a total of 2864 IEDs (range 3–897) were analyzed. Twenty‐three patients (92%) had EMSI results (>5 IEDs), whereas EEG/fMRI resulted in significant statistical fMRI responses in 14 patients (56%). Precisely, among the 25 included patients, 5 had no IED recorded during EEG/fMRI, and 6 showed recorded IEDs but no significant fMRI cluster. For EEG/MEG, two patients had fewer than five recorded IEDs. Consequently, 12 patients had contributive results from both modalities.

text: In the EEG/MEG group (n = 23), patients with good surgical outcome showed significantly higher AUC (mean ± standard deviation: 0.70 ± 0.14 vs 0.56 ± 0.18; p = 0.04, (r (rb)) = −0.51), shorter DLE (4.83 ± 6.80 mm vs 17.98 ± 14.39 mm; p = 0.02, (r (rb)) = 0.57), and lower but not significant SD (24.45 ± 17.07 mm vs 34.21 ± 14.22 mm; p = 0.08, (r (rb)) = 0.43) compared with patients with poor outcome (Figure 3). Patients with good surgical outcome showed significantly higher precision (0.77 ± 0.15 vs 0.36 ± 0.39; p = 0.02, (r (rb)) = −0.55) compared to those with poor outcome (Figure S1). No statistically significant difference was found when considering the recall (Figure S1). In the EEG/fMRI group (n = 14), similar but not statistically significant differences were observed between outcome groups across the three spatial metrics (AUC: 0.68 ± 0.18 vs 0.58 ± 0.22; p = 0.73, (r (rb)) = −0.15, DLE: 11.16 ± 17.14 mm vs. 13.55 ± 18.37 mm; p = 0.62, (r (rb)) = 0.20, and SD: 27.07 ± 16.85 mm vs 30.82 ± 27.40 mm; p = 0.84, (r (rb)) = −0.10; Figure S2). No statistically significant differences were found between good and poor outcome groups when considering precision and recall metrics (Figure S1). Regarding the correlation between these spatial metrics, for EEG/MEG, we found that AUC correlated negatively with DLE (ρ = −0.64, p < 0.001) and with SD (ρ = −0.57, p = 0.005), whereas DLE correlated positively with SD (ρ = 0.40, p = 0.05; Figure 4). Similarly, for EEG/fMRI (Figure 4), AUC correlated negatively with DLE (ρ = −0.68, p = 0.006) and with SD (ρ = −0.60, p = 0.02), whereas DLE and SD showed a positive trend of correlation (ρ = 0.49, p = 0.07). No significant association was found between surgical cavity surface area (cm2) and postoperative outcome (50.46 ± 35.26 cm2 vs 41.49 ± 26.89 cm2; p = 0.56, (r (rb)) = −0.14).

text: Using the combined threshold of AUC > 0.70 and DLE = 0 mm to assess the ability of each modality in predicting postoperative outcome at the patient‐level, EMSI achieved a PPV of 57% [95% confidence interval [CI]: 25%–84%], NPV of 62% [39%–82%], and an accuracy of 61% [41%–78%]. EEG/fMRI showed a PPV of 100%, NPV of 83% [55%–95%], and an accuracy of 86% [60%–96%]. When considering DLE = 0 mm alone, EMSI predictive values increased with a PPV of 67% [35%–88%], NPV of 71% [45%–88%], and an accuracy of 70% [49%–86%]. Results from EEG/fMRI remained the same (Table S1). Of the 12 patients with contributive results from both modalities, two showed spatially concordant findings, with the maximum localization of both EMSI and the most significant fMRI cluster located within the surgical cavity; both patients achieved good outcome (Figure 5, P#16). The remaining 10 patients displayed discordant localizations between modalities. Among them, only two patients achieved good outcome, one with the EMSI localization resected (DLE = 0 mm), whereas the maximum fMRI response was relatively distant from the cavity (DLE = 36.16 mm; Figure 5, P#15), and the other one with both EMSI and fMRI results near the resection margin (DLE = 8.50 mm for fMRI and DLE = 18.10 mm for EMSI). Among the eight patients with poor outcome (Figure 5, P#18), none had the maximum fMRI response inside the surgical cavity, whereas the EMSI maximum was resected in three of them.

text: This study quantitatively assessed how EMSI primary source and EEG/fMRI most significant fMRI cluster relate to the surgical cavity and seizure outcome in drug‐resistant focal epilepsy. For EMSI results, patients with good outcome showed greater spatial overlap, shorter distance to the resection cavity, and a trend toward lower spatial dispersion around the cavity compared with those with poor outcome. Although EEG/fMRI metrics did not differ significantly between outcome groups, similar trends were observed (Figure S2), and, importantly, not resecting the most significant fMRI clusters was strongly predictive of poor outcome. When both modalities were available, patients with concordant and resected localizations (n = 2) achieved a good outcome, supporting the complementary value of integrating source localization and hemodynamic information in the presurgical workup. Our EEG/fMRI findings are consistent with previous large‐scale studies (70 and 84 patients) demonstrating that when the peak of the most significant fMRI cluster was not resected, the likelihood of achieving a good outcome was low, especially in cases where the difference in absolute t‐values between the most significant and the next cluster was large, indicating high‐confidence results. 19 , 21 In our cohort, 10 of 12 patients (83%) whose peak voxel of the most significant fMRI cluster was located outside the surgical cavity had poor outcome. Among the two remaining patients, one did not have a high confidence result (Figure S3), whereas the other exhibited a high confidence result with a DLE of 8.5 mm. Under our strict criterion (DLE = 0 mm), this latter case was classified as non‐resected; however, using a broader 2 cm distance criterion, including both complete and partial concordance with the surgical cavity, as in a previous study, 21 the same patient would have been considered resected. This interpretation aligns with prior results showing that this cluster often co‐localizes with the seizure‐onset zone, the main clinical proxy of the p‐EZ, identified by intracerebral EEG. 10 , 18 Regarding EEG/MEG, our results showed a significant association at the voxel level between resection of the EMSI cluster with the largest number of IEDs and good outcome. This finding aligns with prior results showing that removal of the source‐imaging localization is associated with good outcome. 9 , 20 , 39 , 40 In a large MEG study of 1000 cases (149 underwent epilepsy surgery and had a follow‐up of at least 1 year postoperatively), the authors reported a PPV of 83%, NPV of 65%, and a sensitivity of 66% for complete MEG resection in predicting outcome, using dipole modeling for source localization. 9 In another EEG/MEG study of 141 patients (57 operated) comparing multiple software packages and different standard source imaging approaches, the authors found a PPV between 60% and 83%, NPV between 42% and 49%, and an accuracy ranging from 44% to 57%, depending on the localization method/software used. 20 In our study, using the same proximity‐based criterion (DLE = 0 mm), we obtained a PPV of 67%, NPV of 71%, sensitivity of 60%, and an accuracy of 70% (Table S1). text: and a sensitivity of 66% for complete MEG resection in predicting outcome, using dipole modeling for source localization. 9 In another EEG/MEG study of 141 patients (57 operated) comparing multiple software packages and different standard source imaging approaches, the authors found a PPV between 60% and 83%, NPV between 42% and 49%, and an accuracy ranging from 44% to 57%, depending on the localization method/software used. 20 In our study, using the same proximity‐based criterion (DLE = 0 mm), we obtained a PPV of 67%, NPV of 71%, sensitivity of 60%, and an accuracy of 70% (Table S1). Some variabilities in predictive performance across studies are expected, as differences in patients electroclinical presentation, in software, source localization methods, and the epileptologist performing IED marking have all been shown to influence outcomes. 20 , 39 Of interest, when combining DLE with AUC to account for both proximity and spatial overlap, the overall predictive performance slightly decreased (PPV from 67% to 57%, NPV from 71% to 62%, and accuracy from 70% to 61%). This reduction may reflect the fact that the p‐EZ may not be a homogeneous entity but a spatially distributed network where certain nodes may be more critical for seizure generation. 25 , 41 , 42 Therefore, resection of these key nodes may be sufficient to achieve surgical success, even if parts of the broader generator remain. Thus, although a good spatial overlap between EMSI localizations and the surgical cavity differentiated good from poor outcomes at the group level in our study, extensive overlap may not be necessary for individual success. Our threshold (AUC > 0.70) might therefore have been a little bit conservative. Future studies with larger datasets are needed to refine optimal spatial thresholds and investigate the network properties of the p‐EZ. Another relevant point is related to the voxel level spatial analyses. In a previous source imaging study of 29 patients, recall and precision values were moderate (0.6) in those with good outcome and slightly lower (0.4–0.5) in those with poor outcome, without significant group differences. 22 In our cohort (n = 23), recall, which represents the overlap between EMSI localization and surgical cavity normalized by surgical cavity, was similar between groups (0.24 in good vs 0.20 in poor outcome, Figure S1), whereas precision, which indicates the overlap between EMSI localization and surgical cavity normalized by EMSI map, differed significantly (0.77 vs 0.36m Figure S1). This discrepancy may be explained by methodological differences, as cMEM may produce more focal maps 14 than the source imaging method used previously. 22 Consequently, with cMEM, a lower sensitivity but higher precision (along with a lower rate of FP) would be expected when comparing to the surgical cavity. These results suggest that EMSI effectively captures part of the p‐EZ (approximated by the surgical cavity). Of note, the significantly higher AUC values observed in patients with good outcome indicate that MEM‐derived estimates of spatial extent remain clinically informative and provide complementary information beyond simple peak localization. text: may be explained by methodological differences, as cMEM may produce more focal maps 14 than the source imaging method used previously. 22 Consequently, with cMEM, a lower sensitivity but higher precision (along with a lower rate of FP) would be expected when comparing to the surgical cavity. These results suggest that EMSI effectively captures part of the p‐EZ (approximated by the surgical cavity). Of note, the significantly higher AUC values observed in patients with good outcome indicate that MEM‐derived estimates of spatial extent remain clinically informative and provide complementary information beyond simple peak localization. However, it is important to mention that the resection cavity generally exceeds the true EZ and may not represent the ground truth, particularly in patients with poor outcome. Surgical success depends more on the proportion of accurately localized epileptogenic tissue (precision) than on the total spatial overlap with the surgical cavity. Of interest, when applying the AUC metric, which integrates both precision and recall into a continuous, surface‐based measure rather than a voxel‐wise binary classification (i.e., precision and recall), we were able to distinguish good and poor outcomes. This indicates that AUC captures more anatomically meaningful and clinically relevant information than simple overlap metrics that are threshold dependent. It highlights that not only the extent but also the intensity and spatial organization of abnormal activity identified by EMSI contain clinically relevant information. 43 In line with this, correlations among spatial metrics further support the structured organization of epileptogenic activity. Higher AUC values were associated with shorter DLE and lower SD, whereas DLE correlated positively with SD. These relationships indicate that regions closer to the surgical cavity tended to be more spatially compact and more strongly overlapping with the surgical cavity. In a recent study involving MEG and intracranial EEG simultaneously acquired, we further confirmed the performance of cMEM in recovering the generators of IEDs with their underlying spatial extents, resulting in similar AUC values. 44 EMSI was contributive in a larger proportion of patients than EEG/fMRI (23/25 vs 14/25), likely because EEG/fMRI requires both sufficient interictal activity during scanning and a statistically significant hemodynamic response after correction for multiple comparisons. In contrast, EMSI can be applied more broadly when sufficient IEDs (>5) are recorded. Although this may suggest greater practical applicability of EMSI, the two modalities appear complementary rather than interchangeable, as EEG/fMRI may still provide additional value, particularly for deep generators, 12 , 13 where EEG/MEG source imaging can be more challenging. 44 Finally, combining these modalities yielded the highest predictive accuracy. All patients with concordant and resected EMSI and EEG/fMRI localizations achieved good outcome, whereas discordant results were associated with poorer outcome (8/10 patients with discordant results had poor outcome). These findings are consistent with a prior multimodal study showing that resection of concordant regions was associated with good outcome. 23 This complementary value reflects their underlying physiology: EMSI captures rapid neuronal discharges with high temporal precision, primarily reflecting the zone generating the most frequent IEDs but also the seizure‐onset zone, 5 , 7

text: EEG/MEG source imaging can be more challenging. 44 Finally, combining these modalities yielded the highest predictive accuracy. All patients with concordant and resected EMSI and EEG/fMRI localizations achieved good outcome, whereas discordant results were associated with poorer outcome (8/10 patients with discordant results had poor outcome). These findings are consistent with a prior multimodal study showing that resection of concordant regions was associated with good outcome. 23 This complementary value reflects their underlying physiology: EMSI captures rapid neuronal discharges with high temporal precision, primarily reflecting the zone generating the most frequent IEDs but also the seizure‐onset zone, 5 , 7 , 10 , 30 whereas EEG/fMRI detects slower, spatially distributed hemodynamic changes in brain regions with highest oxygen consumption, typically corresponding to the spike‐onset and seizure‐onset zones. 12 , 17 , 18 The strengths of this study include the integration of multimodal data on a common cortical surface, allowing direct spatial comparison across modalities, and the use of quantitative, continuous metrics that extend beyond categorical classifications. However, this study also has limitations. The sample size was relatively small. In our center, EEG/MEG and EEG/fMRI are performed primarily in complex cases; therefore, the clinical yield of each modality across all presurgical patients is unknown. This was particularly true for patients with contributive results from both modalities, which further reduced statistical power. In addition, multimodal concordance analyses were restricted to patients with contributive findings from both modalities. Therefore, the predictive performance of concordant vs discordant results applies only to this selected subgroup and may overestimate the clinical utility of multimodal concordance in an intent‐to‐treat perspective. Only the most significant fMRI cluster was analyzed, potentially omitting clinically relevant information from other clusters. However, this cluster has been shown to best correlate with intracerebral findings and surgical outcome. 8 , 17 , 18 , 21 Similarly, for EMSI, only the cluster with the largest number of IEDs was included. 10 Although this approach has been shown to yield more reliable and physiologically consistent results, 15 , 16 it may have excluded relevant information from smaller clusters. At the individual level, the interpretation of AUC should be made with caution, as our results are derived from group‐level analyses. AUC reflects the proportion of the EMSI, EEG/fMRI results contained within the surgical cavity and may be clinically informative. To mitigate the effects of postoperative brain deformation and cavity shrinkage, the resection cavity was smoothed with a 5‐mm kernel and projected onto the preoperative cortical surface. A strong correlation between cavity size measured in the original volume space and after projection onto the cortical surface was found, supporting the validity of our surface‐based approach (Figure S4). Higher AUC values, particularly when associated with high precision and short distances to the resection, suggest that the identified region is well captured by the planned surgery, whereas lower AUC values may indicate partial overlap or extension beyond it. text: This study quantitatively shows that EEG/MEG and EEG/fMRI provide complementary spatial information relevant to presurgical evaluation in drug‐resistant focal epilepsy. By assessing overlap, proximity, and dispersion relative to the surgical cavity, we gained a more nuanced understanding of how EEG/MEG and EEG/fMRI localizations relate to surgical outcome. Notably, when both modalities were spatially concordant and resected, patients tended to achieve surgical success, whereas discordant results were associated with poorer prognosis.

text: Epilepsy can have profound impacts on an individual's life, with increased risk of premature mortality, poor mental health outcomes, and decreased quality of life. For most people, antiseizure medications can control seizure occurrence, mitigating negative impacts of epilepsy on life expectancy and quality of life. However, one third of people with epilepsy will be drug‐resistant, meaning they will continue to have seizures despite two adequate trials of different antiseizure medications. 1 For patients with drug‐resistant epilepsy, surgery has been shown to promote seizure remission, reduce associated mortality and morbidity, and improve quality of life. 2 , 3 , 4 Increased success of seizure‐free status postsurgery is associated with earlier referrals after diagnosis of drug‐resistance is established. 5 Current guidelines suggest that surgery should be considered as a treatment in these cases, but despite positive outcomes, surgery remains underutilized. 6 The underutilization of epilepsy surgery has been attributed to a variety of reasons, including patient fears regarding surgery risks and a lack of high‐quality resources to inform and guide patients and their caregivers in making these decisions. Interest in epilepsy surgery has been shown to change when additional information on benefits and complications is provided, reinforcing the role of patient education in decision‐making. 7 , 8 Because misconceptions about the risk of surgery are prominent, 9 it is important that information shared with people living with epilepsy is accurate and informed by their needs. Information resources that focus on epilepsy surgery are highly variable in the content provided, readability, and information quality and often fail to address the specific needs of this patient population. To address the above gaps, the primary aim of this study was to conduct a scoping review to identify the information needs of people considering epilepsy surgery. This includes the specific type of information content, timing and delivery of information, and quality of information desired by patients, caregivers, and family members. Our secondary aims were to identify the barriers and facilitators that exist in deciding to undergo epilepsy surgery and establish what elements are needed when creating a resource to support patient decision‐making about epilepsy surgery. Findings from this scoping review could inform the future development of high‐quality resources that could help patients and their care partners with epilepsy surgery decision‐making.

text: Our search strategy (Appendix S1) incorporated the following databases: American Psychological Association PsycInfo (Ovid), CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature; EBSCO), Education Research Complete (EBSCO), EMBASE (Ovid), MEDLINE (Ovid), SocINDEX (EBSCO), Social Services Abstracts (ProQuest), Sociological Abstracts (ProQuest), and Web of Science (Clarivate). We searched these databases from 1990 to March 2025 to capture studies released after the introduction of clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for epilepsy, because MRI has been instrumental in the surgical evaluation process. 11 Furthermore, this captures most studies that have been completed since the creation of the internet, and our literature review suggested the most common place for patients to access resources was online. Our search was not limited by language. Reference lists of included studies were reviewed to identify additional sources.

text: Our research question was guided by the Population, Concept, Context Framework. We included studies that addressed informational needs of patients or caregivers considering surgical intervention for epilepsy management. Additionally, we included studies that discussed information‐based resources that are available to epilepsy patients regarding surgery. Studies that focused on information needs of health care providers were excluded in addition to abstracts, conference proceedings, protocols, case series, case reports, editorials, opinion pieces, and dissertations.

text: Data charting was completed by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved through consensus. Due to the nature of the scoping review, a narrative synthesis was undertaken. For all included studies, we used calibrated forms for data charting. We collected the following study characteristics: year of publication, data collection years, country, study type, sample size, and demographic characteristics of the study population. When available, we collected specific data on the type of surgical intervention being considered and the type of epilepsy of the patient population. For qualitative studies, data outlining information needs, facilitators and barriers to decision‐making, and descriptions of resources were collected to address information needs of this patient population. Additionally, information on the perceived or objectively scored quality of information resources was collected. For clinical trials, we also collected a description of the resource being evaluated, intervention target, and measured outcome.

text: Risk of bias assessment was completed by one reviewer for all included studies using design‐appropriate tools. Assessment of study quality was completed by a single reviewer. To enhance consistency, the reviewer followed standardized assessment frameworks as follows. The Risk of Bias in Non‐Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS‐I V2) 12 tool was used to appraise interventional studies, and the published algorithm was followed to assess the overall degree of bias. For cross‐sectional studies, risk of bias was categorized by subheading using the Appraisal Tool for Cross‐Sectional Studies (AXIS). 13 Low risk of bias was assigned when all questions within a given AXIS subheading were adequately addressed. Moderate risk of bias was assigned when one or two subquestions within a subheading were not addressed, and severe risk of bias was assigned when more than two subquestions were not addressed. AXIS scoring was applied as a point per item method, assuming equal weighting of items. Finally, Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) 14 was followed for qualitative studies and reported by each question in the tool to identify sources of bias.

text: Table 1 summarizes study characteristics of studies included in the analysis. Six studies were published from the United States, 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 five from Europe, 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 three from Australia, 26 , 27 , 28 two from Canada, 7 , 29 and two from Asia. 30 , 31 Twelve studies explored information needs of patients, 7 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 21 , 23 , 25 , 27 , 28 , 31 nine 15 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 23 , 25 , 27 , 28 , 29 of which used qualitative methods whereas three 7 , 16 , 21 used cross‐sectional surveys. Five clinical trials were also included evaluating existing resources, 22 , 26 , 29 , 30 , 31 as well as two cross‐sectional readability analyses of information‐based resources. 20 , 24 Of these studies, one included both qualitative interviews and a quasiexperimental evaluation of an education program. 31 The study populations of included studies were heterogenous, with seven focused broadly on patients with epilepsy, 7 , 15 , 16 , 21 , 26 , 27 , 28 four on both patients and caregivers/family members, 22 , 25 , 30 , 31 and four on exclusively pediatric patients and their caregivers. 17 , 18 , 23 , 29 Additionally, six studies elicited perspectives about the information needs of patients and their caregivers from various health care professionals involved in epilepsy care including epileptologists, general neurologists, neurosurgeons, primary care physicians, and nurses. 19 , 22 , 25 , 27 , 28 , 29

text: Risk of bias was assessed and is presented in Figure 2A–C. The nine qualitative studies were appraised using the CASP checklist. All qualitative studies demonstrated at least one potential source of bias, most commonly related to insufficient reporting of the relationship between the researchers and participants, which limited assessment of the research team's influence on data collection and interpretation. Five cross‐sectional studies were evaluated using the AXIS‐I tool. All cross‐sectional studies exhibited methodological bias, most frequently due to small, unjustified sample sizes that were identified as limiting data analysis. No study was able to provide information on nonresponders, limiting assessment of response bias. The ROBINS‐I tool was used to assess risk of bias for interventional studies. Primary sources of bias among these studies included failure to identify and control for confounding variables and lack of blinding both participants and researchers to intervention. We were unable to complete risk assessment for one study 27 outlining development of an implementation science model for patient decision‐making as no validated appraisal tool was identified.

text: Figure 3 provides an infographic summary of the main findings. Results of individual studies are summarized in Tables 2 and 3. From the 12 studies that discussed specific information needs of patients, recurring themes included discussion of risks and benefits, personalized prognoses, guides for presurgical assessments, steps that go into decision‐making, and what to expect during recovery. 7 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 21 , 23 , 25 , 27 , 28 Additionally, two studies from the United States emphasized increased need for information on navigating the health care system including insurance procedures. 17 , 18 Four studies focused on information needs of caregivers for pediatric patients. 17 , 18 , 23 , 29 Themes of informational needs for this population encompassed the same categories. In addition, one study emphasized the need for information on how children are prioritized for surgery and the limitations of assessments and surgical procedures that are related to a pediatric patient's age. 23 Additionally, another study emphasized how providing increased education on epilepsy and management can decrease caregiver burnout and improve quality of life for both caregivers and patients. 31 Across studies that included caregiver perspectives, the psychological burden of caregiving was addressed in five. 17 , 18 , 23 , 25 , 31 One study evaluated the impact of addressing information needs on burnout and found that addressing informational needs of caregivers led to increased quality of life and feelings of empowerment toward providing care. 31

text: Ten of the 12 studies that addressed informational needs commented specifically on what is needed in a resource to support decision‐making or how this information should be delivered. 7 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 23 , 25 , 28 , 31 Six studies highlighted the value and need of including testimonials from previous patients. 15 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 25 , 28 Vicarious experiences were identified as being especially valuable if patients shared the same specific illness or potential procedure. Six studies also mentioned the importance of incorporating clinical data presented by field experts in epilepsy alongside patient testimonials. 19 , 22 , 25 , 27 , 28 , 29 Three studies mentioned the importance of a multimedia format utilizing analog, digital, and video means of delivering information. 15 , 19 , 23 Three studies that included family members as participants suggested there is also a desire for family‐specific interventions. 19 , 25 , 31

text: In general, most studies highlighted the heterogeneity of information available for people considering epilepsy surgery and how high‐quality information is usually lacking. Available resources were considered too broad and not specific enough to fit individual patient circumstances. Increased descriptions of the surgical process from preprocedure assessment to potential complications during recovery increased patients' confidence in their decision‐making. 15 Patients who received conflicting information were also driven to seek clarification through online sources including social media 15 , 23 ; however, accuracy of this information was identified as being difficult to discern. 15 , 31 Two studies explored the readability of patient‐focused web‐based resources addressing epilepsy surgery. The first found the Flesch–Kincaid Reading Ease score to be 37.35 (interquartile range [IQR] = 26.80–14.53) and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level to be 12.20 (IQR = 10.87–13.91) across 82 websites. 20 Similarly, a second study found that the average readability across 49 websites was found to score at or above college level when using seven distinct readability formulas. 24 Additionally, one qualitative focus group study found that patients were overwhelmed by information that was provided and suggested the need for a glossary of terms to be provided when discussions of surgery emerged. 15

text: Five clinical trials aimed to evaluate existing resources that were developed to support the decision‐making process surrounding epilepsy surgery. 22 , 26 , 29 , 30 , 31 Three studies addressed intensive information programs, with one addressing patients 26 and two focusing on caregivers. 30 , 31 The information program designed for adult patients found significant reductions in depression and anxiety following use. 26 Another mixed reality tool found that when compared to teaching with a rubber brain model, adult patients had increased comprehensibility and a decrease in presurgical anxiety. 22 The authors hypothesized that the change in presurgical anxiety could have resulted from the use of three‐dimensional MRI imaging in the mixed reality tool, enabling a deeper understanding of brain anatomy and the procedure, ultimately leading to a reduction in fear. Among the two information programs for caregivers, one showed a similar decrease in anxiety and depression as seen among patients. 30 The other also indicated added benefit through decreased difficulty in managing epilepsy, increased knowledge about epilepsy, and increased quality of life among caregivers following use. 31 A final study focused on pediatric patients through the implementation of a personal decision coach for parents, showing significant improvement in decisional conflict, uncertainty, and preparedness for decision‐making. 29 No studies we identified directly engaged pediatric patients.
