text: MPF was calculated as follows: power spectrum analysis was performed—using the discrete Fourier transform “fft” function in MATLAB—on the band‐pass filtered recording (see Signal recording and analysis in animals and Human recording and analysis sections for more filtering information). The MPF was defined as the frequency at which the total spectral power is equally distributed, with 50% below and 50% above this value. Hence, MPF calculation is a technique of dimensionality reduction providing a global picture of the spectrogram with a single metric. As described, 18 , 37 MPF was calculated in 2‐s‐long signal epochs with 1‐s overlap. This MPF calculation then allowed further characterization of both PSWE and non‐PSWE epochs. Median power frequency was defined as the frequency bin at which the cumulative spectral power reached 50% of the total power within the analyzed epoch; thus, it represents the 50th percentile of the spectral power distribution.

text: Local changes in channel activity during PSWE in remote brain regions were investigated. For each “local” channel, MPF was calculated and then averaged, either during PSWE and non‐PSWE epochs in specific remote brain regions. MPF variation was then defined as: (1) ΔMPFlocalHz=MPFlocalt=remotePSWE−MPFlocalt=remotenoPSWE where MPFlocalt=remotePSWE and MPFlocalt=remotenoPSWE are the mean MPFs in the “local” channel during PSWE and non‐PSWE activity in the “remote” channel, respectively. Δ power, estimated as mean squared amplitude [V2], was calculated similarly. First, mean‐squared amplitude was calculated by squaring the voltage values of the 1–45 Hz band‐pass filtered recording. Then, within each segment, percentage change was calculated as: (2) ΔVlocal2%=Vlocal2t=remotePSWE−Vlocal2t=remotenoPSWEVlocal2t=remotenoPSWE×100 For correlation analysis, MPF and power variation were calculated as ratios: (3) ΔrMPFlocal=MPFlocalt=remotePSWE−MPFlocalt=remotenoPSWEMPFlocalt=remotenoPSWE for the MPF and (4) ΔrVlocal2=Vlocal2t=remotePSWE−Vlocal2t=remotenoPSWEVlocal2t=remotenoPSWE for the power. To conduct the Pearson analysis of Figure 2C, mean ΔrMPF as well as mean ΔrV2 were both calculated for each combination of remote channel and local brain region (in which MPF and voltage were measured in parallel with PSWE detection or when no PSWE was recorded in the remote channel) for each of the 10 animals (timeline shown in Figure S1B) giving a total of more than 500 mean ΔrMPF and mean ΔrV2 coupled values. Because those calculations rely on means rather than events, no animal was overrepresented (e.g., with a higher number of events than average).

text: Additional pharmacological experiments were performed in paraoxon‐treated rats with established epilepsy (8–12 weeks post‐injection). Here, montage and recording settings were identical to those shown in Figure S1A but the experimental timeline differed (not shown). Animals received intraperitoneal injections of the pro‐convulsant GABAA receptor antagonist, pentylenetetrazol (PTZ, 10 mg/kg, n = 3) or the anticonvulsant barbiturate pentobarbital (PENTO, 4 mg/kg, n = 3), five times at 30‐min intervals. Intracerebral activity was recorded before and during treatment to assess effects of GABAergic modulation on PSWEs. Animals were killed 20 min after the last injection. To analyze treatment effects, we first constructed correlograms aligned to injection time and quantified PSWE occurrence (Figure 3E,F). For each animal, the pre‐injection baseline interval −1200, 0s was compared with the 0, 1200s interval following each of the five injections. Correlograms were constructed using 60‐s bins. Correlogram data were analyzed using the Friedman test followed by false discovery rate (FDR) correction with the two‐stage step‐up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli, allowing comparison of each time bin with the others. For the summed analysis, all baseline bins from −1200, 0s were pooled and compared with the pooled post‐injection bins from each injection window separately (∑ baseline vs ∑ injection 1, ∑ baseline vs ∑ injection 2, etc.). This yielded five comparisons per animal (yielding 15 observations per group). Statistical differences in summed data were assessed using the two‐tailed non‐parametric Wilcoxon test.

text: The retrospective study of anonymized patient data was approved by the Rabin Medical Center institutional review board (IRB). Stereo‐encephalography (sEEG) with simultaneous scalp EEG was performed during routine pre‐surgical evaluation. Five depth macroelectrodes (8–10 contacts, 5‐mm spacing; Ad‐Tech, USA) were stereotactically implanted (CRW frame, Integra, USA), targeting the amygdala, anterior and posterior hippocampus, and posterior temporal and occipitotemporal cortex (for electrode coordinates see Table S2). Planning was based on pre‐operative 3 T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Philips, Netherlands) co‐registered with intraoperative computerized tomography (CT) (O‐arm, Medtronic, Ireland) using Stealth 8 navigation (Medtronic); post‐operative CT confirmed electrode placement. Recordings began 24 h post‐surgery, sampled at 2 kHz, and downsampled to 250 Hz. Scalp EEG (10–20 system, 19 electrodes) was sampled at 250 Hz. Patients pressed a trigger button at seizure onset. Data were preprocessed in EEGLAB 38 as reported previously 18 , 19 , 21 : band‐pass filtered (1–45 Hz), decomposed with independent component analysis (ICA), and artifact components (muscle, eye, heart) removed using ICLabel. 39 Preprocessed EEG was segmented into 2‐s windows (50% overlap) and MPF calculated. PSWEs were defined as an MPF of 1–6 Hz for ≥5 s in ≥2 electrodes. For scalp EEG during long‐term monitoring, data were stored in 1‐h blocks (University of Freiburg SQL servers). The block containing a seizure and the preceding hour were retrieved, merged, and aligned to seizure onset, yielding 60 min preictal and 20 min postictal data. Recordings with ictal activity in the 1‐h period preceding the seizure onset or data gaps >3 s were excluded.

text: Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 9. When PSWE features (occurrence, duration, MPF) failed normality, data were analyzed with the Kruskal–Wallis test. Normally distributed measures (% time in PSWE, MPF during PSWE) were tested with mixed‐effects analysis of variance (ANOVA; Geisser–Greenhouse correction). Correlogram data were analyzed with non‐parametric tests. FDR correction (two‐stage step‐up, Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli) was applied to ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis, Friedman, and two‐way ANOVA. Q values (q) represent FDR‐adjusted significance with q min/p min = strongest significance and q max/p max = weakest. Because several analyses involved numerous and partially interdependent comparisons, particularly in temporally structured correlogram data, family‐wise correction methods such as Bonferroni were considered overly conservative. We therefore used FDR correction, which better balances sensitivity and false‐positive control in datasets with dependent comparisons, such as neurophysiological recordings.

text: Consistent with prior results, 18 PSWE occurrence, duration, and time in PSWEs increased in epileptic rats vs pre‐SE baseline (Figure 1E; Figure S2A), with no change in controls (PSWE/min, p = 0.0052; percent time in PSWE, p = 0.0006, Wilcoxon two‐tailed tests). PSWEs were detected across all electrodes but occurred more frequently in the right medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC R.) and lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC R.) than in the visual cortex (V1 R.) (1.37 ± 0.16, 1.16 ± 0.43 and 0.25 ± 0.25 PSWE/min, respectively, Kruskal–Wallis p < 0.0001, statistic = 47.37; Figure 1F). Likewise, the percent time in PSWEs was higher in mPFC R. and LEC R. than in V1 R. (73.14% ± 10%, 47.6% ± 22.5%, and 8.01% ± 10.17%, respectively, mixed‐effects analysis p < 0.0005; overall p < 0.0001, F(2.922, 25.46) = 31.30, Geisser–Greenhouse ε = 0.4174; Figure 1G). Similarly, PSWE duration was longer in mPFC R. (32.7 ± 6.7 s) and LEC R. (24.1 ± 8.3 s) than V1 R. (15.02 ± 5.17 s; p < 0.03; Figure S2C). MPF was lower in mPFC R. (2.85 ± 0.3) but not in LEC R. (3.18 ± 0.31), compared to V1 R. (3.55 ± 0.4; p = 0.005; Figure S2D). These findings indicate region‐specific PSWE patterns. For details of the Kruskal–Wallis and mixed‐effects analysis, see the corresponding matrices (#Q, ##Q; Figure 1F,G). In contrast, analysis of the relative change in MPF showed that the drop during PSWE (expressed as percent baseline) was greatest in the epidural electrodes (Epi. Ant. R. and Epi. Post. R., Figure S2E). The largest MPF decrease was observed in the Epi. Ant. R., whereas the smallest decrease was in the LEC L. (−49.23% ± 3.74% vs −29.84% ± 3.19%, respectively; p < 0.0001, mixed‐effects analysis; Figure S2E). Overall, the magnitude of MPF reduction during PSWEs, relative to baseline, differed across electrodes (Figure S2E) and the corresponding z‐scores are shown in Figure S2F.

text: To test whether PSWE in one region was linked to remote changes, we measured MPF across channels during PSWEs recorded in any given channel. PSWEs in one channel were associated with a slowing (MPF reduction) in others (−1.22 ± 0.8 Hz; Figure 2A; two‐way ANOVA, q max = 0.0228, q min < 0.0001; corresponding normalized z‐score can be found in Figure S2G), and with increased power (94.32% ± 102.5%; Figure 2B). MPF reduction correlated with power increase (r = −0.514, p < 0.0001, Pearson correlation; Figure 2C), suggesting greater network synchronization during PSWEs. Correlogram analysis showed that PSWE rate rose in mPFC R. and LEC R. 60–1 s before detection in the anterior epidural electrode (Figure 2D,G; q max = 0.0040, q min < 0.0001, and q max = 0.063 and q min < 0.0001, Friedman test for the mPFC R. and LEC R., respectively). PSWEs in the posterior epidural electrode appeared with a delay relative to the anterior epidural electrode (Figure 2E), indicating propagation. Across channels, PSWE peaks coincided with or followed onset in LEC R. (Figure 2F,G). These findings suggest that PSWEs are associated with ictogenic regions and induce slowing (see Discussion).

text: Spontaneous seizures were recorded in all paraoxon‐treated rats. Video‐EEG showed behavioral arrest with or without jerks or tonic seizures. Correlogram analysis revealed that PSWE occurrence was higher during seizures than in preictal period (−60 to 0 s; Figure 3A,B; two‐way ANOVA, q max = 0.0315, q min < 0.0001). Across channels, time in PSWE was greater during seizures compared to overall baseline (Figure 3C, q max = 0.0067, q min < 0.0001). MPF was the lowest during a PSWE, higher during seizures, and highest outside PSWEs (Figure 3D). To test whether PSWEs reflect an hyperexcitable state or more inhibitory drive, epileptic rats received the pro‐convulsant GABAergic antagonist PTZ or positive GABAA modulator PENTO. PTZ application concurrently increased PSWE occurrence and triggered epileptiform activity and seizures (2/3 rats after one injection; one rat developed SE after the fifth; Figure 3E). PTZ Friedman test's overall p‐value was < 0.0001 for the correlograms. Summed pre‐injection −1200, 0 time bins had significantly lower total number of PSWEs compared to post‐injection 0, 1200 interval (1 ± 1.46 vs. 7.26 ± 11.37, p < 0.0156 two‐tailed Wilcoxon). PENTO reduced PSWE rates and spontaneous movement (Figure 3F). Friedman test's overall p‐value was < 0.0001 for the full correlograms. Summed pre‐injection −1200, 0 time bins had significantly higher total number of PSWE compared to post‐injection 0, 1200 interval (3.66 ± 4.65 vs 0.86 ± 1.59, p < 0.0078 two‐tailed Wilcoxon). These findings suggest that PSWEs reflect hyperexcitable, hypersynchronized, network states suppressed by GABAA transmission.

text: To examine PSWEs in human patients, we analyzed retrospective EEG data from 18 individuals with TLE (137 seizures; European database, see Methods). PSWEs were detected during interictal, preictal (~3 min) and post‐onset periods (Figure 4A). The percent time in PSWEs was lower in the interictal interval compared to the preictal interval (61.29% ± 29.98%, 66.03% ± 29.31%, respectively; p = 0.0006, Mann–Whitney U test) and lower in the interictal interval compared to the postictal interval (61.29% ± 29.98%, 66.81% ± 28.94%, respectively; p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test). PSWE duration in the interictal interval was lower compared to the preictal interval (34.61 ± 20.37, 38.49 ± 19.65 s, respectively; p = 0.0002, Mann–Whitney U test) and in the interictal interval compared to the postictal interval (34.61 ± 20.37, 38.49 ± 19.67 s, respectively; p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test). There were fewer channels detecting PSWEs in the interictal interval compared to the preictal interval (65.72% ± 32.22%, 71.39% ± 30.66%, respectively; p = 0.0004, Mann–Whitney U test) and in the interictal interval compared to the postictal interval (65.72% ± 32.22%, 73.54% ± 30.35%, respectively; p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test). MPF during PSWEs was higher in the interictal interval compared to the postictal interval (2.99 ± 0.71 Hz, 2.67 ± 0.78 Hz, respectively; p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test) and in the preictal interval compared to the postictal interval (2.87 ± 0.85 Hz, 2.67 ± 0.78 Hz, respectively; p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test).

text: Rodent and human data indicated that PSWEs are linked to network hyperexcitability and seizures. To test whether surface PSWEs reflect remote epileptiform activity, we averaged spike–wave (SW) discharges during seizures in rats (Figure 5A). SWs consistently originated in the LEC followed by hippocampus and mPFC R. (Figure 5B). Wave components were simultaneously observed in epidural electrodes with inverted polarity, but was absent in V1 R. electrode (Figure S3D). Correlation between LEC R. and ipsilateral epidural signals was stronger and more negative during PSWEs vs background activity (no PSWEs) (r = −0.35 vs r = −0.21, n = 10, p < 0.0001, paired t test; Figure 5B). These findings suggest that PSWEs reflect cortical slowing driven by deep epileptiform discharges. We next analyzed simultaneous surface and sEEG recordings from a right‐handed man in his 30s with drug‐resistant TLE (tumor in the right temporal lobe, extending to the temporal horn of the right lateral ventricle, involving the head and body of the hippocampus; Figure S5). Because seizure onset could not be localized using video‐EEG long‐term monitoring, five sEEG electrodes were implanted in the right temporal lobe, specifically in the amygdala, anterior and posterior hippocampus, and posterior temporal cortex and temporo‐occipital junction. sEEG showed seizure onset in the posterior hippocampal electrode (Contacts 1 and 2) with spread to the posterior temporal cortex (Contact 1, Figure 5C). Clinical onset (color distortion, staring, oral automatism) occurred 9 s later (indicated by “Trigger 2” in Figure 5C.2), whereas EEG remained silent until spread. Across four seizures, PSWE occurrence, percentage time in PSWEs, and duration rose in the right temporal electrodes 20–60 s before clinical onset and the appearance of the electrographic seizure on the scalp EEG (Figure 5D,E). As in rats, hippocampal SWs were associated with surface slowing (Figure 5F).

text: Recent work suggests that paroxysmal slow‐wave events (or PSWEs) may mark epileptic brain states. 18 , 21 , 37 We show that PSWEs preferentially arise in temporo‐frontal networks, increase pre‐ictally, correlate with deep temporal epileptiform activity, and are bidirectionally modulated by GABAergic drugs. Together, these findings support PSWEs as a noninvasive index of ictogenic activity. In rats, PSWEs were most prominent in entorhinal cortex and ventral mPFC, two regions strongly implicated in TLE. Occurrence in one site coincided with global slowing and power increases, consistent with widespread network synchronization. Correlogram analyses further suggested initiation in anterior temporal structures with subsequent neocortical spread (Figure 2D–G, Figure S3A–C). Notably, q values were lowest around time 0 across several channel comparisons, indicating tight temporal coupling between regional events. However, some apparent backward extension of PSWE peaks into earlier pre‐ictal bins may reflect volume conduction or remote contamination of local signals rather than true early onset. This limitation should be considered in future applications of PSWEs for seizure prediction and presurgical localization. In addition, the smaller MPF decrease observed in the LEC and mPFC relative to epidural electrodes (Figure S2E) may reflect lower baseline MPF in these structures, due either to ongoing subthreshold epileptiform activity or to physiological slow oscillations that reduce the dynamic range for further slowing during PSWEs. PSWEs increased during seizures, consistent with a transition to a hyperexcitable state (Figure 3, Figure S4). Several caveats should be acknowledged. In the animal recordings, seizure onset and offset were identified by visual inspection, which may have limited the precision of interictal, preictal, and ictal boundaries. Moreover, spectral leakage during ictal activity could influence estimation of the PSWE frequency band. Nevertheless, the pharmacological experiments provide convergent support for a mechanistic link between PSWEs and network excitability: PTZ increased PSWE occurrence while also provoking epileptiform activity and seizures, whereas pentobarbital reduced PSWEs together with behavioral activity. These data strongly support an association between PSWEs and seizure‐promoting network states. Mechanistically, several observations link PSWEs to excitatory drive from deep foci: (i) PSWEs increased during seizures and SE; (ii) PTZ (GABAA antagonist) increased PSWEs, whereas pentobarbital (positive GABAA modulator) decreased them; (iii) in rats, hippocampal/entorhinal/mPFC SW activity co‐occurred with epidural slowing and stronger negative correlations between deep and surface signals during PSWEs; and (iv) in the sEEG/scalp case, hippocampal fast activity preceded clinical onset, whereas scalp EEG showed synchronized slowing, with PSWEs increasing minutes before scalp ictal patterns emerged. Together, these findings suggest that at least a subset of surface PSWEs reflects the influence of deep epileptiform activity on distributed cortical networks (Figure 6). At the same time, an inhibitory contribution to PSWE generation cannot be excluded. 40 GABAA‐mediated transmission can promote seizure‐like events in the rat hippocampus via back‐propagation from the CA3/hilus to the dentate gyrus. 41 Hypersynchronous GABAergic‐mediated transmission was also described in the BBB breakdown model of epileptogenesis, in which low‐dose application of the GABAergic antagonist bicuculline led to short‐term inhibition of both spontaneous and evoked epileptic paroxysmal activity. 42 Thus, PSWEs may not

text: patterns emerged. Together, these findings suggest that at least a subset of surface PSWEs reflects the influence of deep epileptiform activity on distributed cortical networks (Figure 6). At the same time, an inhibitory contribution to PSWE generation cannot be excluded. 40 GABAA‐mediated transmission can promote seizure‐like events in the rat hippocampus via back‐propagation from the CA3/hilus to the dentate gyrus. 41 Hypersynchronous GABAergic‐mediated transmission was also described in the BBB breakdown model of epileptogenesis, in which low‐dose application of the GABAergic antagonist bicuculline led to short‐term inhibition of both spontaneous and evoked epileptic paroxysmal activity. 42 Thus, PSWEs may not simply reflect a linear shift toward excitation, but rather a network state in which excitation, inhibition, and synchronization interact. In this framework, GABAergic phase‐coupled networks, such as medial septum‐driven hippocampal theta rhythms, 43 or broader coordination systems such as the claustrum, 44 could contribute to PSWE generation and inter‐regional synchronization. In addition, surround inhibition via interneurons activation and GABAB‐mediated K+ conductance 28 , 29 , 30 , 45 , 46 may also generate slow waves of inhibition, as seen during SW discharges. 40 As such, the remote opening of GABAB channels might be synchronized with increased Ca2+‐dependent K+ conductance within the epileptic foci. 40 Such surround inhibition could explain the remote hypersynchronized slowing we observed. Hence, PSWEs may arise from hypersynchronized network interactions rather than from excitation alone. Far‐field effects also remain a plausible explanation for some PSWEs recorded simultaneously with remote epileptiform activity. In some cases, PSWEs and deep epileptiform discharges may represent the same underlying event recorded at different sites and distorted by the filtering properties of brain tissue. However, several observations argue against a purely passive far‐field explanation. In rats, epidural PSWEs showed inverted polarity relative to distant SWs (Figure 5B) and lacked the spike component. In addition, synchronized activity was absent in V1 R., despite its proximity to the entorhinal electrode (Figure S3B), although differences in electrode geometry may also contribute to this finding. These data suggest that at least some PSWEs are generated through active network processes rather than simple passive conduction. Still, dipole effects, far‐field conduction, and surround inhibition are not mutually exclusive, and all may contribute to PSWE detection at the cortical surface during deep epileptiform activity. Overall, PSWEs likely capture a heterogeneous spectrum of pathological slowing that includes—but is not limited to—intermittent rhythmic delta activity (IRDA, 2–4 Hz). 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 By design, our detector targets prolonged (≥5 s in humans; ≥10 s in rodents) 1–6 Hz events with notable theta content. This profile previously distinguished patients with epilepsy from controls with good diagnostic performance (AUC >0.8). Together with the observation that localization of PSWEs may predict BBB dysfunction 18 and focal structural abnormalities, 36 the present findings support PSWEs as a biomarker for atypical epileptiform activity generated within deep brain structures, specifically within the ictogenic zone. text: 49 , 50 By design, our detector targets prolonged (≥5 s in humans; ≥10 s in rodents) 1–6 Hz events with notable theta content. This profile previously distinguished patients with epilepsy from controls with good diagnostic performance (AUC >0.8). Together with the observation that localization of PSWEs may predict BBB dysfunction 18 and focal structural abnormalities, 36 the present findings support PSWEs as a biomarker for atypical epileptiform activity generated within deep brain structures, specifically within the ictogenic zone. Compared with previous studies, 18 , 37 control rats showed relatively high PSWE rates, possibly reflecting electrode‐related injury or known susceptibility of Sprague Dawley rats to SW activity. 51 Nevertheless, PSWEs increased during epileptogenesis and remained higher in epileptic animals than in controls, supporting their association with disease‐related network dysfunction. The human data mirrored the animal findings. In 18 TLE patients (137 seizures), time in PSWE, duration, and spread were greater pre‐ and post‐onset vs interictal, with MPF reduction post‐onset. In the simultaneous sEEG/scalp case, hippocampal epileptiform activity aligned with scalp slowing, and right temporal scalp PSWEs increased 20–60 s before clinical onset and before clear scalp ictal activity emerged. These findings suggest that PSWEs may provide clinically useful information even when conventional EEG appears relatively unrevealing. This study has several limitations. The simultaneous EEG/scalp analysis was limited to a single patient case, possible drug/state confounds, lack of coverage of extra‐temporal brain regions that may be important for propagation of epileptiform activity (e.g., the thalamus), 52 , 53 and uncertain generalizability to extratemporal epilepsies. Prospective, multi‐center studies with source‐localized PSWEs, thalamic recordings, and standardized pharmacological challenges are warranted, as is testing whether PSWEs can guide imaging in remote areas (specifically in low‐ and middle‐income countries), 36 inform presurgical planning or quantify pharmacodynamic response. Because PSWEs are also elevated in subgroup of patients with Alzheimer's disease, 18 they may also serve as markers of subclinical seizures in neurodegeneration. 54 In conclusion, PSWEs provide a scalable, quantitative, noninvasive marker of deep epileptiform activity and seizure propensity. Used alongside conventional IED detection, PSWE metrics may improve the identification of deep or scalp‐silent epileptic foci, and offer a practical readout for monitoring network excitability in both clinical and research settings.

text: Epilepsy is a major neurological condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures, affecting over 50 million people globally 1 (World Health Organization, 2024). Despite advances in pharmacotherapy and surgical interventions, about one‐third of patients continue to experience drug‐resistant epilepsy, 2 contributing to substantial disability, psychosocial burden, and premature mortality, particularly in low‐resource settings. 3 Seizure occurrence can be influenced by psychological and environmental stressors, 4 , 5 highlighting the complex interplay between these stressors and neural excitability. These challenges underscore the need for complementary and more accessible non‐pharmacological interventions, such as meditation, which has been studied widely for its psychological and neuromodulatory benefits. 6 , 7 However, its effects on seizure outcomes and underlying neural activity in patients with epilepsy remain poorly understood. Meditation encompasses diverse mental techniques aimed at cultivating attention, mindfulness, and awareness, and is typically grouped into two broad categories. Focused attention meditation (FAM) involves voluntarily directing attention to a single chosen object such as breath, whereas open monitoring meditation (OMM) involves maintaining a receptive, non‐judgemental awareness of the field of experience without focusing on any specific object. 8 Evidence suggests that meditation can modulate both subjective experience and neural activity, with consistent changes in large‐scale brain networks involved in attention and emotion regulation. 9 , 10 , 11 In healthy populations, electroencephalography (EEG) studies have revealed reliable spectral changes during meditation, including alterations in theta, alpha, and gamma power, associated with relaxation and attentional engagement. 12 , 13 , 14 These findings support meditation's neuromodulatory potential, yet it remains unclear whether such effects are observed in patients with epilepsy. Early studies investigating the relationship between epilepsy and meditation yielded mixed outcomes. Some suggested that meditation might reduce seizure frequency and improve quality of life, 15 , 16 , 17 whereas others cautioned that it could increase susceptibility to seizures, potentially due to neural hypersynchrony and paradoxical activation. 18 , 19 , 20 Most of these investigations, conducted over two decades ago and restricted to a specific technique (i.e., Transcendental Meditation), relied on scalp EEG recordings. The observed inconsistencies, therefore, may partly reflect methodological limitations of scalp EEG, including low spatial resolution and limited sensitivity to focal epileptiform discharges. In addition, self‐reported measures of seizure frequency have inherent limitations as they are subject to reporting bias, recall errors, and both under‐ and over‐reporting, 21 , 22 making conclusions difficult to interpret and undermining their reliability as an efficacy measure in anti‐epileptic treatments. Therefore, approaches that more accurately quantify seizures or related clinical phenomena can provide a more objective, temporally precise and robust marker of cortical excitability, overcoming many of these methodological limitations. Intracranial EEG (iEEG), routinely employed in the presurgical evaluation of drug‐resistant epilepsy, 23 enables direct recording of local field potentials with high spatial and temporal precision. 24 A few studies have investigated meditation using iEEG in patients with epilepsy, demonstrating changes in different aspects of the EEG signal during meditation. 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 Of note, iEEG also facilitates the detection of clinically

text: measure in anti‐epileptic treatments. Therefore, approaches that more accurately quantify seizures or related clinical phenomena can provide a more objective, temporally precise and robust marker of cortical excitability, overcoming many of these methodological limitations. Intracranial EEG (iEEG), routinely employed in the presurgical evaluation of drug‐resistant epilepsy, 23 enables direct recording of local field potentials with high spatial and temporal precision. 24 A few studies have investigated meditation using iEEG in patients with epilepsy, demonstrating changes in different aspects of the EEG signal during meditation. 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 Of note, iEEG also facilitates the detection of clinically relevant neurophysiological markers of epilepsy, such as interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), which are brief, pathological bursts of activity occurring between seizures, and generated by hyperexcitable neuronal populations. 29 , 30 To date, only one published case study 31 has examined the effects of meditation on IEDs and reported an increased rate of IEDs during meditation compared to a mind‐wandering control condition in a single patient with mesial temporal epilepsy. Whether such modulation of IEDs generalizes across individuals with different forms of epilepsy and whether it depends upon the type of meditation remains unknown. The present study addresses this gap by systematically examining whether meditation affects IEDs that are observed in iEEG recordings in patients with drug‐resistant epilepsy. Individuals with no prior meditation experience briefly engaged in two classical mindfulness practices, FAM and OMM, along with two control conditions, music and story listening. IEDs were quantified during each condition and statistically compared between the meditation and control conditions (Objective 1). Patients' self‐reported meditation depth experience was measured using a validated scale following each condition and its association with IED occurrence was evaluated (Objective 2). Given the mixed findings in the literature, we hypothesized that meditation would modulate IED occurrence relative to control conditions but did not predict a specific direction. Such modulations would reflect changes in clinically relevant neural activity, which may be associated with meditative depth. By integrating objective neural measures with measures of subjective experience, this exploratory work seeks to clarify the neurophysiological and clinical implications of meditation in epilepsy and inform the development of safe, accessible, and evidence‐based complementary interventions, while establishing a baseline framework for future prospective studies with larger, stratified cohorts.

text: Twenty‐seven patients (mean age = 35.70 years, range = 20–55 years, 15 female, 24 right‐handed) undergoing stereotactic EEG monitoring for drug‐resistant epilepsy in the seizure‐monitoring unit participated in the study. All participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the guidelines approved by the Research Ethics Board of the University of Calgary (REB‐20‐0598). Inclusion criteria required participants to have the ability to understand and follow instructions, perform the cognitive task, and have normal or corrected to normal vision. Although most patients (n = 15) had no diagnosed psychiatric and behavioral comorbidities, a significant subset (n = 10) had stress‐related conditions including anxiety, depression, hypertension, and migraines. Notably, no patients were experiencing active, symptomatic episodes such as a panic attack, depressive crisis, or an active migraine at the time of the experimental recordings. None of the patients exhibited cognitive deficits that impaired their ability to maintain a standard conversation while the consent form and task requirements were being explained to them, or to follow the instructions provided; nor did they report engaging in regular meditation practice of any kind prior to participation. Participant demographic details and clinical information are presented in Table 1.

text: As part of standard clinical care, each patient was implanted with 9 to 20 multi‐contact depth electrodes placed stereotactically to identify the seizure‐onset zone. Electrode implantation covering several cortical and sub‐cortical regions was determined solely by clinical needs. Each electrode (made of platinum plates with a diameter of 1–2 mm) consisted of 4–10 contacts of 2 mm length with a center‐to‐center gap of 5 mm (AdTech Medical instruments). Across all patients, a total of 353 electrodes comprising 2303 contacts were implanted, with 194 electrodes (1260 contacts) in the left hemisphere and 159 electrodes (1043 contacts) in the right (see Table S1 for detailed electrode information). For patients with bilateral implants, the number of contacts ranged from 10 to 83 (mean = 46.67 ± 26.21) and 24–80 (mean = 38.63 ± 28.24) in the left and right hemispheres, respectively. To determine contact locations, post‐implantation structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans were obtained from a 3 T scanner. For each patient, T1‐weighted scans were preprocessed in the Fieldtrip toolbox, aligned to the anterior and posterior commissures, and then saved in .nifti format. 32 Subsequent anatomic processing followed the iELVIS pipeline, 33 including segmentation, reconstruction of various brain structures (recon‐all), and co‐registration with the post‐implantation images using an online neuroimaging software suite (FreeSurfer, Charlestown, MA, USA; version 7.4.1) in MATLAB (Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA). Electrodes were displayed on each patient's reconstructed three‐dimensional (3D) cortical surface and then manually annotated with the Bioimage Suite software. 34 Raw electrode coordinates obtained through labeling were then imported into MATLAB for visualization onto the average 3D brain, with corrections for potential brain shift (Figure 1 shows implanted electrodes within mesial temporal structures where IEDs were observed in most participants). Finally, electrode locations for individual participants were verified by a neurosurgeon (author F.G.).

text: Participants completed a task where they engaged in two different meditation practices as separate conditions: FAM, and OMM. During FAM, participants were instructed to direct and maintain attention on their breathing. In OMM, they were asked not to anchor their attention on a specific mental object, but instead to remain aware of any thoughts, bodily sensations, or experiences arising in their awareness. Detailed and standard instructions were read aloud by the experimenter and simultaneously displayed on‐screen immediately before each meditation condition (see Supporting Information). The experimenter ensured that participants clearly understood all instructions and participants were offered opportunities to raise questions throughout the instruction period. There was no ongoing auditory guidance provided during the meditation conditions to allow participants to meditate without any external distraction. Two control conditions involving listening to a story (STL) and listening to a classical music piece (CML; Mozart's Piano K.467) were also included. In both conditions, participants were asked to relax, listen attentively, and refrain from thinking about anything in particular. The control conditions were chosen to match key aspects of each meditation condition: STL paralleled the sustained attention demands of FAM on an external object, whereas CML was intended to match the open and receptive awareness of OMM. This design allowed us to distinguish meditation‐specific effects from general attention or open awareness effects. Each condition lasted for 5, 8, or 10 min, considering participants' comfort and alertness. Each recording session, therefore, lasted for ~30–60 min. The four conditions were separated by brief periods of up to 3 min and presented in a pseudo‐randomized, alternating sequence. For the majority of the cohort (n = 24), meditation conditions (FAM/OMM) were interleaved with control conditions (STL/CML) to facilitate a functional cognitive reset and minimize order effects. In a small subset (n = 3), clinical constraints necessitated the consecutive presentation of meditation blocks. To maintain environmental consistency, recordings were performed in private monitoring rooms with restricted access, and an experimenter was present all the time for continuous monitoring of behavioral signs of exhaustion and drowsiness (i.e., head drooping or prolonged unresponsive eye closure). The clinical staff was provided with “notified that Research is in progress” beforehand to minimize interruptions, and non‐urgent clinical interventions were coordinated during inter‐condition intervals. Furthermore, the testing was scheduled during periods with no visitors and scheduled doctor rounds to ensure a quiet environment. Notably, recordings were conducted 3–4 days post‐implantation to ensure that patients reached a stable, reduced anti‐seizure medication regimen for clinical monitoring (see Table S1 for a detailed medication list). To avoid post‐ictal confounds, sessions were performed only on days when the patient had remained seizure‐free for at least 24 h. To avoid vigilance and sleep‐intrusion confounds, the recordings were strictly coordinated when patients were not sleep deprived the previous night and were performed only during waking hours. Furthermore, we collected self‐ratings on fatigue levels from all participants on a 5‐point scale (1: not tired at all, 5: completely exhausted) before the experiment began. To avoid post‐ictal confounds, sessions were performed only on days when the patient had remained seizure‐free for at least 24 h. To avoid vigilance and sleep‐intrusion confounds, the recordings were strictly coordinated when patients were not sleep deprived the previous night and were performed only during waking hours. Furthermore, we collected self‐ratings on fatigue levels from all participants on a 5‐point scale (1: not tired at all, 5: completely exhausted) before the experiment began. The average fatigue score was 2.8 ± 0.85 (mean ± standard deviation) indicating their cognitive alertness and wakefulness. To validate task adherence, participants retrospectively evaluated the quality of their experience during that condition by completing a short, post‐condition questionnaire adapted from the Meditation Depth Questionnaire (MEDEQ). 35 The MEDEQ was designed to assess the depth of meditation across five progressive levels: L1 (hindrances), including difficulties such as drowsiness and distraction while practicing meditation; L2 (relaxation), capturing subjective ease and calmness; L3 (concentration), including experiences such as effortless attentive control over the mind, internal focus, or mindfulness; L4 (transpersonal qualities), including interpersonal and positive affect experiences often observed in advanced practitioners; and L5 (nonduality), characterizing states of diminished subject–object distinction and self‐dissolution, typically demanding extensive training. The meaning of each question was explained beforehand to ensure that the participants understood the question. Participants rated their experience on a 5‐point scale (1 = Not at all; 2 = Rarely; 3 = Sometimes; 4 = Often; 5 = Completely) for each level. These self‐ratings data also served as a behavioral proxy for task engagement and were used to ensure that participants were able to differentiate between the distinct cognitive demands of each condition. To ensure precise synchronization of behavioral and neural data, a photodiode attached to the presentation laptop was used to time‐lock the beginning and ending of all events within each condition, including instructions, the experimental block (meditation, CML, or STL), and the questionnaire, to the ongoing iEEG recordings. Most participants finished all conditions on the same day, whereas three participants performed the task across two consecutive days (two conditions per day, one meditation and one control). Data from four patients were incomplete due to fatigue or loss of motivation (two patients), or technical issues with the photodiode signals in between some conditions (two patients).

text: Electrophysiological data were recorded with a clinical video‐EEG monitoring system (Natus, NeuroWorks, Middleton, WI) at a sampling rate of 2048 Hz (12 participants) or 1024 Hz (15 participants). The raw signals were then imported into MATLAB 2024a (Mathworks, Inc.) for preprocessing and analyses using custom scripts and the Fieldtrip toolbox. 36 Following visual inspection, electrode contacts exhibiting poor signal quality due to amplifier saturation, excessive environmental noise within the hospital room, or poor contact with brain tissue were excluded. Signals were down‐sampled to 1000 Hz, high‐pass filtered at 1 Hz, low‐pass filtered at 200 Hz using Butterworth filters, and notch filtered to remove line noise (59–61 Hz) and its harmonics (119–121 Hz, 179–181 Hz). Electrode contacts contaminated by movement artifacts or large transients were manually removed from further analysis. The continuous iEEG recordings were not divided into separate trials, but instead, four separate blocks corresponding to the experimental conditions, with onset defined at the beginning of each experimental block and offset just prior to the questionnaire period. Across participants the dataset comprised 27 FAM blocks (2 × 5 min; 17 × 8 min; 8 × 10 min), 25 OMM blocks (3 × 5 min; 15 × 8 min; 7 × 10 min), 27 CML blocks (2 × 5 min; 18 × 8 min; 7 × 10 min), and 25 STL blocks (2 × 5 min; 16 × 8 min; 7 × 10 min) for subsequent analysis. IEDs, including sharps, spikes, and spike–wave discharges, were annotated by a neurologist and certified EEG reader (author K.B.) in accordance with the criteria recommended by the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology (e.g., di‐ or tri‐phasic waveform, sharp peak and duration <70 ms, and the presence of logical physiological field spread across adjacent contacts). 30 To prevent over‐counting of networked activity, synchronous discharges occurring across multiple contacts or distant regions within a 50 ms window were treated as a single event. Consecutive spikes were distinguished as separate events only if a clear return to the background rhythm was observed. Complex waveforms, such as spike‐and‐slow‐wave complex or polyspikes or bursts were marked as a single event representing a discrete period of increased cortical excitability. All annotations relied on expert clinical judgment without additional assumptions. Considering the standard clinical practice in epilepsy research, we chose IEDs as the primary outcome measure, as participants were more likely to exhibit IEDs than seizures during the brief experimental blocks. The IEDs were identified through visual inspection of condition‐specific signal epochs using the ft_databrowser function in the FieldTrip toolbox (Figures S1 and S2). Reference and ground contacts were strictly excluded from quantitative analysis. text: IEDs were identified through visual inspection of condition‐specific signal epochs using the ft_databrowser function in the FieldTrip toolbox (Figures S1 and S2). To preserve the integrity of the spatial distribution of neural signal and minimize signal cancellation or subtraction artifacts, we utilized a monopolar montage referenced to a patient‐specific inactive lead (typically located far from the suspected seizure zone or in non‐cortical tissue). Reference and ground contacts were strictly excluded from quantitative analysis. All identified IEDs across all artifact‐free stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG) contacts, regardless of their anatomic location, were included to enable us to capture the effect of meditation on the whole brain. To examine the impact of meditation on neurophysiological markers of epilepsy, we quantified IED density, defined as the number of IED per minute for all conditions. This measure, instead of raw IED counts, was used as the dependent variable to account for variability in block duration across conditions and participants. We additionally implemented a control analysis to examine whether IED density was associated with the number of minutes of meditation completed. The Pearson correlation was non‐significant (r = .25, p = .09), suggesting that the duration of meditation condition did not systematically influence our measure of IED density.

text: Statistical procedures were performed using custom scripts in MATLAB (2024a) using the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox. Descriptive data are reported as mean ± SD unless otherwise specified. For group‐level analyses, linear mixed‐effects models (LMMs) were fit using the fitlme function with maximum likelihood estimation, including a random intercept for participants to account for repeated measurements. Model coefficients are reported as estimates (β), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), standard errors (SEs), t‐statistics, and p‐values (alpha = .05). Planned hypothesis‐driven comparisons were conducted, testing whether meditation conditions differed from the story listening (STL) control and the classical music listening (CML) control conditions. As these were planned a priori orthogonal contrasts embedded within the experimental design, no corrections were made for multiple comparisons. Pairwise contrasts between conditions were computed using model‐based linear combinations of fixed‐effect coefficients. For models that were used to test interactions between two fixed‐effects predictors, a likelihood ratio test was first performed using compare function to evaluate whether including an interaction term improved model fit. In the absence of a significant interaction, the final model included only main effects. The significance of fixed‐effects predictors was assessed using the F‐tests obtained from anova(lme). In LMMs, STL served as the reference for the condition predictor and L1 (hinderances) as the reference for the level predictor, unless stated otherwise. Individual‐level comparisons were conducted to evaluate the consistency and directionality of changes in IED density across participants and were quantified as symmetrized percentage change. This approach reduces the asymmetry inherent in traditional percent change scores, accounts for non‐linear scaling of increases vs decreases, and provides a more balanced measure of relative change across participants. 37

text: To test our main hypothesis of whether meditation modulates interictal epileptiform activity relative to control, we examined IED density across all conditions: STL, CML, FAM, and OMM. Data from one participant were excluded prior to this stage because no IEDs were observed in any condition, resulting in a final sample of n = 26. To evaluate the effects of meditation on IED density, we implemented an LMM in which condition predicted IED density. Although the omnibus main effect of condition on IED density was not significant (F(3, 91) = 1.95, p = .106), we proceeded with a priori planned contrasts, which revealed higher IED density during both meditation conditions relative to STL (Figure 2A): FAM vs STL (t(91) = 2.25, p = .027) and OMM vs STL (t(91) = 2.07, p = .041). Crucially, the 95% CIs for these effects ([.79, 12.90] and [.26, 12.51], respectively) did not cross zero, further supporting the directionality of the meditation‐induced modulation. In contrast, the CML condition did not differ significantly from STL (t(91) = 1.64, p = .104). Other planned comparisons between conditions showed no significant differences in IED density between the meditation conditions and CML, as well as between the two meditation conditions (see Table 2, Panel A for all parameter estimates). 38 , 39 Variance component estimates indicated high between‐subject variability in baseline IED density (random intercept SD = 21.46 IEDs/min), which likely reduced sensitivity to detect an overall effect. Estimated marginal means of IED density were highest for FAM (M = 22.19, 95% CI 6.76–37.63) and OMM (M = 21.73, 95% CI 6.22–37.24), followed by CML (M = 20.27, 95% CI 4.93–35.62), and lowest for STL (M = 15.35, 95% CI 5.96–24.73). At the individual‐level, condition‐specific symmetrized percentage changes relative to STL confirmed the directionality of meditation‐related effects based on numerical comparisons (Figure 2B). After excluding four participants with incomplete data (i.e., no data in the STL condition), subsequent analyses included 22 participants. Consistent with group‐level trends, most participants exhibited higher IED density during meditation compared to the STL condition (FAM > STL = 17/22; OMM > STL = 16/22), whereas IED density was comparable between the meditation conditions and CML (see Figure S3). To explore the potential differences between the two meditation conditions, we numerically compared IED density between FAM and OMM within individuals (Figure 3). This revealed a heterogeneous pattern: approximately half of the participants exhibited higher IED density during FAM (12/22), whereas the others showed higher density during OMM (10/22).
section: Meditation increased IED density relative to control

text: To evaluate how subjective experiences varied across different levels of meditation depth and conditions, we first fitted an LMM with self‐reported ratings for the MEDEQ as the outcome measure, with condition, level of meditation depth, and their interaction as fixed effects, and a random intercept for participants. The condition × level interaction did not improve model fit (χ 2 (12) = 15.14, p = .23), indicating that the effect of condition did not vary systematically across levels (see Table S2). The final model revealed a significant main effect of condition (F(3, 1252) = 3.84, p = .009). Specifically, self‐report ratings of perceived meditation depth increased significantly during meditation conditions relative to the STL control condition (Figure 4A): FAM vs STL (t(1252) = 2.09, p = .037) and OMM vs STL (t(1252) = 3.07, p = .002). In addition, CML showed higher self‐reported ratings than STL (t(1252) = 2.78, p = .006). No other pairwise differences between conditions were statistically significant. Furthermore, there was a significant main effect of level (F(4, 1252) = 45.83, p < .001), such that self‐report ratings for the MEDEQ systematically increased with meditation depth. The largest increases were observed at L2 (relaxation) and L3 (concentration) relative to L1 (p < .001), with smaller but significant increases at L4 and L5 (transpersonal qualities and non‐duality (p < .005), respectively). Model coefficients and pairwise differences are reported in Table 2, Panel B and estimated means with 95% CI for all conditions and levels are summarized in Table S3. Together, these results suggest that meditation heightened participants' perception of meditation depth compared to the STL control condition, and that this conditional effect was consistent across levels, with overall self‐reported ratings systematically changing by meditation depth.
section: Meditation increased subjective perception of meditation depth

text: To investigate the relationship between IED density and subjective experience of meditation depth, we first tested a full LMM with a three‐way interaction between IED density, condition and level as fixed effects, self‐reported ratings for the MEDEQ as the outcome measure, and participants as a random intercept. The three‐way interaction did not improve model fit over a model including all possible two‐way interactions (IED density × condition, IED density × level, condition × level) additively (χ2(12) = 6.72, p = .87). Next, all two‐way interactions were examined. The IED density × level interaction was significant (χ2(4) = 12.65, p = .013), indicating that the association between IED density and self‐reported ratings varied across levels of meditation depth. In contrast, the IED density × condition interaction (χ2(3) = 1.86, p = .601) and the condition × level interaction were not significant (χ2(15) = 15.33, p = .428), suggesting that condition did not moderate the relationship of subjective experience of meditation depth with IED density or with meditation depth level. (These results are reported in Tables S4 and S5). Follow‐up analyses on the significant IED density × level interaction revealed that IED density negatively predicted self‐reported ratings at L1 (β = −.011, 95% CI −.018 to −.004, SE = .004, t(407) = −2.96, p = .003), whereas this association was reversed at L2 (β = .014, 95% CI .005 to .023, SE = .004, t(407) = 3.18, p = .002) and L3 (β = .011, 95% CI .002 to .019, SE = .004, t(407) = 2.47, p = .014) and was non‐significant at higher levels (L4 and L5, p > .07). These results indicate that IED density is differentially associated with the subjective experience of meditation depth at different levels of meditation depth. These results are visualized in Figure 4B, and detailed model‐derived parameters are reported in Table S6. Overall, these findings suggest that IED density appears to be functionally relevant, such that it corresponds to subjective experience of meditation depth, with the association being more pronounced at lower levels and weakens at deeper levels of meditation.
section: The association between IED density and self‐reported experiences varied with levels of meditation depth

text: Using iEEG, the present study investigated whether meditation modulates IEDs in meditation‐naïve patients with drug‐resistant epilepsy. Both FAM and OMM practices showed modest increases in IED density (IEDs per minute) relative to a non‐meditative control condition (STL), with no such effects when comparing meditation practices to another control condition (CML). Individual‐level patterns also converged on higher IED density during meditation than the STL control, with notable inter‐individual variability in responses to distinct meditation types. Of note, participants reporting fewer hinderances and greater relaxation and concentration exhibited higher IED density, suggesting a functional link between iEEG‐measured clinically‐relevant neural dynamics and the subjective perception of meditation depth.

text: Our findings suggest that meditation can influence interictal epileptiform activity in meditation‐naïve individuals with epilepsy. The observed increase in IED density during meditation compared to a non‐meditative STL condition aligns with a previous case report that also reported elevated IED rates during meditation compared with a mind‐wandering control condition. 31 One possible explanation is that meditative states modulate neural excitability in regions overlapping with epileptogenic zones. Supporting this view, recent iEEG studies have demonstrated that meditation reorganizes local field activity across both epileptic and non‐epileptic areas, including the hippocampus and amygdala, 25 , 27 , 28 shifting oscillatory dynamics and enhancing transient synchrony. In our cohort, the majority of IEDs were detected in the mesial temporal structures. The similarity in the timing of spike activity observed between adjacent structures, such as the hippocampus and amygdala, likely represent the temporally synchronized activity of well‐connected epileptogenic network in these patients. Accordingly, the increased IED density observed here may reflect transient changes in neural synchrony associated with meditation engagement within circuits prone to epileptiform activity, highlighting a functional coupling between these types of internally directed cognitive states and epileptic network dynamics. Although the presence of IEDs in other regions, including frontal and parietal regions, suggests that meditation may impact a whole‐brain epileptic network, the lower IED density in these extra‐temporal areas precluded a secondary analysis of these subregions. The absence of differences in IED density between meditation and music listening likely reflects that music listening, characterized by attention to sounds, silences, and musical elements, could act as a form of contemplative focus, 38 , 39 particularly for novice meditators, producing similar effects. However, the discrepancy between our finding and well‐established reports of anti‐epileptogenic effects during music may be attributed to the state‐dependent nature of IED modulation. Unlike passive listening protocols, where music serves as a background stimulus, our participants were instructed to listen in a relaxed manner but attentively, fostering a state of active sensory monitoring. Such heightened attentional arousal can lead to transient increases in synchronization, manifesting as higher IED density. Notably, although both conditions showed a similar directional trend compared with the STL control, meditation significantly modulated the epileptic network, whereas the effect of music listening was quantitatively lower and failed to reach statistical significance. This suggests that compared to music, meditation provides a more effective and reliable way for probing and engaging deep functional epileptogenic networks. From a clinical perspective, an intervention with higher effect size offers a more robust framework for therapeutic interventions. An alternative explanation for our results is that the observed differences across conditions may partly reflect variations in cognitive load. Listening to a story or music likely imposes comparatively lesser demand, involving externally directed attention, whereas meditation (FAM, OMM) demands sustained internal attention and continuous monitoring of thoughts, making it potentially the more cognitively demanding condition, especially for novice practitioners. An alternative explanation for our results is that the observed differences across conditions may partly reflect variations in cognitive load. Listening to a story or music likely imposes comparatively lesser demand, involving externally directed attention, whereas meditation (FAM, OMM) demands sustained internal attention and continuous monitoring of thoughts, making it potentially the more cognitively demanding condition, especially for novice practitioners. At first glance, it seems possible that the observed conditional differences in IED density may be attributed to task difficulty. However, given that increased IED density during the meditation conditions was only observed in comparison to the STL condition and that cognitive load likely would not differ between the two control conditions, it is unlikely that IED density solely reflected cognitive load differences across conditions. Future work could systematically manipulate or measure cognitive load to clarify its role relative to meditative state in IED occurrences. Notably, differences in the pattern of IED density between FAM and OMM conditions may reflect their distinct attentional demands. 40 FAM requires deliberate redirection of attention to a chosen object, engaging top‐down attentional control via dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal regions, whereas OMM emphasizes non‐reactive awareness of ongoing experience supported by monitoring‐related activity within insular and anterior cingulate cortices. 10 , 41 The observed heterogeneity across meditation types may therefore reflect individual differences in how these attentional demands interact with the underlying epileptiform network. (See Supporting Information for more details regarding the clinical differences in patients showing more IEDs in FAM than OMM and vice versa).

text: We also found that the meditation conditions were associated with significantly higher self‐reported ratings of meditation depth compared with the STL control condition estimated across all five levels. The greater perceived depth during meditation is consistent with prior work 42 and confirms that engagement in structured mindfulness practices yields measurable experiential benefits compared to a control state such as listening to a story. Notably, self‐reported ratings enhanced at deeper levels of meditation, particularly for relaxation and concentration. This suggests that brief mindfulness practices can elicit systematic progression toward deeper meditative states, even in meditation‐naïve individuals. 42 Of note, the association between IED density and participants' subjective perception of meditation depth varied across five depth levels, as indicated by changes in the slope of this association. At the initial level, participants who reported fewer hinderances showed higher IED density. One possible interpretation is that transient increases in cortical excitability or neural synchrony, indexed by increased IED activity, may co‐occur with early internal engagement, thereby reducing the subjective experience of distraction or challenges. Conversely, reduced IED density during experiences of greater hinderance may reflect states of lower cortical excitability or less coordinated neural activity, making it harder to maintain focus and leading to more frequent distractions. This relationship, however, shifted at intermediate levels, where higher IED density was associated with higher self‐reported relaxation and concentration, indicating that heightened neural excitability may support arousal regulation and attentive control over the mind, facilitating the transition into deeper meditative states. At the deepest levels, the non‐significant association suggests that changes in neural excitability may have minimal influence on meditation‐naïve participants' deeper internal engagement. Although speculative, these findings suggest that iEEG‐measured IEDs may be behaviorally meaningful rather than purely pathological events, potentially reflecting transient reorganization of neural synchrony within epileptogenic networks 43 , 44 that coincide with moments of heightened engagement in meditative states.

text: The clinical implications of these findings depend upon the role IEDs play in the broader context of seizure dynamics and disease severity. The relationship between IEDs and seizure occurrence remains divided: some studies report no association between IEDs and seizure frequency, 45 whereas others have proposed that IEDs may inhibit ictal discharges by engaging adaptive inhibitory mechanisms within the epileptogenic networks. 46 Experimental evidence suggests that IEDs are often followed by a period of network inhibition or refractoriness, transiently reducing excitability and stabilizing local circuits. 46 Consequently, increases in IEDs, in certain contexts, could signal functional engagement of epileptogenic networks rather than necessarily indicating pathological consequences. Nevertheless, elevated IED occurrence has conventionally been viewed as a marker of increased cortical excitability and potential pathological risk, and recent evidence also shows that the presence of IEDs may lead to seizure recurrence. 47 However, it is important to note that no clinical seizures were observed during any meditation or control sessions in our study. In this context, meditation‐related increases in IED density observed in our study should be interpreted cautiously and should not discourage the use of meditation as a supportive practice for managing the comorbidities (i.e., anxiety and depression) of drug‐resistant epilepsy. Longitudinal clinical assessments tracking meditation‐related IED changes with seizure outcomes will be crucial for determining the therapeutic relevance of these findings. Furthermore, although the current study did not focus on a formal stratification by “epileptic terrain,” such as distinguishing between specific lesion types and seizure‐onset zone locations, and sought to investigate the overall impact of meditation on IEDs, these factors could influence spike dynamics and responses to interventions such as meditation. However, the observation of a consistent IED modulation across a heterogeneous cohort, including a majority of non‐lesional cases, suggests that meditation‐induced shifts in network excitability may be a generalized physiological response. Future research with larger, multi‐center cohorts is warranted to determine systematically if specific pathologies exhibit distinct sensitivities to the cognitive demands of meditation or if the magnitude of this effect is influenced by the underlying structural differences.

text: The findings of this study should be interpreted with consideration of some limitations. First, all participants were novice meditators with no prior training, which limits the generalizability of our findings to long‐term practitioners who typically exhibit more stable attentional control and distinct neural signatures of meditation. 42 , 48 Future studies including experienced meditators could help determine whether sustained meditation practice leads to more robust or qualitatively different effects on interictal activity. Furthermore, the brief, single‐session meditation design likely constrained the depth of experiential engagement achievable during the experiment. The absence of meditation‐related effects at deeper levels suggests that participants may not have reached advanced meditative states, potentially limiting the expression of stronger neural–behavioral coupling. Longitudinal designs with repeated or extended meditation sessions would better capture meditation‐related variations in IEDs. A significant limitation is the lack of formal, standardized neuropsychological assessing baseline attention and executive functions for patients in the present study. Although our within‐subject design partially controls for individual variance, it is difficult to determine how specific cognitive traits influenced the observed spike modulation. Future research building on this work should aim for better‐stratified patient cohorts based on age, sex, epilepsy localization, etiology, and comprehensive neuropsychiatric profiles. This would allow for a more robust investigation into the mechanisms and predictors of responsiveness to cognitive interventions. Furthermore, although the current study focuses on transient interictal events (IEDs), the absence of spectral composition analysis (e.g., theta/alpha power) prevents a granular verification of the objective brain states achieved during sessions. Future studies integrating EEG spectral measures with IED detection will be a logical and valuable extension of our findings to determine how specific frequency bands relate with the observed changes in network excitability. We also observed variability in IED density between the two meditation types at the individual level, indicating that different meditation styles may interact differentially with the epileptogenic network across individuals. Given the diversity of existing techniques, each emphasizing different attentional and affective processes, 40 these findings should be interpreted within the specific context of the two practices tested. Furthermore, although IEDs provided a practical proxy for neural excitability in epilepsy, seizure counts would remain the clinically preferred outcome measure. Regarding procedural concerns, carry‐over effects stemming from the sequence of conditions could potentially confound the modulation of IED density. We mitigated this by interleaving meditation blocks with control blocks, combined with brief inter‐block gaps, to facilitate a cognitive reset. Notably, participants who performed meditation blocks consecutively also exhibited IED density modulation similar to those who followed the alternating sequence. This suggests that observed changes in IED density are driven by the cognitive state rather than carry‐over effects from the preceding block. Similarly, changes in anti‐seizure medication levels could potentially modulate IED density and therefore influence our results; however, almost all participants completed all conditions on the same day with the condition order pseudo‐randomized, with up to 3 min gaps between them. text: participants who performed meditation blocks consecutively also exhibited IED density modulation similar to those who followed the alternating sequence. This suggests that observed changes in IED density are driven by the cognitive state rather than carry‐over effects from the preceding block. Similarly, changes in anti‐seizure medication levels could potentially modulate IED density and therefore influence our results; however, almost all participants completed all conditions on the same day with the condition order pseudo‐randomized, with up to 3 min gaps between them. Therefore, substantial variation in pharmacological effects is unlikely across conditions, suggesting that the observed changes in IED density cannot be attributed directly to medication effects. Finally, there are anatomic and statistical constraints to consider. Our study did not distinguish whether meditation primarily modulates the primary generators of the seizure‐onset zones or the secondary propagation pathways. Individual differences in network architecture likely influence the spatial and temporal distribution of the observed spike changes. Moreover, although our findings were robust across a diverse cohort, we cannot rule out the possibility that specific clinical syndromes (e.g., temporal vs frontal lobe epilepsy) could exhibit distinct sensitivities to meditation. Although we attempted to account for individual differences using mixed‐effects models, future studies with larger, balanced sub‐groups are recommended to determine if meditation‐induced changes are syndrome‐specific and localized to the onset zone or represent the propagation to other regions. Finally, the modest sample size, further reduced by the exclusion of five participants with incomplete or non‐detectable IED data, may have limited statistical power of the omnibus test and sensitivity to conservative post hoc corrections. Consequently, our iEEG findings are reported as planned comparisons highlighting the modulatory potential of meditation. Larger, multi‐center iEEG studies will be essential to validate these findings and establish their reproducibility across heterogeneous patient populations.

text: In conclusion, this study provides direct intracranial evidence that meditation can modulate interictal epileptiform activity in patients with drug‐resistant epilepsy. Both focused attention and OMM increased IED density relative to a control condition (STL). Inter‐individual variability in IED density in response to distinct meditation practices further indicate that epileptiform networks are differentially sensitive to internal cognitive states. Notably, higher IED density was associated with fewer perceived hinderances, but showed a positive association with greater relaxation and concentration, suggesting a functional link between neural excitability and the subjective ease of meditation. Future research should determine whether meditation‐related modulation of IEDs simply represents transient increases in neural excitability or more permanent adaptive neural mechanisms and assess whether meditation can be used as a clinical tool in the treatment of epilepsy.

text: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS) is the most common developmental and epileptic encephalopathy of infancy, with an estimated incidence of 30–40 per 100 000 live births. 1 It requires rapid diagnosis and treatment compared to other infantile epilepsy syndromes. Etiologies vary across geographic and economic settings. Structural etiologies, particularly perinatal brain injuries, predominate in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), and infectious causes contribute to IESS burden in endemic regions. Genetic etiologies are more frequently identified in high‐income countries (HICs), where testing is more accessible. 2 , 3 , 4 Access to diagnostic tools such as video‐electroencephalography (EEG), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and genetic testing varies dramatically across settings, with particularly limited availability in LMICs, where approximately 80% of people with epilepsy reside. 5 However, no standardized consensus exists regarding the extent of etiological evaluation in IESS, contributing to clinical practice variability. In 2015, the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) published a task force report on infantile seizures management, followed by a Child Neurology Society quality measure set in 2016. 6 , 7 Both emphasize the importance of initiating standard therapy within 1 week of diagnosis, identifying adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), high‐dose prednisolone, and vigabatrin as first‐line treatment options. Initiating standard therapy is important, as earlier intervention has been associated with a more favorable prognosis. 8 However, important gaps remain, including optimal treatment sequencing, duration, and monitoring strategies. Although evidence suggests that ACTH and high‐dose prednisolone may produce comparable response rates, there is no clear consensus on whether these therapies should be administered sequentially or in combination with vigabatrin. 9 In addition, recommendations regarding second‐line therapies, ketogenic diet, surgery, and adverse effect monitoring remain inconsistent, with no existing standardized guidance. Recent studies examining IESS management found that although 88% of centers recommended standard first‐line therapy, reflecting substantial consensus on core treatment, meaningful variation persisted in treatment sequencing, dosing protocols, and monitoring practices. 10 It is likely that even greater differences exist in clinical practice globally. This variability stems from limited evidence for IESS treatment, particularly in the setting of randomized control trials (RCTs). A 2022 network meta‐analysis identified only 22 RCTs comparing first‐line treatments; however, the majority of RCTs have been small, with only two trials enrolling more than 100 patients. 9 , 11 , 12 Treatment delay directly impacts neurodevelopmental outcomes. 13 Yet, in many LMICs, the treatment gap remains unacceptably long, with many preventable IESS causes, including hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy, neonatal hypoglycemia, and infectious etiologies. 2 , 14 , 15 This prolonged treatment gap worsens outcomes and confounds assessment of treatment efficacy across settings. Understanding the global management of IESS is critical, given its profound neurological consequences. Despite current multiple national and regional guidelines, no comprehensive synthesis comparing international recommendations exists. In this scoping review, we synthesize the current evidence and summarize international IESS guidelines to provide a comprehensive overview of global practices, identify areas of consensus and variation, and highlight disparities in care.

text: The search strategy was developed by a pediatric neurologist (G.E.) and a medical librarian (Y.F.). The search was conducted in November 2024 across PubMed (1809–present), Embase (Embase.com, 1974–present), and Cochrane CENTRAL Register of Controlled Trials (Wiley). See Data S1 for search terms. Results were imported into Covidence, duplicates were removed, and results were screened independently by two authors (G.E. and C.K.R.). Full texts were assessed using predefined criteria, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Eligible studies included national or international guidelines providing diagnostic or treatment recommendations. Nonrelevant or duplicate studies were excluded. Search results from each database were imported into systematic review software (Covidence [www.covidence.org]), and duplicates were removed. Two authors (G.E. and C.K.R.) independently screened the remaining citations by title and abstract. Full‐text articles were subsequently reviewed for relevance, eligibility, and quality by the same two authors using preestablished criteria. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. To address underrepresentation of non‐Western regions, unpublished guidelines were obtained through personal and professional pediatric neurology organizations, including ILAE and International Child Neurology Association, and translated when needed by local neurologists or by coauthor A.F.P. The number of individuals contacted and the response rate were not formally tracked. Extracted variables included guideline characteristics, diagnostic evaluation, treatment strategies, dosing, response assessment, and monitoring. Variables were informed by prior Pediatric Epilepsy Research Consortium methodology. 10 See Data S1 for additional details on data extraction.

text: Descriptive statistics summarized recommendations by region and used the World Bank income classification for guideline classification as either LMIC or HIC. Comparisons between LMIC and HIC guidelines were performed for selected binary outcomes. Given small sample sizes, Fisher exact test (two‐sided) was used for exploratory comparisons, with effect sizes reported descriptively as proportions. All statistical comparisons were considered exploratory, given the descriptive intent of this review, and no adjustment was made for multiple comparisons. A sensitivity analysis was performed restricting the LMIC versus HIC comparison to national and international guidelines only, excluding institutional protocols, to assess whether conclusions were robust to differences in document type and development rigor.
